issues.body:
### Description

Match query works with semantic_text fields in the query DSL and it applies prefiltering to other bool queries used with it (https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/132068).

When using `MATCH` on semantic_text fields on ES|QL, it is possible that other filters are not pushable to Lucene. This means that they won't be included in the bool query that will be issued to Lucene, and thus won't be applied as pre-filters.

The way around this for the `KNN` function was to change the KNN query into an exact query, and apply the non-pushable filters as post-filters (see https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/132944). Having KNN as an exact search function means we will find as much results as needed and the non-pushable filters will be applied, but as much results as possible will be retrieved back.

We can apply the same mechanism to `MATCH` when using a semantic_text field to ensure filtering is consistent when filters can't be pushed down.
issues.title: ES|QL - MATCH function with semantic_text fields with non pushable filters

issues.body:
I think there are interesting queries where we're interested both in per-group stats and global stats, like so:
```
...
| INLINE STATS total_median = MEDIAN(field)
| STATS per_group_median = MEDIAN(field), total_median = VALUES(total_median) BY group
```
or so:
```
...
| STATS per_group_min = MIN(field) BY group
| INLINE STATS total_min = min(per_group_min)
```
or:
```
...
| STATS ... BY b = BUCKET(field, 1 year), group
| INLINE STATS min_b = MIN(b)
```

Normally, `INLINE STATS` needs to run the first part of the query twice. That's wasteful. We're already aggregating. It'd be much nicer if we could compute the `INLINE STATS` alongside the `STATS`.

That's currently not possible because the `INLINE STATS` do not have a `BY` in these examples - so we'd need a way to compute an agg function over all values alongside agg functions that are per grouping.
issues.title: ESQL: merge STATS | INLINE STATS

issues.body:
Multivalue support appears inconsistent in our conversion functions.

We should
- decide the multi-value semantics we want for conversions
- correct differences between the desired semantics and current behavior
- add tests for those semantics
- address gaps in the documentation for these functions

issues.body: ## The ask We would like a way to signal to Elasticsearch not to return partial results before an async search is completed, so that we can efficiently use the `GET /_async_search/{id}` endpoint for long-polling. ## The why After creating an async search, Kibana currently uses the async status endpoint `/_async_search/status/{id}` for polling. The reason is that if we use `GET /_async_search/{id}`, we will always receive partial results if they are available. Partial results are not used in the UI prior to search completion and they introduce overhead during polling. However, using the status endpoint has two main drawbacks - it doesn't support long-polling (`wait_for_completion_timeout`) - it requires us to make two requests to detect a finished search and then load results This limitation, together with our [polling backoff strategy](https://github.com/elastic/kibana/blob/d99c16354e142b0fbb4b034e138ef639f2e502f9/src/platform/plugins/shared/data/common/search/poll_search.ts#L39-L46), creates a delay (up to the length of the polling interval) between when an async search is completed, and when the results are delivered to the client. In practical terms, this means that every panel on a dashboard is being unnecessarily slowed down. This enhancement will allow results to be delivered to the client _as soon as they are ready_. ## Visuals **Today** **The proposal**
issues.title: Allow delaying partial results in `GET /_async_search/{id}`

issues.body:
Both `_search` (when using batched execution) and ES|QL use batch-style shard execution, but we still don’t have a way to avoid querying cold shards when a timestamp-sorted request is already satisfied by hot data. Today we largely execute shard queries broadly/concurrently, so older backing indices run even when they cannot affect the top-N results.

We want “latest events” queries (`SORT @timestamp DESC`) on data streams to naturally prioritize hot data and stop early, without requiring users to add a restrictive time range.

Add a range-aware execution strategy for data streams when the request is sorted by `@timestamp desc`, and when:
* there are no aggregations, and
* we don’t need accurate total hits (or can avoid computing it).

Changes needed in **both** paths:

1. **Serial / ordered batch execution across shard ranges (search layer)**

* Partition shards/backing indices into ordered ranges using shard-level min/max `@timestamp`.
* Execute ranges hottest → coldest.
* Stop dispatching further ranges once top-N is satisfied and colder ranges cannot compete.

2. **Make batch execution on a single node min/max-aware (intra-node skipping)**
   Even within “hot ranges”, avoid executing shard requests that cannot compete:

* Track the current worst (oldest) `@timestamp` among the top-N results collected so far.
* For any pending shard in the current batch, if `shard.max_timestamp < current_worst_topN_timestamp`, skip executing it (it cannot produce a document that would enter the top-N for `@timestamp desc`).

This is complementary to existing segment-level skipping: it pushes the decision up to shard/batch scheduling so we don’t pay query+fetch costs for shards that are provably non-competitive.

**Examples**

*Query DSL (`_search`):*

```json
GET index/_search
{
  "query": {
    "bool": {
      "filter": [
        { "term": { "user.value": "user_a" } }
      ]
    }
  },
  "sort": [
    { "@timestamp": "desc" }
  ],
  "size": 10
}
```

*ES|QL:*

```esql
FROM index
| WHERE user.value == "user_a"
| SORT @timestamp DESC
| LIMIT 10
```

We could also change the default sort for datastreams (or just logsdb indices) to be on timestamp desc, making any query where the sort is omitted a fast query.
issues.title: Range-aware serial batch execution for `@timestamp desc` searches on data streams

issues.body:
### Related

#139664 (MV_UNION implementation)
#139435 (MV_CONTAINS null handling discussion)

### Description
Following the MV_UNION implementation, refactor MV_UNION and MV_INTERSECTION to reduce code duplication by extracting shared logic into a common base class or helper.
### Context
As noted by @ioanatia and @markjhoy in the [MV_UNION PR review](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/139664), there's significant overlap between MV_UNION and MV_INTERSECTION implementations. The value extraction, index handling, and result building logic is largely identical, only the set combination operation differs.
### Proposed Approach
Create a shared helper method (e.g., processFieldSets) that handles:

- Getting value counts and indices from both input fields
- Building LinkedHashSet collections from field values
- Applying the combination function (union/intersection/difference)
- Building the result block

The combination logic would be passed as a BiFunction<Set<T>, Set<T>, Set<T>> parameter.

Makes adding future set operations easier (MV_DIFFERENCE, MV_COMPLEMENT, etc.)
### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ]  Common base class or helper extracted
- [ ]  MV_UNION refactored to use shared logic
- [ ]  MV_INTERSECTION refactored to use shared logic
- [ ]  All existing tests pass
- [ ]  No behavioral changes
issues.title: Refactor MV_UNION and MV_INTERSECTION to share common base class

### Description

When running ILM on clusters at scale, you can end up running the same ILM policy against [tens of] thousands of indices in the same cluster.

issues.body:
### Description

Due to a bug in Elasticsearch, it was possible for a data stream to have a mismatch between the UUID of the index that exists and the UUID of the index in the data stream. This was exacerbated by the modify data stream API not allowing the removal of the offending index because it was marked as the write index of the stream.

In these cases, it may be necessary or helpful to have an escape hatch for how we can _either_ remove the offending index from the data stream, or delete it. If we force-deleted the index, we could potentially designate a different index as the write index for the data stream.

Possibly we could enhance the [modify data stream](https://www.elastic.co/docs/api/doc/elasticsearch-serverless/operation/operation-indices-modify-data-stream) API to allow this, with appropriate flags opting in to skipping some checks.

A couple of potential ideas: We have discussed in the past making the write index an actual attribute on the data stream, which would allow us to add APIs to modify it. We've also discussed having backing indices lazily created for data streams, which means that we could allow removing all backing indices for a data stream (even the write index) and having it be created as necessary.
issues.title: Add escape hatch for modifying data stream backing indices

- allocation explain yields `"can_allocate" : "yes"` for this shard(s)
- `"explanation": "the node is above the low watermark cluster setting [cluster.routing.allocation.disk.watermark.low.max_headroom=200gb], having less than the minimum required [200gb] free space, actual free: [166gb], actual used: [99.1%]"` for the desired node is shown as reason using this command : 

```
# this will filter allocation explain API for the node that desired balance designated the unassigned shard to be located onto
jq --slurpfile desired internal_desired_balance.json '
    .index as $index
    | .shard as $shard
    | ($desired[].routing_table[$index][$shard|tostring].current[]|select(.state != "UNASSIGNED")|.node) as $currentNode
    | $desired[].routing_table[$index][$shard|tostring].desired.node_ids[] as $desiredNodes
    | .node_allocation_decisions[]
    | select(.node_id == $desiredNodes)
    | select(.node_id != $currentNode)
    ' allocation_explain.json
```
- This can leave cluster health yellow for potentially hours or days

In the example there are 90 nodes in the zone that could accept the unassigned replica shards that are below low watermark and 2 nodes above low watermark cause multiple indices to remain yellow (https://support.elastic.co/knowledge/b713270a)

There is a high level of unbalance and rebalance recovery working at full capacity based on `cluster.routing.allocation.cluster_concurrent_rebalance`- increasing this may mitigate but this issue but the issue is raised to track whether elasticearch should make sure desired balance does not cause replica shard to be directed to node above low watermark

issues.body:
### Description

There are various places were we are inconsistent or frankly, silly, in our IO patterns for vector search.

- [ ] All our *flat formats should load vectors with `normal` MMAP. It is debatable on if we want to prefetch here. But, making these `normal` makes the most sense. You will generally be searching blocks of these at a time, and read aheads will help significantly.
- [ ] Non-quantized vectors should load via `random` MMAP, and access to them should take advantage of prefetching. Generally, access of the non-quantized vectors only occurs during merging and rescoring. Specifically, in rescoring, we should consider prefetching heavily, and possibly prefetching across segments before attempts at scoring (to account for scenarios when a segment only has one vector we care about, then per-segment prefetching is basically useless). 
- [ ] Quantized vectors & indexing structures should always be `normal` MMAP. Basically, we always want to load as much as possible as we know those vectors will be used and the index structure will always be used. Random here likely only hurts us in the end.
- [ ] Quantized and index files should be easily set to pre-load in the directory. I am not 100% sure if we want to do this by default or not (e.g. if we see a `.veq` that is used in an HNSW field, load it). But, at a minimum, we need to make this experience better (like, who the crap actually knows that they should load `vex` and `veq` and sometimes `veb`...we need to do this better).
- [ ] For DiskBBQ, we need to consider more aggressive pre-fetching of postings lists, right now we only prefetch a single postings list at a time. Our scoring is at times so fast, especially for short lists, we still spend time waiting on IO. Let's fix that.


I hope it goes without saying, we should benchmark to validate each of my assertions.
issues.title: Improve our IO patterns for Vector Search

# Context
In ESQL we have the `ImplicitCasting` Analyzer rule, that takes string literals and fields and casts them to some types, like dates, so you can do `FN("2020-10-10")` instead of `FN("2020-10-10"::date)`.

The TRange function, however, manually handles the string conversion. Leading to some minor code duplication, and the keyword type accepted as a parameter in documetnation, which deviates from the rest of ESQL.

# What
To avoid having special cases like this, it would be convenient to remove that parameter type, and let the planner take care of the automatic conversion.

# <ins>**Breaking change**</ins>

The (only?) side effect of this is that it will accept not just string literals and fields, but also results of other functions, like: `TRANGE("2020-10-10", CONCAT("2020-10", "-10"))`. This isn't currently allowed as an implicit conversion, and existing queries with it would fail, turning this into a breaking change.

This change was attempted in this PR, but reverted after finding that it is a breaking change:
https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/139911/changes/471b21cc01a1cbb5f7cf6cd50bc83c317b08ca8a..90a08920fa4701fe7642485cccc533587a9b2f8d#diff-2e779eeed533ffd0ffa9931179dad92045d2ba9deaed1c99893bd497954a44f5
issues.title: ESQL: TRange manually handling string-to-date param conversion

issues.body:
### Description

## Summary

Elasticsearch needs a simple way to configure JVM log paths (GC logs, error dumps) via environment variable, without the complexity of parsing configuration files. This would enable separation of read-only installation directories from read/write runtime directories.

## Background

Related issues:
- #39091 - Declined due to complexity of coordinating multiple log path configurations (path.logs, log4j2.properties, JVM options)
- #39090 - Declined due to concerns about general environment variable substitution causing unexpected issues

The Windows service already uses `SERVICE_LOG_DIR` for `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Apache Software Foundation\Procrun 2.0\Instance\Parameters\Log\Path`, but this variable is not available in `jvm.options`.

I don't know how `SERVICE_LOG_DIR` is stored or utilized in linux machines, so I accept that it adds further complexity and consideration.

## Current Problem

**jvm.options currently uses hardcoded relative paths:**
```
-XX:ErrorFile=logs/hs_err_pid%p.log
-Xlog:gc*,gc+age=trace,safepoint:file=logs/gc.log:utctime,level,pid,tags:filecount=32,filesize=64m
```

These resolve relative to the working directory, not to any configured log location. Users cannot externalize JVM logs without editing jvm.options at installation time.

## Proposal

Make `SERVICE_LOG_DIR` available for substitution in `jvm.options`:

```
-XX:ErrorFile=${SERVICE_LOG_DIR}/hs_err_pid%p.log
-Xlog:gc*,gc+age=trace,safepoint:file=${SERVICE_LOG_DIR}/gc.log:utctime,level,pid,tags:filecount=32,filesize=64m
```

**Implementation:** Startup scripts perform simple string replacement of `${SERVICE_LOG_DIR}` before passing options to JVM. Default to `logs` if unset, but having installed without `SERVICE_LOG_DIR`, I believe it already defaults to `<Installation Directory>\logs`.

### This Does NOT Require:
- Parsing elasticsearch.yml
- Parsing log4j2.properties
- Coordinating multiple log configurations
- General environment variable substitution (avoiding edge cases like `:` or `_` in keys, which, per example, causes IConfiguration to break in dotnet)
- Changes to Elasticsearch application logging

### This ONLY Provides:
- **One specific variable** (`SERVICE_LOG_DIR`) for **one specific purpose** (JVM-level logs)
- String substitution in startup scripts (same pattern as `ES_TMPDIR` on line 56)
- Consistency with existing Windows service configuration
- The opportunity to configure jvm.options with a subdirectory (`/jvm/`) to organize JVM logs separately from application logs

### This COULD Provide:
- A way to use the variable within the elasticsearch.yml, if you want.
- A way to use the variable in log4j2.properties, if you want.

## Use Cases

**1. Security Hardening**
```
C:\Program Files\Elasticsearch\        (read-only, executables only)
C:\ProgramData\Elasticsearch\data\     (read/write, data)
C:\ProgramData\Elasticsearch\logs\jvm\ (read/write, JVM logs)
```
Following principle of least privilege by preventing write access to installation directory.

**2. Unified Log Location**
All logs (application + JVM) in one place for backup, monitoring, or export:
```
/var/log/elasticsearch/           (application logs via path.logs)
/var/log/elasticsearch/jvm/       (JVM logs via SERVICE_LOG_DIR)
```
Single directory to mount/export/monitor. No need to search multiple locations.

**3. Windows Service Alignment**
Currently `SERVICE_LOG_DIR` controls procrun logs but not GC/error logs, creating inconsistent locations. This would unify them.

## Why This Avoids Previous Objections

- **Not an edge case:** Read-only installation directories are a standard security practice
- **No configuration complexity:** Only affects JVM logs, not the multiple application log configurations
- **Minimal scope:** One variable, not general substitution that could cause parsing issues
- **Follows existing pattern:** `ES_TMPDIR` already works this way (line 56 of jvm.options)

## Backward Compatibility

Default to `logs` if `SERVICE_LOG_DIR` not set, maintaining current behavior.
issues.title: Support SERVICE_LOG_DIR environment variable in jvm.options for JVM log paths

issues.body:
### Description

I maintain numerous ES clusters that have tens of thousands of indices that generally have literally identical mappings (via data streams using a consistent template), except in the rare instance where we add a mapping (then it will become identical again for the next rolled over batch). The only practical difference between each index is the number of shards, which we control by monitoring ingest and adjusting for the next rollover, per data stream. In other words, the mappings stay the same, but the settings may change.

I recently came across https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/83846 and I think it is a step in the right direction, but I think that this is superficial because it is giving a custom response for what is a whollistically bigger problem.

Can (Does?) Elasticsearch do this directly in the cluster state where Elasticsearch literally merges identically mapped index mappings? In my cluster, that would mean that it would just be all of the internal system indexes and then literally _one_ index mapping, for tens of thousands of indexes.

Relates https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/77466
issues.title: [Cluster State] Combine Index Mappings when identical

This is a tough one.

issues.body:
We should be able to optimize stats of the form SUM(X + a) where a is a constant to SUM(X) + a*COUNT(X). This should result in fewer addition operations, and reuse of SUM(X) if it is used elsewhere in the query.

There is a problem with doing this optimization due to multivaluedness. Specifically, if a document has multiple values for X then X+a is null, and does not contribute to the result.

For example if there are two documents one with X value 3 and one with values [5, 10], then the query `STATS SUM(X), SUM(X + 4)` evaluates to 18, 7 because both single and multi values are in the first sum, but only single values are in the second sum.

This breaks the equality: `SUM(X + a) == SUM(X) + a * COUNT(X)`. Is there still a way to do this optimization in some form?
issues.title: Query planner rewrite SUM(X+a) as SUM(X) + a*COUNT(X)

issues.body:
The MMR algorithm follows a simple but effective process:

1. Start by selecting the most relevant item
2. For each remaining item, calculate an MMR score that combines:
   - Its relevance to the query
   - Its dissimilarity to already selected items
3. Select the item with the highest MMR score
4. Repeat until you have enough results


The MMR score formula at step 2 is:

```
MMR(Di) = lambda * similarity(Q,Di)) - (1-lambda)(max(similarity(Di, Dj))
```

where:
- Di is the current doc we compute the MMR score
- Dj represent the docs from the diversified result set
- Q is the query vector (which can be optional)

Let's assume we have N docs that we need to diversify.
In our current implementation of MMR, we maintain two sets of caches:
- a cache that holds the similarity scores between the query Q and all documents (N size)
- a cache that holds the similarity scores between pairs of documents Di,Dj (N*N size)

At step, for each document that we have not selected we recompute the MMR score, using these two caches.

We can reduce the number of computations, the cache size and the number of cache lookups by maintaining:
- a cache that holds the similarity scores between the query Q and all documents (N size)
- a cache that holds max similarity between the current doc and the diversified set of docs (N size)

We no longer need a cache for all pairs of `similarity(Di, Dj)`.

Assume we have selected document `Dx` at step 2 and we are now looking at adding a new document to the diversified set.
The new MMR score becomes:

```
// update the cache for maxSimilarityToSelected 
maxSimilarityToSelected(Di) = max(similarity(Di, Dx), maxSimilarityToSelected(Di))

MMR(Di) = lambda * similarity(Q,Di)) - (1-lambda) * maxSimilarityToSelected(Di)
```

With this method we no longer have to iterate through all the already selected documents, when we compute a new MMR score.
We only need to take into account the last document we added to the list of diversified results.
issues.title: MMR: Reduce cache size by reusing previous MMR scores

### Description

Issue is related to implementation of `@ParametersFactory`. Runner creates multiple instances (one per parameter set), and for each instance it runs all test methods it discovers, including inherited ones. `InferenceServiceTestCase` base class has 2 test methods:

- `testRerankersImplementRerankInterface`
- `testRerankersHaveWindowSize`

- Performance concerns on adding unlimited synonyms
- 10k is the default `index.max_result_window` that is used for the internal synonyms index to perform synonyms retrieval

We want to raise the synonyms limit to allow customers with larger synonyms sets to use the synonyms API. There are a few elements to this:

- Set the limit based on the number of terms in the synonyms map, instead of the number synonym rules in the synonym set.
- Determine a default limit that is a good balance of "large enough" and "performant enough". Somewhere between 200k-500k terms is probably feasible. Performance is measured across a couple dimensions:
   - The amount of memory used by the synonym map, including during construction
   - How long it takes to build the synonym map. It should be less than 30 seconds so that the reload analyzers API call does not time out.
- Add a cluster setting to make the synonym limit configurable in ECH and self-hosted.

issues.body:
### Description

In the current implementation of `SliceBuilder.toFilter(...)`, slicing logic is applied at the shard level. That is: **every shard receives the search request**, and only inside the shard does the logic determine whether the slice ID matches that shard or not. If it doesn't, the shard returns `MatchNoDocsQuery` (i.e., "not part of slice").

This means the coordinating node does not prune irrelevant shards ahead of time when executing a sliced search. Even when slice count matches shard count (or is a clean multiple/divisor), *all* shards are contacted for *every* slice.

This behavior contrasts with what might be an intuitive expectation: that slicing would reduce cross-shard traffic up front — e.g., sending slice 0 only to shard 0, slice 1 only to shard 1, etc., when `maxSlices == numShards`.

For context: I'm in the process of getting large amounts of documents out of ES that match a certain query. I am using the combination of search, PIT, search_after and slicing to do so. I obviously don't care about cross-shard/slice ordering for this scenario (I understand that this would be impossible); search order within the shard/slice is important though to make search_after work correctly.

I would be of the (as per this issue: naive) assumption that if I pick my number of slices equals to the number of shards [or some whole number fraction thereof], the work for each slice gets directed to a single [or exact multiple] number of shards *only*.

However, even just observing the runtimes of the individual slices' queries makes me think this is not so: they start low but then quickly run up, and never come down. 


for clarity: this isn't about scan/scroll. (I'm just mentioning that because most of the slice-related docs are about that interface)
issues.title: Slicing with search/PIT/search_after does not prevent irrelevant shards from being queried
Add new "lookup" for `query_vector_builder`

issues.body:
### Description

Currently, the ESQL Lookup Join is driven by the left table joining the right table. That is, the data matched from the left table, together with push-down filter conditions, is sent to the shards of the right table. For each row, a Lucene query is constructed and executed on the right table, and the results are then returned to the left table to complete the join.

When the number of rows matched from the left table is large, the performance overhead is very high. One reason is the cost of network I/O, since the left table data needs to be transmitted over the network to the right table nodes. Another reason is that each row requires a separate query execution on the right table.

If, in a given business scenario, the data volume matched on the right table after filter push-down is only one or two thousand rows and the right table has very few fields, would it be possible to first push down the filter conditions and execute them on the right table nodes, then construct a hash table from the result set, and broadcast it to the shards of the left table to complete the join? If the right table replicas can be distributed such that there is one replica per node, the broadcast step could even be avoided, resulting in better performance.

Is there a plan to support this kind of scenario?
issues.title: [ESQL] Optimization of ESQL lookup join when the result set is small after filter push-down on the right table

issues.body:
Meta issue to collect suggestions on how to improve our functions, which currently sometimes exhibit inconsistent and surprising behavior.

The goal is to make the behavior of our functions predictable, by grouping them clearly in our docs, naming them well, maybe provide SETtings to control behavior, maybe provide some other tools to users to prevent headaches.

Related issues:
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/139772
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/139435
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/121286

# Some interesting behavior

## Type conversions are applied to each value inside a multivalue:

```
row x = ["1.0", "2.2"] | eval x = x::double

       x       
---------------
[1.0, 2.2] 
```

## String functions sometimes are applied to each individual value, sometimes they just return null

```
row x = ["FOO", "BAR"] | eval x = to_lower(x)

       x       
---------------
[foo, bar] 
```

```
row x = [" foo ", " bar "] | eval x = trim(x)

       x       
---------------
null
```

## operators and numeric functions normally return null

```
row x = [1.0, 2.2] | eval x = x*x
row x = [1.0, 2.2] | eval x = sqrt(x)

       x       
---------------
null 

```

## The IN-operator always returns null

That's consistent, but not always useful.

```
row x = [1.0, 2.2]
| eval x = [1.0, 2.2] IN (x)

row x = [1.0, 2.2]
| eval x = 1.0 IN (x)

       x       
---------------
null
```

## Some pass-through functions return multi-values as they are

```
row x = [1.0, 2.2], y = [3.0, 4.4]
| eval x = coalesce(x, y) | keep x

       x       
---------------
[1.0, 2.2]
```

```
row x = [1.0, 2.2], y = [3.0, 4.4]
| eval x = case(true, x, y) | keep x
       x       
---------------
[1.0, 2.2]
```

## Multi-value functions sometimes treat null as empty set, sometimes not

```
row x = [1.0, 2.2, 4.4], y = null
| eval x = mv_contains(x, y) | keep x

       x       
---------------
true
```

```
row x = [1.0, 2.2]
| eval x = mv_append(x, null)

       x       
---------------
null
```
issues.title: ESQL: consistent and predictable behavior for functions when applied to multivalues and nulls

issues.body:
**Update**: the current discrepancies were fixed in PR #141651, but we keep this issue open as we really need to refactor this and generate those files from annotations on the production code and not a mix with hand-crafted declarations in tests.

While working on ESQL query builders in client libraries, @miguelgrinberg found a discrepancy between the [parameters doc for `absent_over_time`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/a618e8c37824dfac10dcd09fa828a5bcb943ed92/docs/reference/query-languages/esql/_snippets/functions/parameters/absent_over_time.md) that has the `field` and `window` parameters, while the [corresponding kibana definition](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/a618e8c37824dfac10dcd09fa828a5bcb943ed92/docs/reference/query-languages/esql/kibana/definition/functions/absent_over_time.json) only has `field`.

Digging in the code, I found out that the parameter list for function definition is [extracted from the parameterized test cases](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/6cf06c9c673fb43ee96a2b0cb44684958b2586eb/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/test/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/expression/function/DocsV3Support.java#L582) produced by the function's test case. And it turns out that `AbsentOverTimeTestCase` [does not produce values](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/d2f591780a1db207022156b96385521a8362b1ba/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/test/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/expression/function/aggregate/AbsentOverTimeTests.java#L35) for the optional `window` parameter, causing it to be omitted from the Kibana definition file.

Documentation on the other hand is [generated from the `FunctionDescription`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/6cf06c9c673fb43ee96a2b0cb44684958b2586eb/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/test/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/expression/function/DocsV3Support.java#L645) found in the `FunctionRegistry`, and built using reflection from the function's implementation class, where `window` will obviously be found.

Why are we building the Kibana definition from test values? Can it use the `FunctionDescription` instead, which is always up to date, and seems to have all the information needed, including acceptable parameter types, optionality, etc.

Asides:
* `AbsentOverTimeTests` should be updated to have values for `window`,
* The Kibana definition file has a lot of repetitions and could probably be simplified by having a single `params` with an array of `types`. But I may be missing something here.
issues.title: ESQL: Discrepancy in docs & kibana generation for function parameters

We don't have descriptions on indices yet, but since [views are an `IndexAbstraction`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/cluster/metadata/View.java), could this be an opportunity to also add descriptions to indices?

/cc @craigtaverner with whom I discussed this.

issues.body:
The [Streaming](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/plan/logical/Streaming.java) interface marks commands that work on a per-row basis and is used to enable more queries with remote ENRICH commands (and likely soon more! like running approximate queries). When a remote ENRICH comes after a Limit or TopN, we are able to still run the query, but only if the commands in between implement Streaming.

We can mark Completion as Streaming and add 2 spec tests for verification:
- `LIMIT | COMPLETION | ENRICH remote:policy`
- `SORT | LIMIT | COMPLETION | ENRICH remote:policy`

issues.body:
ESQL has multi-values, which are similar to arrays:

```
ROW x = [1,2,3], y =[4,5,6] | EVAL z = MV_APPEND(x, y) | KEEP z

z:integer
-------------
[1,2,3,4,5,6]
```

However, they cannot represent null-values inside of them. `null` is equivalent to a multi-value that has 0 values. So there is no multi-value corresponding to the (JSON) array `[1,null,3]`, for instance.

Some of our functions really want to use arrays and we use multi-values instead for lack of proper arrays.  E.g. in the [computation of confidence intervals](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/131828#discussion_r2727032568) we need proper arrays that can contain nulls, and we resort to using NaN instead (a value that doesn't exist in ESQL and is only incidentally supported in the compute engine!)

Unfortunately, other functions really want to use sets and also use multi-values. This leads to annoying inconsistencies. For instance, `MV_CONTAINS` treats `null` as empty set so `MV_CONTAINS(foo, null)` is always `true`. But `MV_COUNT` treats  `null` as missing value so that `MV_COUNT(null)` is `null`. This wouldn't be an issue if we had proper sets so that we can specify an empty set - which would be different from `null`, which is a missing value.

Let's see if we can actually have _proper_ arrays and sets in ESQL.
issues.title: ESQL: Proper arrays and sets in ESQL

issues.body:
When a shard relocation occurs, in-flight indexing operations wait to acquire a primary permit until the relocation completes. Upon successful relocation, these operations receive a [`RetryOnPrimaryException`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/c3f07ad1ec13ba9c688adbea9c094563cfd69bff/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/action/support/replication/TransportReplicationAction.java#L484-L494), which [marks the request as retried](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/c3f07ad1ec13ba9c688adbea9c094563cfd69bff/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/action/support/replication/TransportReplicationAction.java#L1088-L1096). This [forces a version lookup](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/184c51b9edcf82fada430492acd28f4e336a0364/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/index/engine/InternalEngine.java#L1516-L1519) during indexing on the new primary, even for operations that could have used the auto-generated ID append-only optimization.

For shards with high indexing throughput, relocations can take a while to complete. During this time, many operations queue up, all marked as retried. When they finally execute on the new primary, they must perform version lookups (requiring at least a terms dictionary lookup) with a likely cold cache. This can overwhelm the new primary shard.

We should detect this situation and avoid marking the request as retried, since we can safely assume the documents were not indexed on the old primary.
issues.title: Do not mark bulk indexing requests as retried after primary relocations

issues.body:
Take the following query:

```
FROM colors METADATA _id, _index, _score
| FORK (WHERE color:"red")
    ( WHERE knn(rgb_vector, [1, 2, 3]))
| FUSE
```

We return an error message `cannot use [rgb_byte_vector] as an input of FUSE. Consider using [DROP rgb_byte_vector] before FUSE.`.

FUSE uses STATS internally and the VALUES aggregate function to collect values when merging rows.
STATS works great for us, however we are dependent on what data types VALUES supports.
VALUES does not support  types like `dense_vector`, `aggregate_metric_double`, `exponential_historgram`, `histogram`, `tdigest` and `date_range`.
When VALUES does not support the data type of a column, we return a validation error, pointing that it cannot be used as an input to FUSE.

A lot times support for VALUES depends on whether we have multivalued support for a data type, `dense_vector` is one of those fields that cannot currently be multivalued.

The other aspect is that using VALUES can have a performance impact and it's doing more than what we need.
With FUSE we can expect that rows that have the same key columns (e.g. _id and _index), have pretty much the same values except for the score column and the column that is used for grouping (_fork).
In this case for columns that are not used for scoring or grouping, a better fit would be to use an aggregate function that only returns the first non-null value it encounters.

We don't currently have anything like this, but we can build it as an internal only aggregate function e.g. `FUSE_VALUES`. We don't register it in the function registry or document it.
If there's a user need, we can choose to have it as a public function.

However, the primary goal at this point is to have a mechanism for FUSE to remove the friction of what data types we can support as input and to speed up performance.
issues.title: ES|QL: Improve how we collect values with FUSE

Currently, the t-digest field, like the histogram field, just accepts whatever data the user sends.  We should consider reencoding this with the digest settings the field was defined with.  This would protect against users mistakenly loading very large fields into what is meant to be a compact format. 

I think there are two options we can adopt: 
- Always re-encode the data; this incurs a memory and compute cost on every ingest, which may not be useful if the user sent the right thing in the first place
- Apply some heuristic, such as `if (centroids.length) > compression * 10)`, which makes a reasonable guess about the shape of the sketch and only re-encodes if the supplied data looks very different from that guess.

issues.body:
### Description

**Issue: Group remaining values as “Other” when using LIMIT PER with time buckets**
**Summary**

Users want to query top N values by a metric (e.g. client IPs by average bytes) over time, while also seeing an “Other” group that represents the aggregate of all remaining values per time bucket.

This pattern is common in visualizations such as histograms or time series charts, but it does not currently work as expected in ESQL when time-based bucketing is involved.

**User problem**

A typical use case is:

Identify the top 3 client IPs by a metric (e.g. average or percentile of bytes sent)

Show those top 3 IPs bucketed per hour

Also show an “Other” series, representing the aggregated metric of all remaining client IPs per hour

This is especially important for dashboards, where users want:

Focus on the most significant contributors

Still understand the behavior of the long tail over time

**Example scenario**

A user wants to:

Get the top 3 client IPs by average bytes sent

Visualize them in a histogram bucketed per hour

Include an “Other” bucket that shows the average bytes sent per hour by all remaining client IPs

This works in some simple cases, but fails when time intervals are introduced (e.g. 12-hour or 1-hour buckets).

**Why this is a problem today**

The current behavior makes it difficult or impossible to express this query pattern in ESQL because:

The query needs to:

Determine the top N values across the dataset

Then separately aggregate the remaining values (“Other”) using the same time buckets

Once the top N values are selected, the information needed to correctly compute the “Other” aggregation per time bucket is no longer available within the same query flow

As a result, users cannot reliably produce a single result set that includes:

Top N series per time bucket

Plus a correctly aggregated “Other” series per time bucket

**Impact**

Because of this limitation:

Common visualization patterns (Top N + Other over time) are hard to express

Tools like Kibana currently work around this by issuing multiple background queries

Users cannot easily reason about or reproduce the same logic directly in ESQL
issues.title: Group other values in a separate bucket in esql

issues.body:
Today (e.g. in #139124) we use `TransportService#newNetworkBytesStream` to access the Netty allocator so that we can accumulate bytes for eventual network transmission, but also want to keep track of those bytes in a circuit breaker so that we can fail the accumulation process before it consumes too much heap. With the existing API the caller must accumulate some amount of memory and then update the circuit breaker to match, but it'd be preferable to adjust the circuit breaker before actually allocating the memory in the first place. The caller must also manually keep track of the bytes tracked in the circuit breaker so as to be sure to release them (as well as the actual pages) on all failure paths. The caller also has no practical way to account for the unused bytes in the last page.

I think instead we should offer a way to track the allocations in a circuit breaker as they occur, by adapting either `RecyclerBytesStreamOutput` or the underlying `Recycler<BytesRef>` to do the necessary accounting directly.
issues.title: Integrate `TransportService#newNetworkBytesStream` with circuit breakers

issues.body:
### Description

Multi-cluster environment means the linked cluster will frequently differ in versions from each other. There was a lot of requests to extend the compatibility range of cross-cluster querying. One of the more complicated scenarios is when a newer (higher version) cluster sends queries to an older (lower version) cluster. 

When we have tests a lot of tests are marked with "requires this capability" and "requires that feature", so when these features are missing, the tests do not run. However, this works only for specific tests - this is not part of the execution engine. So if we imagine the same setup as we have in our BWC test - new cluster linked to old cluster - and the user now initiates the same "unsupported" query, what would happen? I mean, we expect some failure, but can we guarantee deterministic "clean" 400 failure? Or we'd get some weird 500s? Or maybe we get broken data? I mean failure is fine, but there are different kinds of failure - there's "it won't work and it will tell you and you will know what to do", and there's "undefined behavior" aka "it can do anything, including wiping your whole database, so don't even do it or we aren't responsible for what happens".

In order to allow the users to run such queries, we need to be able to tell them that it is "safe" to do so - that in this scenario, if the query is not supported by all clusters participating, they'd get either an error message, or a partial result with unsupporting cluster excluded. But we should not find ourselves in a situation where such query would produce 500s, or even worse, broken data. We need to ensure this is indeed the case.
issues.title: ES|QL handling version discrepancies between clusters

issues.body:
In a large shard under write load the peer recovery process must replay into the target shard all operations received by the source shard since acquiring the recovery commit $C_1$ at the start of phase 1. The number of operations to replay is determined by the indexing rate and the size of the data to be copied in phase 1. Replaying operations is a relatively slow process (see e.g. https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/68513) so it'd help if we could reduce this number.

Yet, in a large shard, most of the segments will remain unchanged for long periods even while the shard is receiving writes. Thus we could reduce the amount of data to copy in phase 1 by optimistically copying an older commit $C_0$ first, before acquiring the recovery commit $C_1$, and then in phase 1 we need only copy the few new segments which differ between $C_0$ and $C_1$. For sufficiently large shards we could even try and do this pre-copy phase repeatedly until it gets close enough to the recovery commit we eventually decide to use.
issues.title: Optimistically copy files before acquiring recovery commit

## Reproducer using the csv tests

```
{
    "dynamic": false,
    "properties" : {

            "type" : "integer"

        }

}
```

Then run

```
| INLINE STATS s = sum(id::integer)
| SORT name, version

and returns

Different column name [1]
Expected :name
Actual   :version
```

issues.body:
Literals, when not folded, are evaluated through their `LiteralsEvaluator` (Inside `EvalMapper`):

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/f1bbdc738ddd45f82ec074d1ce24e1bca9ccdf9b/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/evaluator/EvalMapper.java#L251-L257

(Moved in this PR: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/144073/changes#diff-886a0e11925494396c218473e9c04aab7fe33dfccfc6a811a332cdbe9c11e6ea)

It uses `BlockUtils.constantBlock()` which, for each page:
1. Uses reflection to know the kind of Constant Block to create
2. If it has multivalues, it uses a `BlockUtils.wrapperFor()` to, value by value, fill a new block with the literal N times (one per page position)
3. Creates a new block per page. _This is quite lightweight, and as pages may have different position counts, this is hard to avoid_

Problem 1 is probably hardly an improvement, as it's 1 check per full Page.
Problem 2 however would be heavier when using literal multivalues. This could affect expressions like:

It would be helpful to provide a way to ensure ilmhistory documents can always be sorted in an accurate and deterministic order.
Either with a sort of incrementing sequence number per index to leverage as a tie breaker or  increasing the timestamp precision from millis to nanos.

The ilm history events currently record the timestamp in millis. issues.body:
## Summary

Kibana's session management relies on Elasticsearch access/refresh tokens for several authentication providers (SAML, OpenID Connect, Kerberos, and Token). The refresh token lifetime is hard-coded to 24 hours, which prevents Kibana administrators from configuring idle session timeouts longer than 24 hours. Elasticsearch should allow clients like Kibana to request a specific refresh token lifetime when exchanging credentials for a token pair.

## Background

When a user authenticates to Kibana via a token-based provider, Kibana obtains an access/refresh token pair from Elasticsearch. While the user is active, Kibana transparently refreshes the access token. When the user is idle, the refresh token is the only mechanism to resume the session without forcing re-authentication.

Kibana exposes `xpack.security.session.idleTimeout` to control how long a session can be idle. Administrators reasonably set this to values exceeding 24 hours (e.g., `72h` for weekends). However, the hard-coded 24-hour refresh token lifetime silently overrides this: once the refresh token expires, Kibana cannot obtain a new access token and the user is forced to re-authenticate, even though the Kibana session hasn't expired.

This is documented as a known limitation in https://github.com/elastic/kibana/issues/83914 (see "Kibana session settings vs access/refresh token expiration").

## Proposal

Allow clients to specify a desired refresh token lifetime when calling the `POST /_security/oauth2/token` API (and the equivalent SAML/OIDC token exchange APIs). For example, Kibana could pass a parameter like `refresh_token_expires_in` when exchanging credentials:

```json
POST /_security/oauth2/token
{
  "grant_type": "password",
  "username": "kibana_user",
  "password": "...",
  "refresh_token_expires_in": "72h"
}
```

Kibana would derive the requested value from its configured `xpack.security.session.idleTimeout`, ensuring the refresh token lives at least as long as the idle timeout window.

### Considerations

- **Default behavior preserved**: If the parameter is omitted, the refresh token lifetime remains 24 hours.
- **Server-enforced maximum**: Elasticsearch could enforce a configurable upper bound (e.g., via `xpack.security.authc.token.refresh_token.max_timeout`) to prevent clients from requesting excessively long lifetimes.

## References

- [elastic/kibana#83914](https://github.com/elastic/kibana/issues/83914) — Documents this as a known limitation
- [Token-based authentication services](https://www.elastic.co/docs/deploy-manage/users-roles/cluster-or-deployment-auth/token-based-authentication-services) — Documents 24-hour refresh token lifetime
issues.title: Configurable timeout for refresh tokens

issues.body:
When a STATS ... BY query groups by a field that functionally determines other fields used as grouping keys, those functionally-dependent fields are currently included as additional hash aggregation keys. This is unnecessary and hurts performance as the BlockHash in the HashAggregationOperator must hash and compare more columns than are actually needed to distinguish groups.

For example, consider the query:
```
  FROM table
  | STATS count = COUNT(*) BY price, price+1
```

`price+1` is a function of `price` and thus does not cause more groups to be produced. But `price+1` is still used are part of the hash key.

This query could instead be tranformed to:
```
  FROM table
  | STATS count = COUNT(*) BY price
  | EVAL price1 = price + 1 
  | keep count, price, price1
```

A special case of this, which is easier to implement, is when a group by key is a constant. In such a case, the constant can be pushed after the aggregation.
issues.title: Push functional dependencies of GROUP BY keys into post-aggregation EVAL

issues.body:
### Description

**Problem Statement**

We currently have a nightly ES|QL performance dashboard, but it does not fully answer the questions we need in order to move ES|QL performance forward in a systematic way.

In particular, the current signal does not clearly cover:

- Where ES|QL underperforms DSL, with a curated and actionable view

- How ES|QL behaves at scale, beyond nightly test sizes

- How ES|QL performs in Serverless environments, which are a primary deployment model

- How ES|QL behaves under realistic workloads, such as multiple concurrent queries and mixed query shapes

As a result, performance analysis and optimization are often reactive and ad-hoc, and it is difficult to track progress over time or prioritize the highest-impact gaps.

**Goal**

Make ES|QL performance systematically observable and actionable by ensuring that existing performance reporting (starting with the nightly dashboard) covers all major gaps:

- ES|QL vs DSL performance deltas
 
- Scale behavior and trends

- Serverless-specific performance characteristics
 
- Realistic workload scenarios, including concurrency

The intent is not to replace existing dashboards, but to extend and structure them so they reliably answer:

Where are we worse than DSL, why, and are we getting better?

issues.body:
### Description

This is a rather general issue that I need to think more about. However, we are immensely naive in our parallelism with scoring over segments. 

One thread per segment is obviously wrong. In real world cases, segment sizes will be dramatically diverse and giving each a single thread for their given percentage of search is wrong.

One option is that we should adopt what was done for regular queries. Chunking along the known doc counts, handling tiny segments within a single thread and allowing large segments to be parallelized.

Another option is some evolution similar to what we are doing with rescoring, aggressively prefetching regardless of segment and scoring according to a global queue. This might be complicated, and need some design. However, it will likely increase our IO throughput and make our query parallelism much better.

The overall goals here are:

 - Improve our parallelism (break away from one thread == one segment)
 - Increase our IO throughput when things aren't loaded into cache.


Note: These concerns are slightly different than "information sharing" between segments  or postings lists for early termination, etc. I think that work is also useful, and should be done, but associated with a different issue.
issues.title: [DiskBBQ] Fix our segment parallelism

issues.body:
Lucene99 format uses the vector scorer supplier when building the HNSW graph - see https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/main/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/codecs/lucene99/Lucene99HnswVectorsWriter.java#L691. This references the byte/float heap vector directly, which means the native scorers in our supplier implementations can't be used, as they need a `MemorySegment` from on-disk vectors.

JDK22 supports creating `MemorySegment`s from heap arrays, so we could create a JDK22 version of `VectorScorerFactoryImpl` that creates memory segments from the byte/float vector values, and uses native code on that.
issues.title: Use native vector scorers when building the HNSW graph

## Description

PromQL trigonometric functions (e.g. `atanh`, `acos`, `asin`) currently throw an `ArithmeticException` when given out-of-range inputs. For example, `atanh(2)` throws rather than returning `NaN`.

In PromQL, these functions are expected to return `NaN` for out-of-range inputs instead of raising errors. This difference affects compatibility with Prometheus behavior.

## Current behavior

```
atanh(2) → ArithmeticException: Atanh input out of range
```

## Expected PromQL behavior

```
atanh(2) → NaN
```

## Affected functions

- `atanh` (input outside [-1, 1])
- `acos` (input outside [-1, 1])
- `asin` (input outside [-1, 1])
- Potentially other trigonometric functions with domain restrictions

## Proposal

Either create PromQL-specific variants of these functions that return `NaN`, or add a wrapping mechanism that catches `ArithmeticException` and returns `NaN` when invoked from a PromQL context.

## Context

Discussed in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/142213#discussion_r2804610138
issues.title: PromQL: Trigonometric functions should return NaN for out-of-range inputs instead of throwing exceptions

issues.body:
Kinda a continuation of https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/140577. Relates #138888 .

`SET unmapped_fields="nullify"` introduced more usage for the `NULL` type that was previously reserved for the `null` literal. A field that is missing from the indices used in `FROM` will be "nullified", that is, treated like the `null` literal and be of type `NULL`.

Unfortunately, we sometimes guess the output type of an expression when it uses the `NULL` type. This applies e.g. to `SUM` and to arithmetic operators. It can lead to queries unnecessarily becoming invalid when a field goes missing (e.g. due to small mapping changes becoming effective after rollover). An example is

```
SET unmapped_fields="nullify";
FROM idx
| STATS s = SUM(field)
| EVAL foo = CASE(bar, 10000::long, s)
```

When `field` is mapped as a long, this query works fine. But when `field` becomes unmapped, this query fails because `SUM(field)` is then assumed to be `double`, which breaks the `CASE` expression due to type mismatch in its output branches.

As commented [here](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/140577#issuecomment-3846250551), I think we may have more useful behavior for the `NULL` data type if we postulate two rules that expressions consuming the `NULL` type must follow:

1. Every function and operator accepts the null type for any argument that can be a field or other non-literal column. That is, if I can write valid queries with `... | EVAL y = function(x, ...)` and `x` is a field or reference of some non-`NULL` type, `function` must also work if we shadow `x` with a `NULL` literal: `... | EVAL x = null | EVAL y = function(x, ...)`. This does not cover function parameters that need to be folded before the query is run, e.g. `PERCENTILE(field, percentage)` does have to accept a `NULL` field, but not a `NULL` percentage.
2. If a function can output different types depending on the argument types, it must output the type NULL if one of the input types that determines the output type is NULL.

This behavior implies no guessing of output types when we cannot really determine this from the expression; it would also mean that more queries remain valid when using `SET unmapped_fields="nullify"` and one of the fields using in the query is unmapped or missing.
issues.title: ESQL: consider better behavior of NULL type in expressions

issues.body:
### Motivation

ES|QL does not currently support a native way to paginate/scroll results.

There are ways to achieve this in ES|QL, but with additional effort.
Take for example the following query:

```
FROM movies METADATA _score, _id
| WHERE title:?query
| SORT _score DESC, _id // _id here serves as a tiebreaker
| LIMIT 10
```

If we wanted to retrieve the next 10 documents, we could:
- reissue the same ES|QL query, but with `LIMIT 20` and then on the client side, skip the first 10 rows
- from the first 10 documents, take the values of `_score` and `_id` of the last row and add a filter:
```
FROM movies METADATA _score, _id
| WHERE title:?query
| SORT _score DESC, _id
| LIMIT 20
| WHERE _score <= ?last_score AND _id > ?last_id
```

### Proposal

Introduce an OFFSET option to LIMIT

```
LIMIT x OFFSET y
```

Explanation: LIMIT will skip the first y rows and then keep x rows.

While OFFSET might not be the solution to all use cases that require pagination, it does cover many of them, the same way `from` and `size` cover most pagination use cases in `_search`.

### Execution

Take the following query:

```
FROM movies METADATA _score, _id
| WHERE title:?query
| SORT _score DESC
| LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20
```

The OFFSET will only be applied on the coordinator.
In order for this to work correctly, the data node plans will still need to return up to 10 + 20 sorted rows.

The OFFSET option will only be allowed if the input is sorted, e.g. if a SORT is used.
If we detect that OFFSET is used without SORT, we will return a verification error.
This means that OFFSET will only be applied by TopN.

Both Limit and TopN have their own unique optimizations in the planner, that will need to be given special consideration when OFFSET is introduced.


### Requirements/implementation checklist

- [ ] syntax change to introduce OFFSET to LIMIT (query params support for OFFSET)
- [ ] verification when OFFSET is used without SORT
- [ ] basic support (no optimization) for OFFSET with sorted input for basic queries e.g. `FROM index | SORT field | LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10`. 

Optimizations that need to correctly handle OFFSET:
- [ ] `CombineTopN`
- [ ] `HoistRemoteEnrichLimit`
- [ ] `HoistRemoteEnrichTopN`
- [ ] `PushDownAndCombineLimits`
- [ ] `PushDownFilterAndLimitIntoUnionAll`
- [ ] `ReplaceLimitAndSortAsTopN`
- [ ] `ReplaceTopNWithLimitAndSort`
- [ ] `PushDownLimitAndOrderByIntoFork`

Release checklist:
- [ ] remove from snapshot
- [ ] documentation
issues.title: ES|QL: Add OFFSET option to LIMIT

issues.body:
## Summary

`XContentParser.getTokenLocation()` returns an `XContentLocation(lineNumber, columnNumber)`. The underlying Jackson `JsonParser` provides byte offsets via `JsonLocation.getByteOffset()`, but `JsonXContentParser` discards this information when wrapping the Jackson location. Exposing byte offsets would enable zero-copy extraction of sub-structures (objects/arrays) from the source byte array.

## Motivation

The `JSON_EXTRACT` ES|QL function (#142375) extracts values from JSON strings. When the extracted value is an object or array, it currently uses `XContentBuilder.copyCurrentStructure(parser)` to serialize the sub-structure back to JSON — walking every token and rebuilding the string from scratch, even though the original bytes are already valid JSON in the source array.

With byte offsets, extraction becomes a direct array slice:

```java
long start = parser.getTokenLocation().byteOffset();
parser.skipChildren();
long end = parser.getCurrentLocation().byteOffset();
builder.appendBytesRef(new BytesRef(bytes, offset + (int) start, (int) (end - start)));
```

This eliminates all intermediate parsing, string allocation, and JSON escaping for the sub-structure.

## Proposed API Change

**`XContentLocation`** — add `byteOffset` with a backward-compatible constructor:

```java
public record XContentLocation(int lineNumber, int columnNumber, long byteOffset) {
    public XContentLocation(int lineNumber, int columnNumber) {
        this(lineNumber, columnNumber, -1L);
    }
}
```

**`XContentParser`** — add `getCurrentLocation()` (the other method already exists):

```java
XContentLocation getTokenLocation();    // already exists — starts populating byteOffset
XContentLocation getCurrentLocation();  // new — position just past the last consumed byte
```

## Implementation Impact

The XContentParser hierarchy has 19 implementations. The change is concentrated in one place.

**Leaf implementations (5):**

| Class | Change needed | Notes |
|-------|--------------|-------|
| `JsonXContentParser` | Pass through `JsonLocation.getByteOffset()` instead of discarding it. Add `getCurrentLocation()` delegating to Jackson. | ~10 lines changed |
| `SmileXContentParser` | None — inherits from `JsonXContentParser` | |
| `CborXContentParser` | None — inherits from `JsonXContentParser` | |
| `YamlXContentParser` | None — inherits from `JsonXContentParser`. Jackson's YAML parser returns `-1` for byte offsets (only char offsets available). | |
| `MapXContentParser` | Return `-1` byte offset (no byte stream) | Trivial |

**Decorators (13):** All transparent — delegate through `FilterXContentParser.delegate()`. Zero changes needed for 11 of 13. The two with overrides:

| Class | Notes |
|-------|-------|
| `DotExpandingXContentParser` | Returns saved location for synthesized tokens — would carry `-1` byte offset for synthetic tokens, real offsets for original content |
| `CompletionFieldMapper.MultiFieldParser` | Returns fixed location — would carry `-1` byte offset |

**Test-only (1):** `ParameterizableYamlXContentParser` — delegates, transparent.

## Byte Slicing Feasibility by Format

Not all content types support raw byte slicing even with offsets available:

| Format | Byte offsets? | Slicing safe? | Why |
|--------|--------------|---------------|-----|
| JSON | Yes | **Yes** | Sliced sub-structure is valid standalone JSON |
| CBOR | Yes | **Yes** | Self-contained data items, no back-references |
| SMILE | Yes | **No** | Back-references for repeated field names/strings — sliced fragment may contain unresolvable references |
| YAML | No (`-1`) | **No** | Whitespace-sensitive grammar, anchor/alias system |

Consumers must check the content type before slicing. JSON and CBOR are safe; SMILE and YAML require the `XContentBuilder.copyCurrentStructure` fallback.
issues.title: Expose byte offsets on XContentParser for zero-copy sub-structure extraction

issues.body:
### Description
Detection Rules in the Security Solution run queries against Elasticsearch that are built up from a variety of sources - users select index patterns, a base query, "exceptions" (essentially additional filters), a relative time range, and in some cases additional grouping fields or more complex use case-specific parameters that we translate to query logic. When detection rules do not generate the alerts that users expect they have trouble identifying which part of the rule logic is not performing as expected. Often we receive questions like "This query returns results in Discover, but the same query in my rule doesn't generate alerts - why?".

We would like to gather information about how many rows are in the result set at specific points of an ESQL query to help users identify parts of the rule logic that they should focus on when rules aren't working as expected. However, we do not want this information to be part of the normal result rows. For Detection Rules we expect every row returned by the query to become an alert. Ideally this extra information would be returned separately from the normal rows, and it would be returned even if there are no normal rows.

### Example Proposal
One way we might gather this information is via a new ESQL command, which I've named `CHECKPOINT` for this example. When used, `CHECKPOINT` calculates the number of rows passed into the command and stores the result in a key-value store _outside_ the normal rows. The query below is an example implementation of "new terms" logic, looking for values that have just been seen for the first time.

```
FROM logs-* METADATA _id, _index
| CHECKPOINT index_rows
| WHERE [rule_exceptions_filter]
| CHECKPOINT after_exceptions
| KEEP _id, host.name, user.name, _index, @timestamp
| WHERE `host.name` IS NOT NULL AND `user.name` IS NOT NULL
| CHECKPOINT after_rule_query
| MV_EXPAND `host.name`
| MV_EXPAND `[user.name](http://user.name/)`
| CHECKPOINT unique_combos
| INLINE STATS first_seen = MIN(@timestamp) BY host.name, user.name
| WHERE first_seen >= "2024-01-15T10:00:00Z"
| WHERE @timestamp == first_seen
| INLINE STATS min_doc_id = min(_id) BY host.name, user.name
| WHERE _id == min_doc_id
```

For a query like this, we would expect to receive a response with the following information, in addition to the normal result rows:
```
{
  index_rows: 5000,
  after_exceptions: 3000,
  after_rule_query: 10,
  unique_combos: 30
}
```

`unique_combos` is higher than `after_rule_query` due to the `MV_EXPAND` command usage - showing that some rows have multiple values of either `host.name` or `user.name`.
issues.title: ESQL: Collect statistics about query results during processing

issues.body:
### Description

On stateless search nodes we eagerly populate the `BitsetFilterCache` (assuming `load_fixed_bitset_filters_eagerly` is `true`).

This will be done for whichever segments happen to have open readers on the local node, which will vary over time as the segments move in and out of the local disk cache. That means that the amount of memory that is needed in the `BitsetFilterCache` is variable and dependent on which segments have been "recently" searched (where "recently" might not be very recent, if we haven't needed to evict from the disk cache).

In some cases we've seen the cache consume ~3GiB of heap on a node with 4GiB of total heap. Retaining these Bitsets in memory is useful because they are necessary for joins (nested fields) but not if they consume so much heap that the node becomes unstable.

In stateless we already accept that segments can be evicted from the disk cache, which closes the reader and evicts their Bitsets from the `BitsetFilterCache`. So we already do not guarantee that every segment has its Bitsets cached, even when `load_fixed_bitset_filters_eagerly` is `true`. We should extend that to heap management: allow evicting Bitsets from the bitset cache when needed to keep heap usage reasonable, even if the segment reader is still open (because the segment is still on disk).

Related:
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/28857
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/105791
issues.title: Consider size limits/expiry for the BitsetFilterCache in Stateless

issues.body:
### Description

The real memory circuit breaker prevents operations (commonly REST requests) that it predicts would cause the JVM to cross a threshold in heap usage (by default 95%).
In generally this is useful when the heap is being consumed by user level operations (common REST requests) and will become available when those operations complete.

However, there are a number of system managed components that consume heap and contribute to the circuit breaker's "in use" tracking. This includes the base memory needed to run Elasticsearch, the memory used to manage cluster state and index mappings, and notably here _a number of caches_.

Some of these caches are unbounded and/or non-expiring. Most have eviction policies (generally based on memory size or count and age) but each cache operates independently. Given the wide range of use case in which Elasticsearch is used, different types of caches are necessary for different work loads, and the optimum (maximum) size for each cache will vary between deployments and work loads.  
For example:
- A deployment with nested fields may need to cache a larger number filter bitsets 
- A deployment with heavy use of Document Level Security may be need to cache a lot of document-visibility bitsets
- A deployment with a large number of independent clients (or users) may need a large cache to provide fast authentication of users or API Keys

Consequently the default size of many of these caches is intended to support use cases that have a heavy reliance on that particular type of data. However, since the caches operate independently it is possible to have situations where each cache is heavily populated and a very large amount of total heap is consumed which causes very little memory to be available for requests.

Or, in other cases there is a single cache that is consuming a large amount of heap and is leading to user requests being rejected with real memory circuit breaker exceptions (CBEs) but the cause is hard to diagnose (since the memory is in a system managed component) and is hard to resolve (because a node that has very high constant heap usage is hard to administer).

If we were able to create a unified view of these system-managed components, and make that view available to the `HierarchyCircuitBreakerService` then we could:
- Include statistics about where/how the heap is being used in circuit break logs
- Allow operators to alert and respond differently depending on how much heap is used by clients vs the system itself
- Request that system-managed caches perform active evictions when heap is unreasonably high and is preventing use activity.
issues.title: Better management and accounting for non-request heap usage

- `allow_no_indices`: If false, the request returns an error if any wildcard expression, index alias, or _all value targets only missing or closed indices. This behavior applies even if the request targets other open indices. For example, a request targeting foo*,bar* returns an error if an index starts with foo but no index starts with bar.
- `expand_wildcards`: Type of index that wildcard patterns can match. If the request can target data streams, this argument determines whether wildcard expressions match hidden data streams. Supports comma-separated values, such as open,hidden. Supported values include:
  - all: Match any data stream or index, including hidden ones.
  - open: Match open, non-hidden indices. Also matches any non-hidden data stream.
  - closed: Match closed, non-hidden indices. Also matches any non-hidden data stream. Data streams cannot be closed.
  - hidden: Match hidden data streams and hidden indices. Must be combined with open, closed, or both.
  - none: Wildcard expressions are not accepted.
- `ignore_unavailable`: If true, missing or closed indices are not included in the response.
- `ignore_throttled`: If true, concrete, expanded or aliased indices are ignored when frozen.

issues.body:
When an ES|Q query does not have an obvious pipeline breaker like STATS or SORT, most of the query ends up running on the coordinator. For example:

```
FROM idx | EVAL y = somethingExpensive(x) | KEEP y | LIMIT 10
```

Where we want the expensive operation to run on the coordinator, because we only want to run it 10 times (due to LIMIT 10). So the data node gets something like `FROM idx | LIMIT 10` and the coordinator then does `LIMIT 10 | EVAL y = somethingExpensive(x) | KEEP y`.

This is, however, not the perfect solution if:
* The LIMIT is a higher number than some filter
  * the filter already reduces the row count below the limit, so we will always run the expensive function the same number of times, and spreading the load to the data nodes is more efficient.
* The function is a shrinking function, like LENGTH or ST_SIMPLIFY where we can reduce the data volumes early and minimize runtime memory usage.
  * This open the opportunity to push the function into the BlockLoader so we do not allocate blocks for the input fields at all, only the result (requires KEEP/DROP as in the example above)

We want to combined shrinking function identification with dropping the original fields. If that combination occurs, we should push it down. Some functions we could consider for this:

* LENGTH
* JSON_EXTRACT
* ST_SIMPLIFY
* ST_ENVELOPE, ST_XMIN, ST_XMAX, ST_YMIN, ST_YMAX
* ST_X, ST_Y (this does not shrink much, or not at all if both are used)

If we also had some measure of the cardinality of a filter, we could push down functions even if they did not shrink the results.
issues.title: Expand cases where ES|QL unctions should run on data nodes instead of coordinator

issues.body:
We configure Jackson to use the [`JsonParser.Feature.STRICT_DUPLICATE_DETECTION`](https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson-core/blob/52f39ad0a8f858afc9788b28594975c007ebd347/src/main/java/com/fasterxml/jackson/core/JsonParser.java#L321-L337) feature in `JsonXContentImpl`:

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/bbeda7bcfffc8ecd0dbd668c6cba836228a35fd6/libs/x-content/impl/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xcontent/provider/json/JsonXContentImpl.java#L57

Note: I'm linking to the JSON version of things, but as far as I'm aware the same story would apply in, say, yaml or smile parsing, etc, since they all build on the same code.

The purpose of that feature is to reject documents that use the same key twice in a single context (e.g. a map with `"foo"` twice). Upstream in Jackson, the feature is implemented via the [DupDetector](https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson-core/blob/2.x/src/main/java/com/fasterxml/jackson/core/json/DupDetector.java) class. There are some optimizations that have already been written in that scheme, for example, maps with just one or two keys don't allocate new internal data structures, and `DupDetector` instances are reset-and-reused in subsequent contexts at the same depth.

As documented on the feature, though, there is a cost to duplicate key checking (naively, one would imagine that we'd need to allocate a `HashSet<String>` and then `Set#add` each key and check the `boolean` result to see if that key has already been seen -- and that's not all that far off from the reality of things).

In more concrete Elasticsearch terms, if we consider everything inside an `IndexShard.prepareIndex` call to be the high level task of 'mapping', then, _in one of our internal benchmarks_, of the cpu time that we're mapping, about 6.5% of it is in `DupDetector`. For the same internal benchmark, of the memory allocated during mapping, about 21% of it is in `DupDetector`. This varies by benchmark (naturally!), depending on the general structure of the documents being indexed. For example, in a different benchmark the cpu time is comparable, but the memory cost is closer to 11%.

There's probably not all too much that can be done about the Big O time here, but this might be a spot where some micro-optimizations could shine.
issues.title: Optimization: faster duplicate map key detection

## Summary

Establish a valid baseline dataset for the `tsdb-metricsgen` Rally track before benchmarking the pipeline codec. The current dataset has precision artifacts and data generation issues that make benchmark results unreliable for evaluating floating-point compression and counter encoding.

The `metricsgenreceiver` tool needs fixes to produce realistic TSDB data, and a new dataset must be generated and published as the baseline for all `ES95` benchmarking (both integer parity validation and float compression evaluation).

This is a prerequisite for #141117 (TSDB Pipeline Codec POC Benchmarking).

### metricsgenreceiver fixes (all merged in [v1.0.8](https://github.com/elastic/metricsgenreceiver/releases/tag/v1.0.8))

- [x] Limited precision for floating point values: https://github.com/elastic/metricsgenreceiver/pull/34
- [x] Per-instance timestamp jitter: https://github.com/elastic/metricsgenreceiver/pull/33
- [x] Align hostmetrics template with EDOT defaults: https://github.com/elastic/metricsgenreceiver/pull/36
- [x] Monotonic long/double counters (already correct in v1.0.3+)

### Upstream OTel precision issues (tracked, not blocking)

The following upstream issues affect real-world compression effectiveness but do not block Rally benchmarking since `metricsgenreceiver` already fixes precision artifacts independently:

- [open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib#46141](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/issues/46141): Excessive float64 precision in scrapers (memory, disk, network, paging). Fixed by [#46153](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/pull/46153) (merged).
- [open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib#46177](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/issues/46177): CPU scraper precision (gopsutil converts integer jiffies to float64 before the scraper sees them). Fix in progress: [#46319](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/pull/46319) (open).

Similar precision issues likely exist in other components (e.g., process scraper reading `/proc/[pid]/stat`, third-party exporters performing float64 divisions on integer counters).

## Scope

- Land `metricsgenreceiver` fixes (PRs #33, #34, monotonic counters)
- Generate a new `tsdb-metricsgen` dataset with the fixed receiver
- Update the `tsdb-metricsgen` Rally track to use the new dataset as baseline
- Run `ES819` baseline benchmarks on the new dataset to establish reference numbers for indexing throughput, query latency, and storage footprint

## Acceptance Criteria

- All `metricsgenreceiver` fixes are merged
- New dataset is generated and published for the `tsdb-metricsgen` Rally track
- `ES819` baseline benchmark results are captured on the new dataset
- Float values in the dataset have realistic limited precision (not 12+ digit noise)
- Counter values are monotonically increasing with realistic reset patterns
- Timestamps have per-instance jitter (not identical across hosts)
issues.title: TSDB Pipeline Codec: Rally Dataset Baseline

When [InternalEngine.acquireLastIndexCommit](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/09e608535540b84ecd73e3de9a0b74c6ef4ad8c4/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/index/engine/InternalEngine.java#L2620-L2632) is invoked with `flushFirst = true`, it flushes the current commit, waits for the flush to complete (including upload when in serverless) and acquires the last index commit.

But this new commit is not flushed and without durability guarantees. This can sometimes be surprising if the caller depends on flush's durability semantics. It would be useful if this method can guarantee the acquired commit is always flushed.
