issues.body:
### Description

Within a dedicated Space, a user should be able to delegate day-to-day Fleet policy management to non-admin users while keeping the installation and upgrade of integrations restricted to admins. 

Currently, granting Fleet permissions that enable users to add integrations to agent policies also gives them the ability to install and update any integration in the Space, which is considered a security risk. A user should be able to leverage already-installed integrations and attach or update packages within their policies without performing installation or version upgrades themselves.

**Environment Details**
Product Area: Fleet-managed Elastic Agent

Version: 9.4

Context: Space-aware Fleet management and RBAC

**Current Limitations**
Setting Integrations permission to READ prevents installation/updates but also blocks adding integrations to policies, breaking the desired workflow.

No known configuration in v9.4 achieves "use but not install/update." Existing options are essentially READ or ALL, and sub-feature toggles do not address this requirement.

**Proposed Feature: Granular Integration Privileges**
Introduce space-aware privileges for Fleet Integrations that separate usage from administration.

A user should be able to:
- View available integrations already installed in the Space.
- Add an installed integration to an agent policy.
- Adjust integration policy settings within allowed bounds.
- Pin to currently installed package versions without the ability to trigger a global upgrade.

Administrative restrictions:
- Only admins should retain permissions for:
- Installing new integrations.
- Upgrading integration packages.
- Removing integrations from the Space.

**Implementation Considerations**
Space Isolation: Ensure behavior is consistent across Spaces so that granting the new permission in one Space does not leak install/upgrade capabilities from another.

UI/UX: Surface clear affordances (e.g., a disabled "Upgrade" button with an explanatory tooltip) when users lack administrative privileges but can still attach integrations.

Auditability: Log attempts by non-privileged users to install or upgrade for security and audit purposes.

**Value & Impact**
Safe Delegation: Enables operational teams to manage policies without exposing the platform to risks caused by unintended integration upgrades.

Least Privilege: Aligns with security best practices and reduces change-management risk in production environments.

Acceptance Criteria
A user should be able to configure a role where users can add installed integrations to policies in a Space but cannot install or upgrade integrations.

Attempting to upgrade or install must trigger a permission error and result in no state change.

The privilege model must be enforced consistently across both the API and the UI.
issues.title: Granular Permissions for Fleet Integrations

issues.body:
### Description

Currently when ILM triggers a rollover, the new index name is derived by incrementing a numeric suffix (e.g. ro_log-2026.01-000001 → ro_log-2026.01-000002). This means the date portion of the index name stays frozen at the bootstrap index's date, making it impossible to deterministically derive an index name from a date alone without querying Elasticsearch.
When index.lifecycle.parse_origination_date is enabled, ILM already understands that the index name encodes a date. It would be a natural and consistent extension for ILM to also use the current date when generating the rollover index name, following the same date format pattern detected from the existing index name.
This is proposed as a fully opt-in feature so existing behaviour is completely unchanged for anyone who does not explicitly enable it.
Current Behavior:
```
Existing index:   ro_log-2026.01
Rollover triggered in May 2026
New index name:   ro_log-2026.01-000002  ← counter incremented, date is stale
```
Expected Behavior:
```
Existing index:   ro_log-2026.01
Rollover triggered in May 2026
New index name:   ro_log-2026.05   ← derived from current month automatically
```
**Why This Matters:**
1. Index names become fully deterministic from a date alone — no ES query needed to resolve which index to write to
2. Eliminates the need for an external cron/scheduler to call _rollover with an explicit target index name each month
3. Backfill and targeted writes become trivial — any service can derive ro_log-YYYY.MM from a document's date field without any coordination
4. Consistent with the existing philosophy of parse_origination_date — if ILM can read the date from the name, it should also be able to write the date into the name
5. Reduces operational complexity for time-series use cases with strict retention requirements (e.g. 24 month rolling windows)
6. Fully opt-in — zero breaking changes, zero impact on existing users

**Proposed Behaviour:**
Introduce two new opt-in index settings:

```
"index.lifecycle.rollover_date_naming": true,
"index.lifecycle.rollover_date_format": "YYYY.MM"
```
**rollover_date_naming** is the opt-in flag — existing behaviour is completely unchanged for anyone who does not set it. rollover_date_format defines how the date is embedded in the new index name on each rollover.
When both are set, ILM derives the rollover index name from the current date instead of incrementing a numeric suffix:

```
index.lifecycle.rollover_date_naming: true
index.lifecycle.rollover_date_format: YYYY.MM

Rollover triggered May 2026  →  ro_log-2026.05
Rollover triggered Jun 2026  →  ro_log-2026.06
Rollover triggered Jan 2027  →  ro_log-2027.01
```
When rollover_date_naming is not set or false, ILM behaves exactly as today:

`Rollover triggered May 2026  →  ro_log-2026.01-000002  (counter incremented, no change)`
issues.title: [ILM] Support date-based index naming on rollover using parse_origination_date format

issues.body:
In https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/128618, we plan to prevent reindex, update-by-query, and delete-by-query from causing OOMs which kill ES nodes. That issue will cover using circuit breakers so that the task will fail with a circuit breaker exception before it can OOM the node. It will not prevent the task failing, perhaps after hours of work.

Although users should be able to prevent this by choosing small enough batch sizes and not running too many reindexes concurrently, this is difficult in practice, especially since the batch size is configured by a doc count and the bytes per doc is not always easy to predict. This is especially bad in serverless where users shouldn't need to know anything about their nodes' heap sizes.

The fix for that would be to have reindex (and friends) automatically limit the size in bytes of the search responses they get. This involves two changes:
 - On the search side, expose a `sizeInBytes`. This would probably go in `SearchSourceBuilder`. Assuming we want this to work for reindex-from-remote as well as local, we'd also need to expose it in the `_search` REST API. When both `size` and `sizeInBytes` are set, both should apply, i.e. the number of hits returned should be capped by whichever is the stricter limit.
 - On the reindex side, set that value on each search request. Assuming we want this to work for reindex-from-remote as well as local, we'd need to ensure that we include it when building the HTTP request for remote. We should do this in addition to setting `size` as we currently do. The `sizeInBytes` should be under the control of the reindex code, though perhaps with a node setting to allow some user/operator overrides. We probably want to default to some reasonable fraction of the node's heap — but this needs to be shared between all the reindex operations being coordinated concurrently on this node.
issues.title: Make reindex and friends limit the size in bytes of their search responses

issues.body:
## Description

Pick a small number of random documents (typically 5) from a stream's matching window — and pick them uniformly, so the LLM that consumes them sees a representative slice. The window might contain anywhere from hundreds of docs to a billion. Any bias (newest first, oldest first, single shard, single time bucket) silently poisons the LLM's view of the stream.

**DSL today (one query)**  

```js  
{  
  size: 5,  
  query: { function_score: { query: ..., random_score: { seed: ... } } },  
  sort: [{ _score: 'desc' }]  
}  
```

`random_score` assigns each matching doc a uniform random score; `sort:_score:desc` picks the top 5. Returns exactly the desired count in random order. Per-doc inclusion probability = `desired count / population`. One round trip.

**ES|QL — no direct equivalent in 9.4/9.5.** `| SAMPLE p` is a Bernoulli filter (each doc kept independently with probability `p`), not a top-N selector. No `function_score` analogue exists. Tracked upstream as [[elastic/elasticsearch#98545](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/98545)](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/98545) (`RANDOM` function).

**What we shipped — count, oversample, shuffle, trim:**  
  
```sql  
-- Pass 1: how big is the population?  
FROM <idx> | WHERE <filter> | STATS total = COUNT(*)  
  
-- Pass 2: oversample, then cap  
FROM <idx> METADATA _id, _source  
| WHERE <filter>  
| SAMPLE <sample probability>  
| LIMIT <cap>  
```  
  
Then in Node.js: **Fisher–Yates shuffle** the returned rows, then take the first 5.

**Concrete production case** — `errorLogsGenerator` sampling 500 error logs from a 1M-doc window:  
  
- Pass 1: `FROM logs-* | STATS total = COUNT(*)` → population = 1,000,000  
- Compute: 
	- sample probability = `(3 × 500) / 1,000,000` = 0.0015.
	- Limit = `10 × 500` = 5,000.  
- Pass 2: `FROM logs-* METADATA _id, _source | SAMPLE 0.0015 | LIMIT 5000`  
- Over the wire: typically ~1,500 rows; cap is 5,000 (almost never hit — overshoot probability essentially zero at this scale); underrun (<500 rows) probability also essentially zero  
- Node.js: shuffle the ~1,500 rows, return the first 500
issues.title: ES|QL: Random sampling

issues.body:
## Problem

Memory tracking in Elasticsearch fails by two structural mechanisms: allocations never registered with a tracking layer remain invisible, and registered values are typically estimates rather than measurements. The recent serverless OOM ([elastic/elasticsearch#147920](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/147920)) was an instance of the first. `NumericEntry` retained `numericFieldReader` instances each holding a 4 KB [`DocValuesForUtil`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/index/codec/tsdb/DocValuesForUtil.java) scratch buffer, and at scale (`field_count * segment_count * 4 KB`) the retained heap dwarfed everything else. The fix removed the retained references but did not close the visibility gap that let the regression ship.

## Today

Elasticsearch already runs several tracking layers, none of which reaches into the affected code path. [`BigArrays`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/common/util/BigArrays.java) registers managed byte, int, long, double, and object array allocations with a circuit breaker via [`addEstimateBytesAndMaybeBreak`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/common/breaker/CircuitBreaker.java#L85); `Accountable` companions (`BytesRefArray`, `BytesRefHash`, `BitArray`, `TDigestState`, `ExponentialHistogramState`) integrate with the same path. [`IndexingPressure`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/index/IndexingPressure.java) bounds bytes in flight during indexing through per role counters (coordinating, primary, replica) that increment at start and decrement on completion, rejecting requests that would push past the configured limit. Field data caches, query caches, and request buffers each maintain their own accounting. None sums across the others, and each sees only what it is instrumented for. Off heap allocations bypass this picture entirely: ZSTD compression in stored fields ([`ZstdCompressionMode`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/index/codec/zstd/ZstdCompressionMode.java) obtains a `CloseableByteBuffer` wrapping a native `ByteBuffer` via `nativeAccess.newConfinedBuffer`) and LZ4 transport compression (`Lz4TransportDecompressor`, `ReuseBuffersLZ4BlockOutputStream`) allocate native buffers outside JVM heap monitoring and outside every circuit breaker.

Lucene's [`Accountable`](https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/main/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/util/Accountable.java) interface is the standard way for a data structure to declare its retained size, but adoption is opt in and the declared value is an estimate based on field declarations rather than a measurement. `ramBytesUsed()` must be manually kept in sync as data structures evolve, so estimates drift from reality over time. Doc value readers and their scratch buffers do not implement `Accountable` uniformly, which is why the bug from #147920 was untracked. The pattern extends beyond doc values: BKD tree state during query execution, codec scratch buffers, the field readers held by `NumericEntry`, `SortedSetEntry`, and similar TSDB producer entry structures, and in memory posting structures during analyzer heavy indexing (see [elastic/elasticsearch#146804](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/146804) for an earlier symptom on the indexing path) are all invisible to Elasticsearch's accounting.

## Directions

Closing the gap requires three layered changes. Wrap more Elasticsearch side allocations in the `BigArrays` path so they enter the existing breaker. Call `ramBytesUsed()` from the accounting breaker on Lucene structures that already expose it, accepting that the returned value is an estimate. Push upstream contributions to make doc value readers, scratch buffers, and the entry types above `Accountable` compliant in Lucene, which is the only way to bring the largest untracked surfaces into any kind of accounting. Small heap stress tests (workloads run on intentionally tight heap to surface memory pressure as test failure) have a place as a coarse canary that flags the symptom without identifying which component retained the memory; their pass and fail behavior is sensitive to JVM version, garbage collector choice and tuning, and workload shape, so they complement rather than replace accounting.

Related to: [elastic/elasticsearch#148761](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/148761).
issues.title: Memory accounting and visibility gaps in Elasticsearch

issues.body:
## Problem

Rally exposes node level [telemetry](https://esrally.readthedocs.io/en/stable/telemetry.html) (`node-stats`, `gc`, and several specialized devices) that Elasticsearch's benchmarks already have the plumbing to use: the internal `esbench` orchestrator that wraps Rally for our benchmark runs forwards `stats.telemetry` and `runtime.telemetry` from each use case to Rally. Adoption is uneven. `mki`, `external`, and the logging cloud variants enable `node-stats` with sensible parameters; `simple`, `machine_learning`, and `many_shards` capture only `gc` or nothing. The result is a benchmark report surface where resource regressions that hold throughput and latency flat, the class of bug that produced the recent serverless OOM ([elastic/elasticsearch#147920](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/147920)), are invisible. The same blind spot covers CPU and IO regressions, and efficiency wins where throughput stays steady while resource consumption drops.

## Today

`node-stats` polls `_nodes/stats` and produces a per node time series including JVM heap and non heap usage, GC counters and time, OS level CPU percent and memory, process CPU and memory, file descriptor count, thread pool depths, indexing and search counters, and file system bytes per data path. Additional devices cover specialized cases: `shard-stats`, `recovery-stats`, `disk-usage-stats`, `segment-stats`. `runtime.telemetry` separately offers `jfr` (Java Flight Recorder) and `heapdump` for forensic captures. All of this is already supported by Rally and already plumbed through `esbench`. The work to close the gap is configuration plus dashboarding, not engineering.

## Directions

Standardize a shared default of `stats.telemetry = ["node-stats"]` plus `runtime.telemetry = ["gc"]` across all `esbench` use cases, with `stats.telemetry.params` setting `node-stats-include-indices: true` and a 10 second sample interval (deliberately larger than Rally's 1 second default to keep storage and indexing overhead manageable for nightly runs). Use cases with documented reasons to remain lightweight, for example to avoid perturbing a controlled comparison, can opt out explicitly. Build trend dashboards over the resulting metrics, charted by commit, on the same axes the team already uses for throughput and latency. Phase sliced attribution (indexing, merging, querying) and metrics not captured by the existing Rally devices are follow up work, not part of this issue.

Related to: [elastic/elasticsearch#148761](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/148761).
issues.title: Capture per node resource usage during Rally benchmark runs

issues.body:
### Description

Query approximation does not support chained `STATS` commands.

These have some fundamental issues, e.g.
```
SET approximation=true;
FROM people | STATS country_population BY country
```
may miss some countries (because of low population count), and next
```
SET approximation=true;
FROM people | STATS country_population BY country | STATS avg_population=AVG(country_population)
```
may be totally wrong. This is a fundamental problem of sampling and must be documented carefully.

On top of this, the source commands `TS` and `PROMQL` use chained `STATS` under the hood (first aggregating per time series, and next across time series), so they also don't work at the moment.

And there's one more issue: the default per-time-series agg is `LAST_OVER_TIME`, which is not supported by approximation due to its `MAX`-semantics.
issues.title: [ES|QL] Query approximation: support TS / PROMQL / chained STATS

issues.body:
## Problem

During node shutdown, `attemptFlushMetrics()` and `attemptFlushTraces()` are called sequentially, each with its own `TELEMETRY_OTEL_FLUSH_TIMEOUT` (default 10 s). With two meter providers plus the tracer provider, the worst-case shutdown delay is ~30–50 s.

## Solution

Use `CompletableResultCode.ofAll(asList(traceResult, metricsResult, ...)).join(timeout, unit)` so all `forceFlush()` calls fire in parallel under a single shared timeout — the same pattern used by the OTel Java agent ([reference](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-java-instrumentation/blob/f1e161dae78b2f95f7efc6d07cd21781f2154799/javaagent-tooling/src/main/java/io/opentelemetry/javaagent/tooling/OpenTelemetryInstaller.java#L57-L66)).

## Files to change

- `OtelSdkExportMeterSupplier.attemptFlushMetrics()` — return `CompletableResultCode` instead of joining internally
- `OtelSdkExportTracerSupplier.attemptFlushTraces()` — same
- `APMTelemetryProvider` — add `attemptFlushAll()` that combines results with `CompletableResultCode.ofAll()`

## Context

Identified in PR #146096 review by @mateuszrzeszutek. Deferred to keep that PR focused.
issues.title: APM OTel SDK: combine metrics and traces forceFlush() under a single shared timeout

issues.body:
## What this looks like from the product side

`EncryptionService.encrypt(byte[]) → EncryptedData` uses a single PEK per project — every byte every consumer encrypts in that project is under the same key. The contract is clean and the service does exactly what it promises. The implication: PEK is the unit of cryptographic isolation. A heap dump on any node yields the active PEK, which decrypts every payload any consumer ever encrypted in that project.

Today there are no production callers of `encrypt`/`decrypt` — `EncryptionService` shipped as a primitive ahead of consumers (verified by grep across the tree on current `main`). The first in-flight production consumer is an ES|QL workstream wiring encryption into data-source secret read/write paths. As more consumers come online (audit logs, snapshots, other secret stores — hypothetical but plausible), the blast-radius concentration compounds across all consumers within a project. Worth a conversation now while there's exactly one user.

## What this looks like from the structural side

The current contract has no notion of "who is encrypting" or "what context". The PEK is opaque to callers (good), and undifferentiated across them (the question this issue raises). Any tightening of the blast-radius property has to happen inside the service: consumers can't construct cryptographic separation in their own layer without adopting KDF conventions that don't belong there.

A reasonable alternative posture: per-consumer (or per-record, or per-purpose) key derivation. The service grows a notion of context, derives a context-specific key from the PEK using a standard KDF, and AES operates on the derived key — the PEK never reaches the cipher directly. Consumers get cryptographically independent keys from a single PEK; decrypt re-derives from the same inputs.

Whether to do this, and at what granularity, is the owners' call. There's a reasonable case for "single-PEK-per-project is the right posture; consumers should not assume cryptographic separation" — in which case nothing changes and this issue closes as won't-fix.

## What this would look like in implementation

One possible shape, sketched to illustrate the design space — not a prescription:

- API grows context: `EncryptionService.encrypt(byte[], String purpose, String identifier)`. Same for `decrypt`.
- Internal derivation: `derived_key = HKDF(IKM = PEK_secret_bytes, salt = projectId.bytes, info = purpose || ":" || identifier)`. IKM is the PEK's secret material (not its public `keyId` — that distinction matters); salt is a per-project diversifier; info encodes the per-consumer + per-record context.
- AES-GCM operates on `derived_key`. The PEK is never used as an AES key directly.
- `EncryptedData.keyId` already exists and can encode the derivation parameters so decrypt re-derives without storing the derived key anywhere.

What this doesn't change: PEK still lives in memory on every node. An attacker with the heap dump still has the master from which any derived key can be reconstructed, *given they also know the per-consumer context inputs* (which may be reachable depending on the consumer's storage). The mitigation isn't "prevent breach" — it's narrowing the impact of partial-leak scenarios: ciphertext escaping without surrounding context, telemetry contamination, audit logs including ciphertext, future envelope encryption or HSM integration.

## Where this surfaced

An ES|QL workstream wiring `EncryptionService` into data-source secret read/write paths initially planned data-source-side HKDF: `HKDF(PEK_secret, projectId, data_source_uuid)`. On reflection, cryptographic-construction conventions belong in the primitive, not in the consumer — so the consumer-side design now uses `EncryptionService.encrypt`/`decrypt` as-shipped. A stable per-data-source identifier (`data_source_uuid`) ships in the consumer regardless of what's decided here, so if the service ever grows a per-consumer derivation hook, the consumer has the natural `identifier` to thread through.

Filing here for the owners to decide whether per-consumer separation is a property worth adding to the primitive, or whether single-PEK-per-project is the intended posture.

## Related

- #145990 — `PrimaryEncryptionKeyService`
- #147418 — `EncryptionService` (this class)
- #149194 — related latent issue on the same service's cache shape
issues.title: EncryptionService: consider per-consumer key derivation to bound PEK blast radius
Address Review Feedback

## What this is about

Follow-ups to #149206, which collapsed the three pre-existing ES|QL SET → request-body plumbing styles into one registry-driven framework. Three items were punted from that PR: one substantive (cluster-level defaults), two polish.

## Items

- [ ] **Cluster-level defaults (`esql.query.<key>.default`)** — a dynamic cluster-wide setting that defines default SET options to prepend to every ES|QL query. Standard precedence applies on top of the existing fold: in-query `SET` > request body > cluster default > setting default. `QuerySettings.resolveSingle` already folds two precedence-ordered sources (body, SET) via per-setting reconcilers; adding a third (cluster default) is one more fold step plus a new input to `resolve(...)` and its single caller in `EsqlSession.analyseAndExecute`. See the "Default SET options" section of the design doc for the user-facing shape.

- [ ] **Lifecycle gate parity for `serverlessOnly`** — `QuerySettings.resolveSingle` gates `snapshotOnly` against body-supplied input via `VerificationException`, and `QuerySettings.validate` gates the same against SET-supplied input via `ParsingException`. The mirror gate for `serverlessOnly` is missing on both paths. `SettingsValidationContext` needs an `isServerless` field, plus the gate inside both methods. Currently dormant — the only `withServerlessOnly` setting (`PROJECT_ROUTING`) is also gated by its `withValidator` check on `crossProjectEnabled`, which catches non-serverless deployments by correlation — but the lifecycle gate should be authoritative.

- [ ] **Nested-path body aliases** — `QuerySettingDef.Builder.withAliasAt(parentPath, name)` accepts arbitrary JSON paths in the data model, but `RequestXContent.declareRegistryAliases` throws at parser-build time for any non-root parent path. Only `withAliasAtRoot()` is wired through today. Wire up nested-path aliases in the parser if/when a setting wants to live under a nested body path.
issues.title: ES|QL: follow-ups to the SET / request-body settings framework

issues.body:
## Background

PR #144937 introduced a live in-flight counter (`clientConnections`) to cap how many concurrent requests ARS probes to stat-less or warming-up nodes across searches. The per-search cap (via `searchCounts`) works correctly. The cross-search cap has a known race.

## The race

The routing decision in `rankNodes` reads `globalCounts` (an unmodifiable view of `clientConnections`) to check whether the probe cap is reached. `clientConnections` is incremented later — inside the `ConnectionCountingHandler` constructor, at transport dispatch time. Between routing and dispatch, concurrent searches all read the same count (e.g. 0), all pass the cap, and all route to the new node before any increment lands.

## Fix direction

Move the increment to happen immediately after the routing decision, before concurrent searches can interleave. The core challenge is the decrement: `decConnectionCount()` is only called from `ConnectionCountingHandler.handleResponse` / `handleException`, which are only reachable if the handler was constructed. If `getConnection()` throws between the routing-time increment and handler construction, the counter leaks — permanently locking the node out of probe traffic.

The fix must decrement in every intermediate failure path between routing and successful handler construction (at minimum the `getConnection()` catch block in `AbstractSearchAsyncAction`).

Making `clientConnections` mutable (rather than introducing a separate reservations map) is preferred to avoid an additional structure with overlapping semantics.
issues.title: Increment ARS in-flight count at routing decision time

issues.body:
## Problem

Kibana now uses three system data streams whose mappings and template lifecycle are managed in Kibana:

- `.workflows-events`
- `.workflows-execution-data-stream-logs`
- `.kibana_change_history`

The Workflows data streams are registered in Elasticsearch via `SystemDataStreamDescriptor` in `KibanaPlugin` ([#145822](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/145822)) and defined in Kibana via `coreDataStreams.registerDataStream()` with TypeScript mappings.

The change history data stream was similarly registered as a `SystemDataStreamDescriptor` in [#154113](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/154113). Its mappings and template lifecycle are also defined in Kibana by `@kbn/change-history` using `@kbn/data-streams`.

`SystemDataStreamDescriptor` currently **requires** a non-null `ComposableIndexTemplate`, and system data stream creation uses that template for new backing indices (`MetadataCreateDataStreamService` uses `systemDataStreamDescriptor.getComposableIndexTemplate()` instead of cluster template lookup).

That forces us to duplicate the full mappings in both repositories:

- Elasticsearch:
  - `modules/kibana/src/main/resources/org/elasticsearch/kibana/workflows-*.json`
  - `modules/kibana/src/main/resources/org/elasticsearch/kibana/kibana-change-history.json`
- Kibana:
  - `workflows_execution_engine` (`registerDataStream` + `WORKFLOWS_*_MANAGED_INDEX_MAPPINGS_VERSION`)
  - `@kbn/change-history` (`mappings.ts` + `DataStreamClient.initialize`)

When the Elasticsearch copy of the Workflows mappings lagged Kibana (for example, `dynamic: true` and minimal `properties` in Elasticsearch versus `dynamic: false` and the full schema in Kibana), new backing indices got **wrong mappings** even though Kibana believed it owned the schema. We patched Elasticsearch to match Kibana in commit `79436ab`, but the dual-definition problem remains.

[#154113](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/154113) extends the same ownership problem to `.kibana_change_history`: registering it correctly as a system data stream required copying its Kibana-owned template and mappings into Elasticsearch. The PR discussion also identified the clash between the descriptor-owned template and Kibana's existing template lifecycle management. Moving that lifecycle entirely into Elasticsearch would still leave cross-repository mapping changes for a Kibana-only writer.

## Why we need Elasticsearch registration

The descriptors are needed so these are proper **system data streams**, rather than data streams incidentally covered by broad system **index** patterns:

- The Workflows streams were covered by `.workflows-*` before [#145822](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/145822).
- `.kibana_change_history` is covered directly as a `SystemDataStreamDescriptor` since [#154113](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/154113).

Registration preserves required cluster behavior:

- DLM / restricted system resource handling ([#143958](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/143958))
- Product origin / security
- Hidden indices, snapshots, and feature state

## Proposed direction

**Split responsibilities:**

| Layer | Owns |
|-------|------|
| Elasticsearch | System data stream status (`SystemDataStreamDescriptor`): security, DLM, hidden, product origin, etc. |
| Kibana | Mappings, composable index template, `managed_index_mappings_version`, and rollover ([#269514](https://github.com/elastic/kibana/pull/269514)) |

We should **not** maintain two mapping copies long term. Unlike Fleet (multiple stack readers/writers), these Kibana-only system data streams do not benefit from shipping canonical mappings in Elasticsearch.

## Request

Support registering a `SystemDataStreamDescriptor` that marks a data stream as **system** without Elasticsearch applying an authoritative composable template body for **mappings**. Backing-index creation should use cluster templates installed by Kibana (`registerDataStream` / `@kbn/data-streams`), while Elasticsearch enforces system metadata and protections from [#145822](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/145822) and [#154113](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/154113).

Possible approaches (for the team to choose):

1. Optional / absent composable template on the descriptor; fall back to `lookupTemplateForDataStream` for mappings when a cluster template exists.
2. Descriptor allows settings/lifecycle-only template; mappings come exclusively from cluster-visible templates.
3. Another pattern you recommend for single-writer, Kibana-registered system data streams.

## Questions

1. Do DLM, security, restricted indices, and snapshot behavior depend on the descriptor-owned template **body**, or only on the data stream being registered as system?
2. Can a placeholder descriptor template defer mappings to a higher-priority cluster composable template?
3. Are other products likely to hit this with Kibana-only system data streams?

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `.workflows-events`, `.workflows-execution-data-stream-logs`, and `.kibana_change_history` remain registered as system data streams.
- [ ] Cluster behavior from [#145822](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/145822) and [#154113](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/154113) is preserved (DLM, product origin, security, hidden indices, and snapshots).
- [ ] New backing indices use Kibana-owned mappings only.
- [ ] Elasticsearch JSON mapping files in `KibanaPlugin` can be removed or reduced to non-mapping metadata.
issues.title: Allow `SystemDataStreamDescriptor` without owning index mappings
Follow up release-test Gradle convention cleanup (CI/build)

issues.body:
Follow-up from #148678 (Nick's inline comment on `DenseVectorArithmeticOperation.java:105`).

`DenseVectorArithmeticOperation` and its subclasses (`Add`, `Sub`, `Mul`, `Div`) currently take 8+ individual evaluator/factory parameters in their constructors — one per `(type, const|var)` pair. The ctor surface is wide and the same set of evaluators gets repeated at every construction site.

Proposal: introduce an `Evaluators` record bundling the per-type evaluators (`ints`, `longs`, `ulongs`, `doubles`, `denseVectors`, `intsConst`, `longsConst`, `doublesConst`), declare one `static final Evaluators` per operator, and pass that single argument through the ctor instead of the long list.

### Affected files (approx)

- New: `Evaluators` record in `x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/expression/predicate/operator/arithmetic/`
- `DenseVectorArithmeticOperation`, `DateTimeArithmeticOperation` — ctor refactor
- `Add`, `Sub`, `Mul`, `Div` — declare and pass `Evaluators` constant
- Corresponding tests

### Considerations

- `DenseVectorArithmeticOperation` has `StreamInput` ctors — wire-format compatibility needs checking. If the wire format is affected, this needs a transport version bump + BWC reads.
- Orthogonal to JIT-folding work in #148678; deliberately scoped out of that PR.
issues.title: Consolidate arithmetic operator ctor surface via an `Evaluators` bundle

issues.body:
Follow-up from #148678. `JitConstantSpinner` uses ASM 9.9 for runtime bytecode emission because `java.lang.classfile` (JEP 484) is only available from JDK 24, and ES still supports JDK 21 as the runtime minimum. The spinner already abstracts the emit path through a `SpunClassEmitter` interface so the swap is mechanical.

When the JDK minimum bumps to 24+, replace `AsmSpunClassEmitter` with a `ClassFileApiSpunClassEmitter` implementation that uses `java.lang.classfile`. Drop the `org.ow2.asm:asm` dependency from `esql/compute` if nothing else needs it.

Suggested by @nik9000.
issues.title: Migrate `JitConstantSpinner` codegen from ASM to `java.lang.classfile` when JDK minimum bumps to 24+

issues.body:
When a shard times out during a search (SearchTimeoutException), the coordinator retries the request on the next available replica copy of that shard. If partial results are not allowed (`allow_partial_search_results=false`), this retry happens transparently before the timeout is surfaced to the user.

The issue was initially raised by @javanna  in [#72349](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/72349).

> "when a shard times out, and partial results are not allowed, that timeout error is sent back to the coord node which will retry on another copy. That feels like the wrong behaviour, in that it defeats the purpose of providing a search timeout."

A related fix (#149506) stopped retrying `BAD_REQUEST` errors on replicas. `SearchTimeoutException` was intentionally left out of that fix.

When a shard fails with `SearchTimeoutException`, the coordinator should treat it as a terminal failure for that shard group and not attempt any replica. The timeout should be surfaced to the user immediately, consistent with the intent of the `search.timeout` parameter.
issues.title: Replica retry on SearchTimeoutException ignores the intent of search.timeout

issues.body:
### Description

Currently `IngestService` in unconditionally created on every node and added as a cluster state applier https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/15a693228cfdaa56ffa688f6f63de5933a368aa1/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/node/NodeService.java#L109

`IngestService` however is not free and it was observed that it can consume decent amount of memory in internal `pipelines` map. This is problematic for tiebreaker nodes (https://www.elastic.co/docs/deploy-manage/production-guidance/availability-and-resilience/resilience-in-small-clusters#high-availability-cluster-design-two-nodes-plus) or any other configurations that don't serve any traffic but still have `IngestService` consuming memory. 

We should consider deactivating `IngestService` if a node doesn't have `ingest` role. Some actions and plugins depend on `IngestService` and need to be considered: `TransportDeleteEnrichPolicyAction`, `IngestIpLocationPlugin`, possibly others.
issues.title: Consider not running `IngestService` on nodes that don't have `ingest` role

issues.body:
### Description

**Problem**
Several customers want KQL searches to be case-insensitive in Kibana. To address this, Kibana is adding a per-space Advanced Setting that opts a space into case-insensitive KQL: elastic/kibana-team#3389.

However, ES|QL's kql() function currently has no awareness of this setting. If a user opts in, Kibana KQL and ES|QL KQL will silently return different results for the same query string — which is confusing and likely to generate support requests.

A related precedent: 
#135772 was filed (and fixed) precisely because ES|QL kql() defaulted to case-insensitive behavior while Kibana KQL was case-sensitive. We worked hard to align the two — we should maintain that alignment as Kibana's behavior evolves.

**Example**
Assume a space has case-insensitive KQL enabled and an index contains:

```
{ "user": "Student01" }
{ "user": "student01" }
```
In Kibana Discover (KQL mode):

`user: "student01"`
→ Returns both documents (case-insensitive setting is active).

In ES|QL (same space):

`FROM my-index | WHERE kql("user: \"student01\"")`
→ Returns only student01 (setting is not respected).

A user switching between Discover and an ES|QL-based lens or rule in the same space would see inconsistent results with no explanation.

**Request**
When a space opts into case-insensitive KQL, kql() in ES|QL queries run in that space should respect the setting and apply case-insensitive matching consistently. This ensures KQL behaves uniformly regardless of which surface the user is working in.
issues.title: Allow ES|QL KQL to be case-insensitive by default via a space setting

issues.body:
## What

Add an anonymized form of the original ES|QL query text as a fifth artifact in the failure-path anonymized log emitted by `EsqlSession` (PR #149633). Lex the query string via `EsqlBaseLexer` and rewrite identifier / literal tokens using the same column / index / literal token maps the plan rewrite builds.

## Why

PR #149633 logs four anonymized artifacts on `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` failures: schema, parsed plan, optimized plan, physical plan. The original query text is intentionally not in that set today because the only viable rewrite mechanism — text-level regex substitution against the token maps — is fragile around:

- backtick-quoted identifiers (`` `weird name with spaces` ``)
- ES|QL triple-quoted strings (`"""multi\nline"""`)
- escape sequences inside double-quoted strings
- numeric literals that happen to overlap with substrings already substituted

A regex pass that handles all of the above accumulates corner cases and silent failures. The right mechanism is the ES|QL grammar itself.

The query text is the form support engineers reach for first during incident triage. Today they have the four plan artifacts and have to reconstruct the original shape mentally. A clean anonymized query short-circuits that step.

## Proposed shape

Use `EsqlBaseLexer` (the ANTLR-generated lexer that the parser already runs on every query) to tokenize the original text. Walk the token stream and rewrite by token type:

- `IDENTIFIER`, `QUOTED_IDENTIFIER` → strip quotes if present; look up in the column-token map (then fall back to index-token map for the FROM-position case). Emit the anonymized token.
- `STRING` (single-double-quote and triple-double-quote both handled by the lexer) → look up the BytesRef content in the literal map; if no match — typical of LIKE patterns where the optimizer kept only the prefix, or dates folded to epoch — emit a `"<STRING>"` placeholder.
- `INTEGER_LITERAL`, `DECIMAL_LITERAL` → literal-token map; emit typed placeholder (same shape as the plan-side `2[LONG]` / `0.1[DOUBLE]`).
- Keywords, operators, whitespace, parameters (`?foo`) — pass through unchanged.

Reconstruct the text from the token stream with whitespace preserved (ANTLR keeps offsets). Result: a syntactically valid ES|QL string with every customer identifier and literal replaced, readable at a glance during triage. The plan-side maps are populated from the same submission so the query and plan artifacts cross-reference consistently — `col_dfa4ac7d` in the query is the same field as `col_dfa4ac7d` in the plan.

Estimated ~200 LOC for the lexer pass + dispatch, plus matching tests.

## Tests

Adversarial coverage:

- Identifier shapes: bare, backtick-quoted with spaces / unicode / dots.
- String literal shapes: single-double-quoted, triple-double-quoted, embedded escape sequences, embedded quotes.
- Numeric literals: integer overflow boundary, decimal, scientific notation.
- Named query parameters (`?param_name`) — should pass through unchanged.
- Malformed queries that fail at parse — the lexer should still produce tokens up to the failure point.
- Determinism: same query / cluster UUID → byte-identical anonymized output across runs and threads.

## Transition

1. Add the new artifact to the existing `AnonymizedPlans` record (five fields → six).
2. Plumb the raw query text from `EsqlQueryRequest.query()` through to the anonymizer (it's already accessible at the `EsqlSession.execute()` entry; just needs to flow into `logAnonymizedPlans` and the anonymize call).
3. Implement the lexer pass.
4. Update the PR body example shape to add a `QUERY:` section.
5. The default-safe refactor (#149693) is orthogonal — that one is about plan-node rendering; this one is about textual rendering of the original input.

## Related

- PR #149633 — the failure-path anonymized log this issue extends.
- Issue #149693 — default-safe `Node.anonymize()` refactor (orthogonal architectural concern).
issues.title: ESQL: anonymized query text via ANTLR-lexer rewrite

issues.body:
### Description

In this line:

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/ff62792a0600bb936f2eb13f3bbc3e496bace797/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/action/admin/indices/rollover/TransportRolloverAction.java#L629

We wait for the allocator after rollover. In some cases, however, it would be nice for the rollover to proceed regardless so as to not be blocking. For example, when ILM invokes rollover, because ILM will immediately turn around and wait for the index to be allocated in a separate step.

ILM already passes `setWaitForActiveShards(ActiveShardCount.NONE)` to the rollover request, so ideally the rollover API would either automatically skip the waiting if the shard count were set to `NONE`, or a new internal-only option could be introduced that would disable waiting for the allocator convergence, of which ILM could then make use.
issues.title: Add a way to disable waiting for allocator convergence on rollover

issues.body:
### Description

Time series data streams (TSDS) index documents based on their `@timestamp` and not the ingestion time because their value depends on this `@timestamp`.

A user can configure lifecycle actions such as downsampling or searchable snapshots that convert indices to read-only. As a consequence, documents with `@timestamp`s that fall within these indices will be rejected. Effectively, a TSDS has a write window within which it should be able to accept documents that fall within this window.

This is not fully supported yet, because new TSDS cannot only go back till [`index.look_back_time`](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/index-settings/time-series), we are working on improving this, but before we do that we need a way to retrieve the write window of a TSDS regardless if the backing indices exist or not.

**Implementation notes:**

To define the write-window we need to:

1. Determine which lifecycle feature is currently managing this data stream (ILM or data stream lifecycle).
2. Determine how does each feature influence the write window, for example, which read-only actions in ILM.
~3. Expose it via the `DataStream` or something more appropriate.~
issues.title: [TSDB++] Define the eligible write window of TSDS

issues.body:
## The problem 

The way [Time Series Data Streams (TSDS)](https://www.elastic.co/docs/manage-data/data-store/data-streams/time-series-data-stream-tsds) work today is that after creating the initial index, users can not load historical data at any point in time, only data going forward from the start time that index supports.

The reason for that is that Time Series Data Streams (TSDS) use time bound backing indices that accept documents based on their timestamp values. A time bound index has a start and end time and accepts documents whose @timestamp belongs to that timeframe, anything else gets rejected. When you add a document to a TSDS, Elasticsearch adds the document to the appropriate backing index based on its @timestamp value.

As time passes, new time bound indexes are added to cover new time intervals. So, all time intervals are supported after the creation of a TSDS, but no data can be added before the initial start time as there is no way to add time bound indexes in the past.

This blocks non greenfield Elasticsearch users with existing time series data that want to migrate to using Elasticsearch TSDS. The most common use case is to start a new index with recent data, to either test how TSDS work or just adopt the feature, and start backfilling historical data at a later point or in the background.

## Proposed solution

### For green field use-cases
The proposed solution enables a TSDB data stream to **lazily create backing indices** in the past of predefined duration, potentially configurable via a cluster setting. The creation of the backing indices is triggered only when a document with a past `@timestamp` arrives and does not match any of the current backing indices while the `@timestamp` falls within the **eligible write window**. 

The **eligible write window** is defined by the lifecycle feature managing a TSDB, specifically, either by the time condition of the first read-only action or the retention. For example, if TSDB should be downsampled after 7 days, this means that we will create new backing indices only for documents whose `@timestamp` falls within now till 7 days ago.

### For historical data of longer periods
Considering the above limitation, we want to offer an alternative path for users who want to load historical data further than the write window. For them, we suggest the following steps:

- Scale their target indexing tier to hold the whole amount of their historical data next to their current ingestion.
- Create a new TSDS, let's call it `historical-ds` using a similar index template as the original one, potentially adjust shards if deemed necessary.
- Start indexing to that `historical-ds` only the historical data and keep indexing current data to the original one.
- When finished, enable DLM if it's not enabled and add any downsampling, frozen or retention configurations.
- Remember to delete the `historical-ds` when retention the data "expires".

#### Caveats

This scenario has a few caveats:

- Queries need to be adjusted to include both original & historical data streams, or the user needs to define a data stream alias.
- When DLM is enabled on a data stream with a lot of data it can trigger a large amount of heavy operations that can overwhelm the master. This is already an issue, but with this proposal we make it more prominent. We would like to add a throttling mechanism to "pace" at downsampling and searchable snapshot operation per data stream.
- This scenario is supported by **DLM only**. We cannot support such throttling in ILM. The user can manually add policies per index if they wish to, but we will not provide any native ILM throttling mechanism.

## Planned work

- [x] Lazily create backing indices:
- [x] (i) Create the transport action that can create new backing indices. (https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/150878)
- [x] Performance test timestamp retrieval in the transport action (@jbaiera )
        - Detection in the transport bulk actions appears to cause no performance regression, so we are moving forward.
- [ ] (ii) Detect when backing indices need to be created (https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/152716). 
- [x] Implement flood gates in DLM to protect a cluster from queuing up a large amount of downsampling and frozen actions per data stream. (https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/150624)
- [ ] Add telemetry
- [ ] Update docs (https://github.com/elastic/docs-content/issues/7252)

issues.body:
### Description

A continuous transform's `sync.time.delay` is a single steady-state watermark: every checkpoint's upper time bound is `now - delay`. The delay has to be conservative enough to tolerate ingest/refresh lag in the source, so it is typically tens of seconds (Kibana SLO transforms use `65s`, for example).

That single value also governs the **very first** checkpoint(s). When a transform starts (or is reset) and there is already data present — or data that lands moments after start — that data is not picked up until it has aged past the full steady-state `delay`. For a single transform that is a one-time delay; for **chained** transforms it compounds.

#### Concrete motivation: Kibana SLO summary latency

Kibana SLOs are two chained continuous transforms: a *rollup* transform writes SLI documents, and a *summary* transform reads those SLI documents. Both use `delay: 65s`. On SLO creation:

1. The summary transform's first checkpoint fires immediately, before the rollup has written any SLI data, so it is empty.
2. The SLI data then lands a few seconds later.
3. Because every subsequent checkpoint uses the steady-state `65s` delay, the just-written SLI data is not summarized until it ages past the `65s` watermark.

The observed result is that the **first SLO summary document appears ~60–120s after the SLO is created**, which shows up as a visible lag in the SLO UI right after creation.

### Proposed enhancement

Add an optional `initial_delay` to `sync.time`:

```json
"sync": {
  "time": {
    "field": "event.ingested",
    "delay": "65s",
    "initial_delay": "1s"
  }
}
```

Semantics:

- `initial_delay` is the reduced delay applied while the transform is still in its **initial catch-up phase** — i.e. until it has processed its first document. Once the transform has processed data it reverts to the steady-state `delay`.
- Keying off "has processed data" rather than literally "checkpoint #1" matters for chained transforms: the source data often lands shortly *after* the downstream transform's first (empty) checkpoint, so a checkpoint-#1-only rule would revert to the steady-state delay before any data was ever seen.
- Defaults to `delay` when omitted, so existing transforms are completely unchanged. Must be `<= delay`.

### Scope / expected impact

This bounds the first-data latency by the transform's `frequency` instead of by `delay + frequency`. For the Kibana SLO summary transform (`frequency: 1m`) a local end-to-end test showed the first summary document dropping from **~122s to ~62s** with no orchestration changes — purely by setting `initial_delay`. Reaching seconds-level latency additionally requires the downstream transform to be *triggered* promptly after the upstream writes (e.g. `_schedule_now` or a shorter `frequency`); that is out of scope here.

### Notes

- Backwards compatible on the wire (guarded by a new transport version) and in the persisted config (`initial_delay` is only serialized to XContent when it differs from `delay`).
- A PR implementing this will follow.
issues.title: Transform: add an initial-delay override to time `sync` to cut first-data latency for continuous transforms

If a node leaves the cluster while this force-merge is in progress then shards of the temporary index may become unassigned, which is reported by the `GET _health_report` API as a problem needing immediate attention. issues.body:
For whatever reason, we once decided to implement `TO_RADIANS` and `TO_DEGREES` via `AbstractConvertFunction` and treat it the very same as other convert functions, like `TO_DOUBLE` and `TO_KEYWORD`.

This is very weird, because they don't actually change the type. They also don't follow other implicit invariants of type conversion functions:
- Double-to-double conversions are not noops.
- They are not idempotent; `to_radians(to_radians(foo))` is different from `to_radians(foo)`.

These should just be treated as normal math functions. Type conversion functions are treated especially with respect to union types (and maybe other places); e.g. you can not pass an integer/double union type to `sqrt`, but you can pass it to `to_radians`. The SETting `unmapped_fields="load"` makes these functions more relevant because https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/148800 introduces auto-casting for partially unmapped non-keyword fields, where type conversion functions _again_ play a role.

Let's update our documentation and have these functions inherit from a different base class.

This is at least mildly breaking because functions union types won't be able to be used in `to_radians` and `to_degrees` anymore. We'll need to check for other side effects, too.
issues.title: ESQL: TO_RADIANS and TO_DEGREES shouldn't be considered type conversion functions

issues.body:
## What this is about
Independent subplans that go through the re-planning execution loop — `IN`-subquery (`SemiJoin`/`AntiJoin`/`LeftSemiJoin`) and `INLINE STATS` (`InlineJoin`) — execute strictly one at a time, even when they have no data dependency on each other.

## Current behaviour
`EsqlSession.executeSubPlans` drives a loop: `findFirstSubPlanJoin` returns the *first* un-executed `SemiJoin`/`InlineJoin`, that subplan is executed to completion, its result is gathered into a coordinator `LocalRelation`, `inlineData` rewrites the plan, and only then does the loop look for the next subplan. So `FROM t | WHERE x IN (subA) AND y IN (subB)` is **two sequential coordinator round-trips**; N independent IN-subqueries are N round-trips in series.

## Why it matters
Each round-trip is a full distributed execution plus a coordinator gather. For multiple independent subqueries the latencies add rather than overlap, with no correctness reason — the subplans are independent.

## What already exists
`ComputeService.SubPlansExecutor` already runs **FORK and FROM-subquery** branches in parallel batches, controlled by the `BRANCH_PARALLEL_DEGREE` pragma (default 2) — #144687. That mechanism covers exchange-sink branches inside a single physical plan; it does **not** cover the `SemiJoin`/`InlineJoin` re-planning loop, which is the gap here.

## Proposed direction
Batch/parallelize execution of *independent* re-planning subplans (no result feeds another), reusing the `BRANCH_PARALLEL_DEGREE` budget so concurrent coordinator memory stays bounded — these subplans materialize their results into coordinator `LocalRelation`s, so heap pressure is the constraint, same as the existing batched path.

## Out of scope
- Subplans with a data dependency (one subquery's result feeds another, e.g. a view nested inside an IN-subquery) must stay ordered.
- Correlated subqueries (unsupported regardless).

Related: #144687 (parallel FORK/FROM-subquery branches), #139197 (WHERE IN / NOT IN subquery meta).
issues.title: [ES|QL] Independent re-planning subplans (IN subquery, INLINE STATS) execute sequentially — run them concurrently

issues.body:
### Description

Data stream lifecycle (DLM) operates on the whole data stream. This means that if a user has a data stream that holds data for the last 6 months and adds any operations that needs to be executed after 7 days, then this operation will be applied to all the eligible indices older than 7 days at the next run.

If this operation is deleting 5+ months worth of data is not a problem, but if this operation is downsampling, this can have side-effects, downsampling is heavier and could overwhelm the master with persistent task updates. If the cluster is scaled properly it will eventually recover.

For this reasons, we want to add a flood gate mechanism so the lifecycle of a single data stream will not overload the cluster.

- [x] Expose actively downsampled indices (https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/150855)
- [ ] Add downsampling flood gate (https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/150802)

Note: this is issue is less probable with ILM because when a policy is changed on the data stream level it will affect new indices, unless specifically applied to all backing indices.
issues.title: Introduce flood gates for downsampling in DLM

issues.body:
## What this is about

`INLINE STATS <agg> BY <key>` is a window aggregation: it preserves rows and attaches a group's aggregate back onto each input row. When the grouping key is **multivalued**, a row belongs to several groups at once, so the aggregates of *several* groups must land on *one* row.

Today there is exactly one behavior for that — **`concat`**: flatten the groups' results into a single multivalue. It's genuinely useful for some cases and a poor fit for others, and it's silent and non-optional. This issue proposes adding a second behavior — **`aggregate`**, which combines the groups as a real aggregation — and letting the user choose between them. Surfaced by #150491.

## Example dataset

`FROM catalog | KEEP product, price, category`:

| product | price | category |
|---|---|---|
| Running Shoes | 90 | `Shoes` |
| Leather Boots | 150 | `Shoes` |
| Canvas Sneakers | 60 | `Shoes` |
| Camping Tent | 200 | `Outdoor` |
| Sleeping Bag | 80 | `Outdoor` |
| Trail Running Shoes | 120 | `[Shoes, Outdoor]` |

`Trail Running Shoes` is cross-listed in two categories — the only multivalued-key row, and the only row whose output differs between the two behaviors.

## Today's behavior: `concat`

`concat` keeps **each matched group's result**, lined up with the groups the row belongs to.

**Where it's good.** For `SUM(price)`, the `[Shoes, Outdoor]` row's `[420, 400]` reads directly as *"420 within Shoes, 400 within Outdoor"* — a real per-category breakdown of the aggregate across this row's categories, exactly the detail a single pooled number would discard. For scalar aggregates (`SUM`, `COUNT`, `AVG`) it's a clean, useful parallel array.

**Where it isn't.**

- *Scalars silently stop being scalars.* `SUM(price)` → `[420, 400]` when the user wrote `SUM` and expected one number — and the entries are unlabeled, so which is `Shoes` and which is `Outdoor` is positional guesswork.
- *Multivalue-producing aggregates collapse incoherently.* `TOP(price, 2)` → `[150, 120, 200, 120]` — four values for a top-2, with a duplicate, and the per-group boundary gone (you can't tell `Shoes`' top-2 from `Outdoor`'s). `VALUES(price)` concatenates the groups' sets and loses distinctness — contradicting its documented *unique (deduplicated)* contract.
- *Easy to miss.* Single-valued-key rows look correct, so the anomaly surfaces only on the subset of rows whose key is multivalued.

So `concat` is a legitimate behavior that simply isn't always what you want — and today it's the only option.

## Why it happens

INLINE STATS rewrites (`InlineStats.surrogate`) to an `InlineJoin` — a LEFT join, on the grouping key, over a `STATS … BY key`. `STATS` **unrolls** a multivalued key: a doc tagged `[Shoes, Outdoor]` contributes to both groups (`BlockHash`), and the grouped result is keyed by single scalar values. The row-preserving join then matches the original (still multivalued) row against both group rows and, with only a flat multivalue available as a container, **concatenates** their values (`Block.lookup`). `STATS` unrolls and stops there; INLINE STATS unrolls *and* must re-roll — and that re-roll is the part with no defined behavior.

## Proposal

Keep `concat` and add `aggregate`; let the user choose. `concat` glues each group's results together. `aggregate` combines them into the aggregate's own value, using its existing combine logic: `SUM` → the summed total, `TOP(x, 2)` → the top-2 of the union, `VALUES` → the deduped union, `SPARKLINE` → one combined sparkline. The result is a single, well-formed value — sometimes a scalar (`SUM`/`COUNT`/`AVG`), sometimes a multivalue (`TOP`, `VALUES`, `SPARKLINE`).

### Syntax

The mode is selected per-command. One option, following ES|QL's existing `WITH { … }` command-options form:

```esql
INLINE STATS TOP(price, 2) BY category WITH { "mv_rollup": "aggregate" }
```

`"concat"` is the current behavior, `"aggregate"` the new one. `concat` stays the default for now; `aggregate` is opt-in; the default can be revisited before GA.

### Semantics

For the `[Shoes, Outdoor]` row (the only multivalued-key row):

| query | before (`concat`) | after (`aggregate`) |
|---|---|---|
| `SUM(price)` | `[420, 400]` | `820` |
| `COUNT(*)` | `[4, 3]` | `7` |
| `AVG(price)` | `[105, 133.33]` | `117.14` |
| `TOP(price, 2)` | `[150, 120, 200, 120]` | `[200, 150]` |
| `VALUES(price)` | `[90, 150, 60, 120, 200, 80, 120]` | `[90, 150, 60, 120, 200, 80]` |

`concat` lays each group's result side by side; `aggregate` combines them with the aggregate's own logic — sum the sums, re-take the top-2, dedup the values, merge the sparkline buckets. The result is one value (scalar or multivalue), never a concatenation. Under `aggregate`, a doc in N groups counts once per group, so SUM/COUNT/AVG pool across the row's categories (matching how plain STATS already attributes a multivalued doc); per-document de-duplication is out of scope.

### Implementation

`aggregate` is a second aggregation grouped by output-row identity, reusing existing machinery — **no new per-aggregate code**. The combiner (`addIntermediateInput`), the partial-state layout (`intermediateStateDesc`), and `ToPartial`/`FromPartial` already exist for distributed aggregation, and `ReplaceSparklineAggregate` already uses the `ToPartial` → `FromPartial` two-phase pattern.

1. Inner aggregation emits **partial** state (`ToPartial`, a `partial_agg` composite block) instead of the finalized value — FINAL is deferred past the join.
2. The join carries the `partial_agg` column, multi-collecting one partial per matched group. This requires **implementing `CompositeBlock.lookup`**, currently a stub that throws (`// TODO: support this`) — the main net-new compute-layer work.
3. The re-roll combines the row's collected partials (`addIntermediateInput`) and finalizes (`FromPartial` → `evaluateFinal`), grouped by a synthetic per-row ordinal.

## Scope

- Local to INLINE STATS (the `InlineJoin` roll-up); `STATS`'s unroll is unchanged.
- No nested-array support required; a breakdown that keeps per-group boundaries (`[[150,120],[200,120]]`) would need a nested type and is a separate effort.
- Snapshot-only, so no backward-compatibility constraint.
issues.title: [ES|QL] INLINE STATS: add an aggregate roll-up for multivalued grouping keys (alongside today's concat)

### Description

**Summary**

When creating an external inference endpoint for Google Vertex AI in Elastic Serverless Observability (or via the Inference API), the GCP Region field is mandatory and directly constructs the service URL as https://{region}-aiplatform.googleapis.com. There is no way to specify or fall back to the global endpoint (https://aiplatform.googleapis.com), which is valid and supported by Google.

**Steps to Reproduce**

In Elastic Serverless / Kibana, navigate to Admin and Settings  → External Inference → Add endpoint.
Select Google Vertex AI as the provider.
Observe that the GCP Region field is required — it cannot be left blank or set to global.
Any value entered is interpolated into the URL: https://<region>-aiplatform.googleapis.com.

**Expected Behavior**

The GCP Region field should either:

Accept an empty / blank value that resolves to the global endpoint https://aiplatform.googleapis.com, or
Expose a "global" option (or equivalent) that explicitly targets that endpoint.

**Actual Behavior**

The GCP Region field is required with no global option. Leaving it blank causes a validation error; entering any string produces a regional URL, making the global endpoint unreachable.

**Why This Matters**

Google's global endpoint is the recommended default for many Vertex AI workloads (especially for globally-deployed models). We currently can't use global endpoint of Elastic's native Vertex AI inference integration.

**Workaround (if any)**

None currently known via the UI or standard API payload.
issues.title: [Inference Endpoint] Google Vertex AI: Cannot use global endpoint (aiplatform.googleapis.com) — GCP region field is mandatory with no "global" option

```json
PUT _cluster/settings
{
  "persistent": {
    "cluster.routing.allocation.enable": "none"
  }
}
```

Disabling shard allocation is a legitimate maintenance operation, but if left enabled accidentally it can lead to unassigned shards and a red cluster following node failures or restarts.

Today, Elasticsearch accepts this change without indicating the operational risk associated with it.

### Proposed Solution

When users modify particularly impactful cluster settings, Elasticsearch should return an additional warning in the API response indicating the potential consequences of the change.

Example:

```json
{
  "acknowledged": true,
  "warnings": [
    "cluster.routing.allocation.enable=none disables shard allocation. Leaving this setting enabled may result in unassigned shards and cluster health degradation."
  ]
}
```

Potential candidates include:

* cluster.routing.allocation.enable
* cluster.routing.rebalance.enable
* disk allocation threshold settings
* destructive operation settings
* other settings identified as high-risk by the Elasticsearch team

### Benefits

* Reduces operational mistakes.
* Provides immediate feedback at the moment the change is made.
* Helps administrators understand the impact of advanced settings.
* May prevent prolonged outages caused by forgotten maintenance settings.

The key argument is that Elasticsearch already knows the semantics of the setting. If it knows that `cluster.routing.allocation.enable=none` is typically a temporary maintenance action, it can proactively tell the user "this is dangerous if left enabled" instead of silently accepting the change. That's harder for users to implement themselves and makes a stronger feature request.
issues.title: Provide risk-aware warnings when modifying critical cluster settings.

issues.body:
### Description

## Summary

We are requesting the ability to selectively include indices in a snapshot based on their current ILM phase or data tier (e.g., warm, cold), rather than snapshotting all indices regardless of their lifecycle state.

## Current Behavior

Snapshot Lifecycle Management (SLM) policies currently support index filtering only via index name patterns (glob expressions) in the `indices` configuration field. There is no built-in mechanism to filter indices based on their ILM phase or the data tier they currently reside on.

## Problem

In clusters with a tiered architecture (hot → warm → cold) and active ILM policies, all indices — including those on hot nodes with ongoing write activity — are included in every scheduled snapshot.

This causes significant unnecessary load on the I/O subsystem of hot nodes during snapshot creation, precisely when those nodes are under the highest write pressure.

The fundamental issue is that indices on hot nodes are continuously being written to, making them the least suitable candidates for snapshotting from both a performance and consistency standpoint. Indices on warm and cold tiers, by contrast, are immutable or near-immutable and are the natural targets for long-term snapshot coverage.

## Why Existing Workarounds Are Insufficient

In our environment, each data source has its own dedicated SLM policy. The `indices` pattern in each policy is scoped to that source's indices only. This is intentional — it provides isolation and per-source snapshot control.

However, the `indices` field supports only name-based glob patterns. There is no way to express "indices of this source that are currently in the warm or cold phase." To achieve tier-based filtering today, one would need to:

- Continuously track which specific indices of each source have transitioned to warm or cold
- Update every affected SLM policy accordingly

Given the number of independent data sources and the dynamic nature of index lifecycles, this is technically prohibitive to automate reliably and completely impossible to maintain manually at scale.

## Desired Outcome

We would like a way to configure an SLM policy so that only indices meeting certain lifecycle or tier criteria are included in the snapshot — automatically, without manual intervention, and in a way that remains correct as indices transition through their lifecycle phases.

The exact mechanism for achieving this is left to the discretion of the development team. We recognize that this may involve changes to SLM, ILM, or the interaction between both systems.

## Use Case

- Cluster with hot/warm/cold tier architecture
- ILM policies managing index lifecycle across all tiers
- High write throughput on hot nodes
- Snapshots scheduled via SLM policies
- Goal: snapshot only warm and cold indices to avoid I/O contention on hot nodes during peak write activity

## Related

This improvement would naturally complement the existing ILM → SLM integration, where ILM already uses snapshot state as a condition before index deletion (`min_snapshot_age`). Extending this relationship in the opposite direction — allowing SLM to be aware of ILM state — would make the two systems more cohesive.

A related request was previously raised in [#76899](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/76899), where the need to exclude actively written indices from snapshots was described in a different context (per-index setting to exclude from all snapshots). Both requests share the same underlying motivation: reducing unnecessary I/O load on active nodes and providing more granular control over snapshot scope. Our request extends that idea to the SLM policy level, enabling lifecycle-aware snapshot targeting without per-index manual configuration.
issues.title: [Feature Request] SLM: Add ability to filter indices by ILM phase or data tier when creating snapshots

```
FROM main_index
| LOOKUP JOIN lookup_index ON lookup_key
| WHERE lookup_field == "foo" 
| KEEP main_idx_field 
| SORT main_idx_field DESC 
| LIMIT 25
```

This query needs to run the JOIN on the full main index before performing the filter and then the sort. This can be too expensive for high cardinality indices.

Possible solutions:
1. replace the JOIN with a subquery

```
FROM main_index
| WHERE lookup_key IN
  ( FROM lookup_index
    | WHERE lookup_field == "foo" 
    | KEEP lookup_key
  )
| KEEP main_idx_field 
| SORT main_idx_field DESC 
| LIMIT 25
```

This is feasible if the cardinality of the subquery result is small enough, but in the general case we still have some limitations

2. push down SORT past JOIN, someway related to https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/121884

### Description

  ## Problem
  `_msearch` batches transport/parsing overhead, but each sub-search is still executed independently.
  For vector search workloads (many similar queries in one request), this may miss opportunities for
  better CPU/cache efficiency and higher throughput.
  ## Motivation
  Today, vector search queries in `_msearch` are not fused at Lucene execution level. We already have
  internal batching patterns in search execution (e.g., per-node batched query phase), but there is no
  explicit multi-query vector execution mode that attempts to reuse work across queries.
  ## Proposal (exploratory)
  Investigate an optional batched vector-query execution path for groups of compatible queries in a
  single request, with strict result equivalence to independent execution.
  Potential scope:
  - only for compatible query groups (same field, similarity, filter shape, k/num_candidates bounds)
  - coordinator groups eligible queries and sends them as a batch to data nodes
  - data-node execution may use tighter loops / shared memory access patterns where possible
  - fallback to current per-query execution for unsupported cases
  ## Open questions
  - For HNSW ANN traversal, where can real reuse be obtained without harming latency?
  - Should this target exact/brute-force and rerank stages first, before ANN traversal?
  - What batching controls are needed (`max_batched_queries`, optional wait window, per-node limits)?
  - How should this interact with `max_concurrent_searches` and `max_concurrent_shard_requests`?
  ## Related
  - #112306 (batched query phase per data node)
  - #33072 (`_msearch` concurrency/load controls)
  - #4227 (`_search`/`_msearch` consistency)

### Description

With the recent addition of https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/147964 and https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/150175, serverless now handles the prefetch signal so that a local file cache miss triggers a blob cache load from the remote store. That means that we will likely see significant benefit to increasing the `PrefetchingCentroidIterator` depth, which is hard coded to 1 currently.

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/219087f9b4c6d6a81a121892d51fa8feb91e30c6/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/index/codec/vectors/diskbbq/next/ESNextDiskBBQVectorsReader.java#L79-L83

I see two solutions:

Short term: use some runtime heuristics to prefetch dynamically based on the maximum number of vectors we want to compare and the average number of vectors we see in the current window of partitions. This approach likely gets us from `n` prefetch batches to `2` batches, where we get the first set, figure out how many vectors we can expect each partition to contribute, and then fetch that many partitions to fill the local cache. Also, there might be a way to use the `length` value from `CentroidOffsetAndLength` to estimate the number of vectors. It won't be exactly right because we use `vint` to encode doc ids, but since quantized vectors dominate on size, it should be directionally helpful.

Long term: evaluate adding a new field to the `CentroidOffsetAndLength` record (and therefore to the `.cenivf` file) to track the `numVectors` per partition. This metadata would make it trivial to decide how deeply to prefetch, allowing for a single round of prefetch calls to get the partitions.

As we investigate more aggressive prefetching, we likely want to make sure that we're using the `PrefetchingCentroidIterator` in all relevant locations to maximize the benefit. In my cursory reading, there might be some other applications of the class where it wouldn't make a big difference on stateful but will on serverless.
issues.title: PrefetchingCentroidIterator: use iterator state to determine prefetch depth

issues.body:
Today a dynamic mapping update during indexing causes the nodes holding copies of the affected shard (both primary and replicas) to wait for the update to be applied, but it does not wait for any other nodes before returning. This means that a subsequent call to e.g. the field-caps APIs may observe a stale mapping, which clients can find surprising.

It is particularly surprising to clients that perform a refresh and then use ES|QL for the search, since this uses the field caps API internally and may therefore fail to return the expected refreshed documents. Technically the visibility of mappings is unrelated to refreshes, but the interplay with ES|QL means we need to consider linking them together.

The proposal here is for indexing requests with `?refresh=wait_for` or `?refresh=true`, and the `POST _refresh` API, also to wait for any relevant mapping updates to be applied on all nodes holding a copy of any shard of the index. I would expect to do this using `TransportAwaitClusterStateVersionAppliedAction` towards the end of the indexing/refresh process, rather than delaying indexing while we wait for mapping updates to be applied on unrelated shards. Ideally I'd prefer to keep track of the appropriate cluster state version, and the appropriate set of target nodes, by including a little extra detail in the responses to shard bulks and refreshes.
issues.title: Ensure mapping updates are visible after a refresh

issues.body:
### Description

Make FUSE return a deterministic value for passthrough columns when FORK branches produce genuinely different non-null values for the same `(_id, _index)` group.

### Problem

After #150220, FUSE rewrites passthrough columns to `FIRST(col, NULL)`. `FIRST(col, NULL)` uses the `Any<T>` aggregator path that returns the first non-null value, with no defined ordering across FORK branches. For the standard hybrid-search case every branch reads the same document and produces the same value, so non-determinism is not an issue. 

In the divergent case: each branch builds its own value via `EVAL` and can potentially reuse the same column name. Under this scenario the passthrough columns FUSE returns can vary across runs of the same query.                                           

### Desired Behavior
  
**First FORK branch wins**, i.e. the value picked for a passthrough column is the one from the lowest- numbered branch (`fork1` over `fork2`, etc.), and thus be stable across runs.

### Solution

Inject _fork_id (integer branch counter) instead of extending FIRST for keyword sort keys.
  
 At analysis time, resolveFuse wraps each FORK branch in Eval(_fork_id = N)  FUSE then emits FIRST(col, _fork_id) for all passthrough columns. The integer sort key routes through the existing AllFirst<T>ByInt aggregator family. _fork_id is stripped from output and field references; it exists solely as the tiebreak key. 
Branch 1 deterministically wins when branches diverge.
issues.title: [ESQL]: Make FUSE passthrough columns deterministic
