### Description

A flattened field can declare explicitly mapped sub-fields under properties. When such a root is loaded as a whole column (e.g. KEEP attributes)  the engine must produce one canonical JSON string that is byte-identical regardless of the loading path. 

To guarantee that identity, PR #151415 made any flattened root that declares mapped sub-fields always load from _source and dropped the doc-values reconstruction path. This is correct but it doesn't provide the best performance.

This penalty applies to every flattened field that declares even one mapped sub-field, including the common case where all mapped sub-fields have doc values.

We can reconstruct the JSON blob from doc values + toString() and fall back to _source only when unavoidable (check if there are such cases).

See the related PRs:
1. #150464 — consistent field_extract on mapped sub-keys
2. #151415 — load flattened mapped-root from _source

### Enhancement

`AnalysisRegistry#build` runs once per index, so two indices with the same analysis recipe each build and hold their own `NamedAnalyzer` — and everything it carries (e.g. a synonyms chain's MB-scale `SynonymMap`, plus the per-analyzer `CloseableThreadLocal` graph). With data streams and templated indices pushing one recipe onto hundreds of indices per node, that recipe is built and held hundreds of times.

This makes the **analyzer the unit of sharing**: indices that resolve to a byte-identical recipe share one reference-counted `NamedAnalyzer`, built once per node and keyed on recipe structure. Each factory exposes a `sharingKey()` — identity by default (never shared; safe), overridden to opt in. Built once (single-flight), reloaded once per request, closed on last release. Gated by the `shared_analyzers` feature flag (off in release). Synonyms motivate it, but it also de-duplicates the default / language / custom analyzers.

Originally implemented end-to-end in #150797; splitting into smaller, focused PRs to ease review. Enabling the flag in release is a separate, macro-benchmark-gated follow-up.

### Plan
- [x] Node-level analyzer cache and sharing-key plumbing #151755
- [x] Per-factory settings-contract test harness #159929
- [ ] `analysis-common` factory opt-ins
  - [ ] Mechanical keys: stateless filters, language analyzers, simple record keys https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/160365
  - [ ] Judgment-call keys: `*_case` filters, identity-keyed, external-resource, `min_hash`, `delimited_payload`
- [ ] Plugin and ML factory opt-ins: icu, kuromoji, nori, smartcn, stempel, phonetic, ukrainian, ml
- [ ] Synonyms
- [ ] Tighten the completeness gate and add a changelog (closes this issue)

### Pre-GA follow-ups (gate the flag flip, not the split)

- [ ] Operator escape hatch — a node-level setting to force `sharingKey()` back to identity (disable sharing) without code changes, so an unexpected analyzer/plugin interaction can be worked around in the field without a rollback. ([raised here](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/151755#issuecomment-4794274834))
issues.title: Share analyzers across indices on a node

issues.body:
## Summary

When using Elasticsearch as a Prometheus data source (e.g. in Grafana), PromQL queries fan out to all TSDS indices matching the configured index scope. If any of those indices have been moved to the frozen tier, queries incur significantly higher latency because frozen-tier shards are fetched from object storage on demand.

Unlike ES|QL — where callers can filter by `_tier` via `METADATA` — the PromQL API provides no mechanism for callers to exclude tiers from query execution. Users with long retention periods who move older indices to frozen have no way to avoid the latency impact short of narrowing the index scope via the URL path (which is a coarse workaround and requires reconfiguring the data source).

As a workaround, PromQL expressions can be executed via the ES|QL `PROMQL` source command, which supports `METADATA _tier` filtering. However, this requires switching away from the native PromQL HTTP API and is not usable directly from a Grafana Prometheus data source.

## Requested behavior

A standard mechanism — for example a query parameter or a header — that allows callers to exclude frozen-tier indices from PromQL query execution, ideally one that maps to an existing Grafana Prometheus data source configuration option to avoid requiring Elastic-specific client changes.

## Context

Tracked as a known limitation in the [PromQL limitations documentation](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/query-languages/promql/promql-limitations#promql-limitations-frozen-tier).
issues.title: PromQL HTTP API: support excluding frozen-tier indices from query execution

issues.body:
### Description

## Problem
We observed node OOM during shard recovery/open-engine on a small-heap node.
  
Heap dump analysis indicates memory concentration in Lucene reader initialization for a shard with very high segment cardinality (~1159+ segments).

The failure occurs in shard recovery/open paths where memory appears insufficiently bounded by circuit breakers.

## Evidence
  ### Stack path at OOM
  ```
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError
 org.apache.lucene.store.DataOutput.copyBytes
 org.apache.lucene.util.fst.FST.readMetadata
 org.apache.lucene.codecs.lucene90.blocktree.FieldReader.<init>
 org.apache.lucene.index.SegmentReader.<init>
 org.elasticsearch.index.engine.InternalEngine.createReaderManager
 org.elasticsearch.index.shard.StoreRecovery.internalRecoverFromStore
 org.elasticsearch.index.shard.IndexShard.recoverFromStore
```

  ### Heap characteristics
  - Dominant retained heap in a recovery thread local context (`generic` thread).
  - Large object graph under Lucene reader structures:
    - `SegmentCoreReaders`
    - `SegmentReader`
    - `PerFieldDocValuesFormat$FieldsReader`
    - many `SegmentCommitInfo` entries
  - Large `byte[]` ownership under Lucene FST/reader structures.
  ### Workload/topology context
  - Incident occurred on a 2 GB node and stabilized after scaling to 4 GB.
  - Recovery involved a shard with very high segment count (order of 1k+).
  ## Why this matters
  Circuit breakers protect many accounted memory paths, but this recovery/open-engine path can still OOM before breaker rejection.
  This creates operational risk on small heaps or while recovering shards after a disruption (e.g., scale up/down, restart, rolling upgrades)

  ## Proposed behavior
  Recovery/open should have stronger memory safety under high segment cardinality:
  - bounded allocations and/or
  - explicit accounting/guardrails and/or
  - adaptive throttling/backoff/fail-fast behavior that avoids node OOM.

  ## Possible directions
  - Add memory accounting/limits for reader initialization during store recovery.
  - Add recovery-time safeguards when segment count per shard is very high.
  - Consider adaptive recovery throttling based on real-time heap pressure.
  - Improve observability: emit warnings/metrics for high segment-count recovery risk.
  ## Related issues
  - #44484 (network read throttling under memory pressure)
  - #98087 (recovery throttling strategy)
  - #148950 (memory accounting visibility gaps)
  - #148761 (memory regression detection)
issues.title: OOM during shard recovery with very high segment count is not bounded by circuit breakers

issues.body:
Follow-up to #152353, which makes columnar `shape`/`geo_shape` store each geometry as a per-document WKB doc value. Two related optimizations, with the format/approach left to the implementer:

1. **Optimize the geometry doc-value format.** A per-document WKB blob compresses poorly; a more columnar-friendly layout (e.g. coordinate-shredded columns, encoded/delta coordinates) would be smaller on disk.

2. **Optionally drop the tessellation doc value.** Once the raw geometry is in doc values, the tessellated triangle-tree doc value (per-doc relations/aggregations/grids) becomes a derived cache. Add an option to skip writing it and tessellate on demand from the raw geometry — trading query speed for storage. This only touches the doc-value compute path; the BKD search index is unaffected.
issues.title: Columnar shape/geo_shape: optimize geometry doc-value storage and optionally drop the tessellation

issues.body:
Follow-up to #152357, which adds `nested` support in columnar index modes and caps nesting at a single level.

Today nested relies on block-join: each child is a separate Lucene document, tied back to its parent by a bitset. This expands the doc id space, and nested values are read by iterating child documents.

With the single-level cap, a nested field is just a flat array of records. The main goal is to store each nested sub-field as an aligned array column, keeping one Lucene document (one doc id) per top-level document, so nested values and `_source` are read directly from the columns and per-parent offsets — no child documents, no parent bitset. (A sub-field that is itself multi-valued within a child needs a second level of offsets.)

Bonus: extend the same layout to nested queries, so block-join can be dropped entirely instead of only for the doc-value path — matching a nested query against the single document while still correlating values within the same child. This is the harder half and can come later.

The exact layout and query mechanism are left open.
issues.title: Columnar: replace nested block-join with aligned array columns

issues.body:
### Description

The Profile API's kNN diagnostics are currently limited to a single kNN-specific metric (vector_operations_count) plus the generic Lucene query timing breakdown. These generic timings mostly capture post-rewrite iteration over the already-computed result set, not the actual vector search work. This makes it difficult to diagnose performance issues in kNN searches, particularly when rescoring with quantized vectors is the bottleneck.

When investigating slow kNN queries, the current profiling output does not provide enough signal to distinguish between slow initial approximate search, slow full-precision rescoring after quantized search (e.g., BBQ or scalar quantization), or slow post-filter retries when filter selectivity is poor. 

For example, RescoreKnnVectorQuery aggregates initial quantized search and full-precision rescore into a single timing blob. If rescoring is the bottleneck, there is no way to see that today. Similarly, PostFilterKnnQuery can execute up to 3 rounds with no visibility into which rounds ran or how long each took.

### Proposed enhancements:
 * Rescore timing breakdown: report separate timings for the initial quantized search vs. the full-precision rescore phase in RescoreKnnVectorQuery
 * Separate vector_operations_count per phase (initial search ops vs. rescore ops)
 * Post-filter round visibility: surface which rounds of PostFilterKnnQuery executed and the time spent in each

### Related: 
 * #109018 (Explain API for vector search, complementary to this request)
 * #116362 (Explain API for retrievers)
issues.title: Enhance Profile API with kNN-specific phase breakdowns (rescore, graph traversal, quantization)

issues.body:
## Motivation

Builds on https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/131054, but for slices.

When merging vector segments partitioned by a slice field, if a slice is contributed by only one segment and has no deleted values, we should be able to skip rebuilding the vector index structures, which should speed up segment building.

This issue is to investigate possible solutions and then implement the most feasible one. The best solution is likely to copy raw bytes (not sure if this is possible though). Otherwise, we should be able to read/deserialize the centroids and posting lists and then write them out without doing any additional computation.

This would particularly benefit auto-sharding (which is implemented with a block of deletes on the out-of-bounds part of the segment file) because slices do not cross shard boundaries. Cheaper segment merge might also make it feasible to have more aggressive segment merge policies.
issues.title: Optimize vector slice merging when slice is contributed by one segment without any deleted values

issues.body:
Follow-up from #149206 (unify `SET` and request-body settings).

ES|QL's `project_routing` "cross-project disabled" error now reads (routed through the settings validator):

> `Error validating setting [project_routing]: cross-project search not enabled`

SQL and EQL emit the original wording for the same field (`RestSqlQueryAction`, `RestSqlTranslateAction`, `RestEqlSearchAction`; asserted in their tests):

> `[project_routing] is only allowed when cross-project search is enabled`

No functional impact and no test breakage — just a cross-engine consistency wart, ES|QL being the odd one out. Either align ES|QL's validator string to the sibling wording (and update the ES|QL test assertions), or consciously accept the divergence.
issues.title: ES|QL: project_routing cross-project error message diverges from SQL/EQL

## Description

When a bulk role operation (bulk put or bulk delete) affects N roles, the role-cache invalidation fans out into N separate invalidations, each acquiring the role-cache invalidation lock and performing a full linear scan of the role cache — rather than a single batched invalidation.

## Call path

1. `NativeRolesStore.bulkResponseAndRefreshRolesCache` collects all affected role names and correctly issues one clear request:
   ```java
   clearRoleCache(rolesToRefreshInCache.toArray(String[]::new), ...); // NativeRolesStore.java:444
   ```
   which builds a single `ClearRolesCacheRequest().names(roles)` (NativeRolesStore.java:853-854).
2. But the node handler expands it back into a per-role loop:
   ```java
   // TransportClearRolesCacheAction.java:79-81
   for (String role : request.getNames()) {
       rolesStore.invalidate(role);
   }
   ```
3. Each `CompositeRolesStore.invalidate(String role)` acquires the exclusive cache-invalidation lock and does a full O(cache-size) scan of the role cache (matching keys whose role names contain `role`), plus a single-key negative-cache invalidate and a counter bump.

## Impact

For a bulk update of N roles: N exclusive-lock acquisitions and N full role-cache scans (cache size defaults to 10,000 entries, unbounded if configured to `-1`). This runs on the MANAGEMENT thread pool, so it does not affect cluster-state application, but it serializes N full scans and repeatedly blocks role-resolution cache writes for the duration of the bulk operation. Cost scales as N × cache-size instead of ~cache-size.

## Proposed fix

Batch the invalidation so a bulk clear does a single lock acquisition and a single cache scan matching all affected role names at once. A suitable primitive already exists:

```java
// CompositeRolesStore.java:866
public void invalidateClusterScopedRoles(Set<String> roles) // one lock, one scan via Sets.haveEmptyIntersection
```

`invalidateClusterScopedRoles` matches cached keys against the whole set of role names in one pass, but it's currently only wired to the file-based `clusterScopedRolesChanged` listener. Options:
- Have `TransportClearRolesCacheAction.nodeOperation` call a single set-based invalidation instead of looping, or
- Add a `CompositeRolesStore.invalidate(Set<String> roles)` that does one scan for the named-roles case, mirroring `invalidateClusterScopedRoles`.

Note the negative-cache handling differs (`invalidate(role)` uses per-project scoped keys via `negativeLookupCache.invalidate(new ProjectScoped<>(projectId, role))`), so the batched version needs to preserve per-project semantics rather than reuse the cluster-scoped predicate verbatim.

## Notes

- Pre-existing behavior; independent of any recent invalidation-locking changes.
- No correctness impact — purely efficiency/contention under bulk role administration.
issues.title: Bulk role updates trigger N separate cache invalidations instead of one batched clear

### Description

# Proposal: Randomized input values for YAML REST tests using `${...}`

## Summary

Elasticsearch's Java tests lean heavily on seed-driven randomisation (`ESTestCase.randomIntBetween`, `randomIdentifier`, ...). YAML REST tests do not have an equivalent, so every value in a `.yml` test is fixed unless it comes from a previous response via the stash.

This proposes adding reproducible randomised input values to the YAML REST runner using the existing `${...}` interpolation and function names matching the equivalent `ESTestCase` helpers. Two mechanisms are proposed for generating random inputs:

- **Inline substitution**: `${randomIntBetween(1, 100)}` usable directly in a `do` params/body for single-use values.
- **Named random values**: a new `stash` section evaluates random calls and stashes their results for reuse through existing `$var` / `${var}` substitution.

## Motivation

YAML REST tests are the first port of call for many developers because of the ease of use yet they are missing this key functionality. During a recent analysis of a newly discovered bug it was noted that YAML test coverage existed and a degree of randomisation probably would have caught the issue earlier. 

- Randomized inputs can expose bugs around value length, naming assumptions, ranges, collisions, and ordering.
- Reusing `ESTestCase` helper names keeps the YAML feature familiar to Elasticsearch test authors.
- Reproducibility remains seed-based: failures reproduce with the usual `-Dtests.seed=<seed>` option.

## Proposed usage

### Inline random calls

```yaml
"single-use random values":
  - requires:
      test_runner_features: [randomized_input]
      reason: uses randomized input values
  - do:
      search:      
        index: my-index
        body:
          suggest:
            text: query text 
            suggest-field:
              completion:
                field: field
                shard_size: "${randomInt()}"
```

A whole-value random call preserves its generated type:

```yaml
count: "${randomIntBetween(1, 100)}"   # JSON number
enabled: "${randomBoolean()}"          # JSON boolean
```

An embedded random call is stringified into the surrounding scalar:

```yaml
name: "index-${randomIdentifier()}"    # JSON string
```

### Named random values with `stash`

```yaml
"random index round-trip":
  - requires:
      test_runner_features: [randomized_input]
      reason: uses randomized input values
  - stash:
      idx: randomIndexName()
      id: randomIdentifier()
  - do:
      index:
        index: $idx
        id: $id
        body:
          title: "${randomAlphaOfLength(10)}"
  - do:
      get:
        index: $idx
        id: $id
  - match: { _index: $idx }
  - match: { _id: $id }
```

The generated values land in the stash. Existing stash semantics continue to apply:

- `$var` preserves the stashed value type.
- `${var}` stringifies the stashed value for embedded substitution.

## Function syntax

Random calls use the same names as `ESTestCase` helpers where possible:

| YAML call | Java helper |
|---|---|
| `randomInt()` | `ESTestCase.randomInt()` |
| `randomIntBetween(min, max)` | `ESTestCase.randomIntBetween(int min, int max)` |
| `randomLong()` | `ESTestCase.randomLong()` |
| `randomLongBetween(min, max)` | `ESTestCase.randomLongBetween(long min, long max)` |
| `randomDouble()` | `ESTestCase.randomDouble()` |
| `randomBoolean()` | `ESTestCase.randomBoolean()` |
| `randomAlphaOfLengthBetween(min, max)` | `ESTestCase.randomAlphaOfLengthBetween(int min, int max)` |
| `randomIdentifier()` | `ESTestCase.randomIdentifier()` |
| `randomFrom(a, b, c)` | `ESTestCase.randomFrom(...)` |

Initial support should stay deliberately small.

## Interaction with existing `${...}` stash syntax

The YAML REST runner already uses `${name}` for embedded stash substitution. The new behavior should be a narrow extension:

1. If the contents of `${...}` exactly match a supported random function call, evaluate it as a random call.
2. Otherwise, leave existing stash behavior unchanged.

Examples:

```yaml
index: "${randomIndexName()}"  # random call
index: "${idx}"                # existing stash lookup
index: "test-${suffix}"        # existing embedded stash lookup
index: "test-${randomIdentifier()}" # embedded random call
```

This reserves stash keys that look exactly like supported random calls, such as `randomIdentifier()`. That is a small compatibility risk, but it is much narrower than treating every `${...}` body as an expression.

Existing escaping should remain intact. Today `\${foo}` produces a literal `${foo}` rather than a stash lookup; the same should apply to random calls:

```yaml
literal: "\${randomIdentifier()}"
```
issues.title: Randomized input values for YAML REST tests using `${...}`

There are likely some simple improvements that we can do to make `unmapped_fields="LOAD"` faster. Let's collect simple improvements here.

1. In `SET unmapped_fields="LOAD"; FROM idx | WHERE partially_unmapped == "foo" | LIMIT 1000`, the filter can generally not be pushed down because it requires loading a field. But during batched execution on data nodes, we might have a batch where the field is fully mapped and we can push down to Lucene. Do we? If not, let's do it! More generally: if during local optimization we run on a batch where a partially mapped field is fully mapped, we should treat it as such.
2. When loading individual fields from `_source`, we use Jackson to retrieve by field name them during block loading. Is this always the fastest approach? Is there any hot code that we can optimize? There might be cases where parsing the entire `_source` and then extracting fields from it is faster.

We should start with a time-boxed spike and keep in mind a set of user-relevant queries before we start optimizing anything.
issues.title: ESQL: low-hanging fruit optimizations for `unmapped_fields="LOAD"`

## Background

#147820 adds a new top-level `dense_vector` query (`DenseVectorQueryBuilder`) that performs exact, brute-force scoring against `dense_vector` fields, as an alternative to the approximate `knn` query.

Unlike `knn`, `match`, and `sparse_vector`, the new `dense_vector` query has no query-rewrite interception support for `semantic_text` fields, so it cannot currently be used against a `semantic_text` field the way those other query types can.

## What needs to happen

Add a `SemanticDenseVectorQueryRewriteInterceptor` (mirroring `SemanticKnnVectorQueryRewriteInterceptor`) that:

- Implements `QueryRewriteInterceptor`, keyed to `DenseVectorQueryBuilder.NAME`.
- When the query targets a `semantic_text` field, rewrites it to an `InterceptedInferenceDenseVectorQueryBuilder`-style wrapper that performs the necessary inference call and rewrites to the native `dense_vector` query against the field's underlying inference-generated subfield, analogous to how `InterceptedInferenceKnnVectorQueryBuilder` works for `knn`.
- Is registered in `InferencePlugin.getQueryRewriteInterceptors()` alongside the existing `knn`/`match`/`sparse_vector` interceptors.

## References

- Base PR: #147820
- Original feature request: #97541
- Existing pattern to follow: `SemanticKnnVectorQueryRewriteInterceptor` / `InterceptedInferenceKnnVectorQueryBuilder`
issues.title: dense_vector query: add semantic_text-aware query rewrite interception

issues.body:
## Summary [RFC 10008: The HTTP QUERY Method](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc10008.html) became a Standards-Track RFC in June 2026, and it's essentially the spec written around what Elasticsearch search actually is: a request that's **safe, idempotent, and cacheable, yet carries a body**. I'd like to propose supporting `QUERY /{index}/_search` as a first-class HTTP method, on equal footing with `GET` and `POST`. The server-side implementation is straightforward and completely additive. And here's the great news: **Netty, the HTTP library Elasticsearch already uses, already recognizes `QUERY`** as [`HttpMethod.QUERY`](https://github.com/netty/netty/blob/4.1/codec-http/src/main/java/io/netty/handler/codec/http/HttpMethod.java#L92). The only piece missing is adding `QUERY` to Elasticsearch's internal `RestRequest.Method` enum. It's a small change with outsized impact. ## QUERY is here now: the ecosystem is already ready QUERY just became a registered HTTP method (June 2026), and support is rolling out across the stack. Here's what's already in place that matters for Elasticsearch: - **Netty** (Elasticsearch's transport layer): `QUERY` is a full `HttpMethod` constant ([`HttpMethod.java` line 92](https://github.com/netty/netty/blob/4.1/codec-http/src/main/java/io/netty/handler/codec/http/HttpMethod.java#L92), described as “requests that the request target process the enclosed content in a safe and idempotent manner”). QUERY requests already traverse Elasticsearch's wire layer without issues. - **Apache HttpComponents Core** (the go-to Java HTTP client): `QUERY` is marked as safe and idempotent ([`Method.java` line 106](https://github.com/apache/httpcomponents-core/blob/master/httpcore5/src/main/java/org/apache/hc/core5/http/Method.java#L106)). This is important because it influences the broader Java ecosystem. - **JDK `java.net.http`** (Java's built-in): Developers can write `HttpRequest.Builder.method(“QUERY”, …)` and it just works ([line 367](https://github.com/openjdk/jdk/blob/master/src/java.net.http/share/classes/java/net/http/HttpRequest.java#L367)). Only `CONNECT` is restricted. - **nginx, Node undici, axios**: All have QUERY support merged or in flight. ([nginx PR](https://github.com/nginx/nginx/pull/1488), [undici PR #5459](https://github.com/nodejs/undici/pull/5459)) - **OpenAPI 3.2**: Officially added a `query` operation ([OAI/OpenAPI-Specification #3033](https://github.com/OAI/OpenAPI-Specification/issues/3033)), so the Elasticsearch REST spec can describe QUERY endpoints. - **The adoption hub**: Central coordination at [jeswr/http-query-adoption](https://github.com/jeswr/http-query-adoption). Bottom line: clients can already send QUERY, proxies can already route it, and specifications can already describe it. Elasticsearch adding support completes the picture and makes ES a reference implementation in the ecosystem. ## Why this matters for Elasticsearch and REST A search is fundamentally a read operation. But today, we're forced to express it in one of two ways that misrepresent what's actually happening: 1. **`POST /_search` with a body**: This works, but `POST` sends a signal to every client, proxy, and cache: “this request might mutate state.” That's wrong. Searches aren't safe, aren't idempotent, and aren't cacheable in the HTTP sense. We lose the ability to safely retry on timeout and we forfeit HTTP-level caching. 2. **`GET /_search` with a body**: This is closer to the intent, but a body on `GET` is [not well-defined in the HTTP spec](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#name-get) and many proxies, CDNs, and client libraries silently drop or reject it. `QUERY` fills exactly this gap. It says plainly what a search is: a safe, idempotent, cacheable operation whose input is a body. Adding QUERY support makes Elasticsearch's REST API **genuinely RESTful**. The HTTP method finally carries the correct semantics. Intermediate caches can cache identical searches by content. Clients get safe-retry behavior without extra logic. It's a small change that elevates the entire search API. ## Current behavior `QUERY /{index}/_search` returns **`405 Method Not Allowed`**: not because the HTTP transport layer can't handle it, but because Elasticsearch's application-level method enum is closed: - [`RestRequest.java` L240-249](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/rest/RestRequest.java#L240): The enum reads `Method { GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, HEAD, PATCH, TRACE, CONNECT }` with **no `QUERY` entry**. - When an unrecognized method arrives, `RestController` catches the `IllegalArgumentException` and routes it to `handleUnsupportedHttpMethod(...)`, which returns `METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED`.
curl: The problem today and the goal ```bash # (1) Today: POST works, but the method mis-signals the semantics (unsafe/uncacheable) curl -sS -XPOST "https://es:9200/products/_search" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"query":{"match":{"title":"wireless keyboard"}},"size":20}' # (2) Today: GET-with-body is semantically closer but fragile across proxies/CDNs curl -sS -XGET "https://es:9200/products/_search" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"query":{"match":{"title":"wireless keyboard"}}}' # (3) Today: QUERY (what we want) is rejected before it reaches the handler curl -sS -XQUERY "https://es:9200/products/_search" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"query":{"match":{"title":"wireless keyboard"}}}' # => HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed (Allow: GET, POST) # (4) The goal: same body as POST, correct semantics, cacheable by content curl -sS -XQUERY "https://es:9200/products/_search" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Accept-Query: application/json' \ -d '{"query":{"match":{"title":"wireless keyboard"}},"size":20}' ```
## Proposed change: three layers, additive and search-only The RFC is more than “add a verb.” To do it right and get the full HTTP benefit, three surfaces are involved: the first is required for QUERY to work, and the other two unlock the semantic payoff: 1. **The method (required).** Add `QUERY` to `RestRequest.Method` and register it on the read routes (`_search`, and in follow-ups, `_msearch` and `_count`). Body parsing is *identical* to `POST /_search`. No handler code changes needed. 2. **Body and Content-Type (RFC 10008 §2).** QUERY defines its query by the `Content-Type` header of the request. For Elasticsearch, that's the existing `application/json` Query DSL. An empty body defaults to match-all (same as today). If Elasticsearch can't parse the `Content-Type`, return **`415 Unsupported Media Type`**. If the Query DSL is malformed, return **`400`** (matching current `_search` behavior). 3. **Cacheability and the Accept-Query header (RFC 10008 §2–§3).** QUERY responses are cacheable with a cache key derived from request content (method + URI + body hash). Optionally advertise `Accept-Query: application/json` on the `_search` endpoint so proxies and CDNs know the endpoint accepts QUERY and understand the caching contract. Let responses carry appropriate `Cache-Control` headers. (The in-node request cache is unaffected. This is about HTTP-level caching at fronting proxies and CDNs, which matters a lot for read-heavy search traffic.) Strictly read-only: no mutating route changes. `GET` and `POST` `_search` behavior is completely untouched.
The change, concretely: illustrative diffs against main **1) Add the method** to `server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/rest/RestRequest.java` ```diff public enum Method { - GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, HEAD, PATCH, TRACE, CONNECT + GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, HEAD, PATCH, TRACE, CONNECT, QUERY } ``` **2) Register it on the search routes** in `server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/rest/action/search/RestSearchAction.java` (`routes()` method, around L94-99) ```diff import static org.elasticsearch.rest.RestRequest.Method.GET; import static org.elasticsearch.rest.RestRequest.Method.POST; +import static org.elasticsearch.rest.RestRequest.Method.QUERY; ... public List routes() { return List.of( new Route(GET, "/_search"), new Route(POST, "/_search"), + new Route(QUERY, "/_search"), new Route(GET, "/{index}/_search"), - new Route(POST, "/{index}/_search") + new Route(POST, "/{index}/_search"), + new Route(QUERY, "/{index}/_search") ); } ``` Because the handler already reads the body the same way for both `GET` and `POST`, no changes to `prepareRequest(...)` are needed for basic support to work. Add `RestControllerTests` + `RestSearchAction` unit tests, then a `rest-api-spec` YAML test for `QUERY /_search`.
End-to-end: Java client using JDK HttpClient ```java // Client side: java.net.http already permits QUERY (only CONNECT is restricted) var body = """ { "query": { "match": { "title": "wireless keyboard" } }, "size": 20 } """; HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://es:9200/products/_search")) .header("Content-Type", "application/json") .header("Accept-Query", "application/json") .method("QUERY", HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)) // safe + idempotent + cacheable .build(); HttpResponse res = client.send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()); ``` On the wire, Netty (`transport-netty4`) decodes the request line into `HttpMethod.QUERY` (already defined). The request hits `RestController`, which once `QUERY` is in `RestRequest.Method` and registered on `RestSearchAction`, dispatches to the same search handler as `POST`. It parses the same Query DSL body and returns the same hits. The only behavioral change is *correct HTTP semantics*: the method now correctly signals safe, idempotent, and cacheable intent.
## Backward compatibility 100% additive. Existing `GET` and `POST` `_search` clients are completely unaffected. `QUERY` is a newly *accepted* method on the same routes. No response shape or DSL changes, so this is purely opt-in for new clients. ## Questions for the team **Server implementation:** - Would you be interested in a PR adding `QUERY` support to `_search` (with follow-ups for `_msearch` and `_count`)? - Should QUERY be gated behind a feature flag or `RestApiVersion` while clients and proxies catch up, or should we enable it directly? - For the first PR, how much of the cacheability contract (`Accept-Query` and `Cache-Control` headers) should we include versus making that a follow-up? **Integration and ecosystem:** - The elasticsearch-java and opensearch-java client libraries will need to add `QUERY` to their `HttpMethod` enums before integration tests can fully exercise QUERY routes. Should the server PR wait for those, or should we move in parallel and coordinate the integration tests afterward? - Should we provide migration guidance for users moving from POST/GET searches to QUERY? What should the adoption story look like? - For higher-level HTTP client libraries (elasticsearch-py, elasticsearch-js, elasticsearch-go, elasticsearch-rs), what does the QUERY API look like from the user's perspective? Are there teams we should loop in early? **Rollout strategy:** - How do we coordinate timing with related projects (Java clients, official client libraries, proxies) to make the rollout smooth? ## References - RFC 10008: The HTTP QUERY Method: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc10008.html - Netty `HttpMethod.QUERY`: https://github.com/netty/netty/blob/4.1/codec-http/src/main/java/io/netty/handler/codec/http/HttpMethod.java#L92 - Apache HttpComponents Core `Method.QUERY`: https://github.com/apache/httpcomponents-core/blob/master/httpcore5/src/main/java/org/apache/hc/core5/http/Method.java#L106 - JDK `java.net.http` `HttpRequest.Builder.method`: https://github.com/openjdk/jdk/blob/master/src/java.net.http/share/classes/java/net/http/HttpRequest.java#L367 - Node `undici` (RFC 10008): https://github.com/nodejs/undici/pull/5459 · nginx: https://github.com/nginx/nginx/pull/1488 - OpenAPI 3.2 `query` operation: https://github.com/OAI/OpenAPI-Specification/issues/3033 - Adoption hub: https://github.com/jeswr/http-query-adoption **Cross-platform coordination:** - A parallel feature request for OpenSearch has been filed at https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/issues/22409. Synchronized rollout across both communities would help the ecosystem understand QUERY as a standard, not a one-off. I'm happy to implement this end-to-end: the RestController routing test, `RestSearchAction` unit test, and `rest-api-spec` YAML test, all under the DCO.
issues.title: Support the HTTP `QUERY` method (RFC 10008) on `_search`

issues.body:
## Summary

Today, all parallelism in the ES|QL compute engine comes from running multiple
`Driver`s, each executing a full copy of the pipeline. For aggregations with a
coordinator/collector split, this means the final merge (hashing + aggregating
partial results from data nodes) runs single-threaded on the coordinator,
which becomes a bottleneck for high-cardinality `GROUP BY` queries.

The proposal is to keep a single driver on the coordinator, but let individual operators
adaptively spawn their own worker threads once some threshold is crossed
(e.g. grouping-key cardinality > 100K, or partitioned pages start arriving
from data nodes) — rather than scaling out via more drivers. Below-threshold
queries keep using the existing single-threaded path with zero added overhead.

This is a new form of parallelism for ES|QL (intra-operator worker pools,
"scatter/gather" within a single driver) rather than the existing
multi-driver model, so we're building it up incrementally, proving the
pattern on a simple operator before tackling the harder final-merge case.

## Phase 1 — Parallelize TopN operator ✅ Done

Used `TopNOperator` as the proving ground for per-operator worker-thread
parallelism, since it's simpler than the final hash-merge case but the
initial partitioned-hash-aggregation POC showed pushing TopN into parallel
final-merge threads gave additional speedup on its own.

- Landed: [elastic/elasticsearch#150148 — Parallel TopN Operator](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/150148) (merged 2026-06-30)
- Design: `TopNOperator` promotes itself to `ParallelTopNOperator` once
  received rows exceed `esql.parallel_topn_promotion_threshold_rows`
  (default 1M). Worker threads (from the `esql_worker` pool) each own a
  `TopNOperator`; the Driver just routes pages to workers. On completion,
  worker outputs are merged into the original (pre-promotion) `TopNOperator`.
- **Known follow-up:** [elastic/elasticsearch#153169](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/153169)
  (open) — fixes a double-release-on-Block bug in `ParallelTopNOperator`
  found via CI flake [elastic/elasticsearch#152904](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/152904).
  Needs review before this phase is fully closed out.

## Phase 2 — Add partitioning on the data nodes

From the initial (data-node) stage of aggregation, partition result pages by
grouping key so that all rows for a given group land in pages with the same
`partitionId`. This is what lets Phase 3's final-merge workers each own a
disjoint set of groups.

Likely design: once the group-cardinality threshold is crossed and
partitioning kicks in, switch from a single hash table to multiple hash
tables, one per partition, behind a higher-level table indexed by
`partitionId`. This physically partitions the hash values, which should
improve emit efficiency since hash blocks are clustered per partition table.

A complication is group handling. Hash aggregation uses the hash table to
assign a `groupId`, which then indexes into a dense array of aggregation
states for the update. With a multi-level (partitioned) hash table, we'll
likely need a matching multi-level aggregation state array, i.e. one dense
state array per partition, parallel to the per-partition hash table.

## Phase 3 — Multi-threaded final aggregation on the collector

Run the final merge stage of an aggregation in parallel, consuming the
partitioned pages from Phase 2. A single driver receives pages and
distributes them to worker threads by `partitionId`, so each worker merges
all pages for its assigned partition(s). The driver thread routes work 
but can help with actual hash and aggregation as needed.

- Worker thread count should scale with hardware execution contexts, but
  should not consume all of them.
- Reuse the worker-pool / promotion pattern from Phase 1
  ([elastic/elasticsearch#150148](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/150148))
  for work distribution.
- **Non-partitioned/threshold handling** — only start partitioning once
  cardinality exceeds some threshold. Before that threshold is hit, rows are
  inserted into a shared, un-partitioned hash table (can be the original
  operator's own hash table). Once partitioning kicks in, a single thread
  drains that shared table and inserts its entries into the new partitioned
  tables.

## Phase 4 — Combine adjacent parallel operators

Once multiple operators in a row are parallelized (e.g. `ParallelHashMerge`
followed by `ParallelTopN`), each needs its own worker pool, and the total
thread count needed grows beyond the hardware thread count as more operators
are parallelized. There's also a thread-affinity concern: in driver-based
parallelism the same thread carries a page through adjacent operators
(cache-friendly); with independent parallel operators, a page is very likely
handled by a different hardware thread at each stage, plus the driver has
to gather/scatter between each parallel stage.

Possible directions (not yet decided):
- Fuse adjacent parallel operators (e.g. `ParallelHashMerge` + `ParallelTopN`)
  into a single operator so one worker thread runs the whole mini-pipeline.
- Have the planner coalesce adjacent parallel sub-operators more generally.
- Note this resembles the original POC's parallel-exchange approach, which
  leaned on driver-based parallelism instead.

## Open items / risks to flag in the ticket

- Phase 1's outstanding double-release bug ([#153169](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/153169)) should probably be resolved before or alongside starting Phase 2/3 work, since Phase 3 reuses the same worker-pool pattern.
- Phase 2 and Phase 3 are tightly coupled (partition scheme choice in Phase 2 directly drives worker assignment in Phase 3) — may be worth designing them together even if implemented sequentially.
- Phase 4 is explicitly speculative/unscoped pending experience from Phases 2-3 ("hand wavy" per the original issue text).
- Worker count / max-in-flight tuning from Phase 1 was never benchmarked on real hardware (defaults are principled guesses) — worth doing before extending the same pattern to Phase 3's heavier final-merge workload.

### Description

Hi team, my name is **Abdul Mateen** and I'm **part of the IPGeolocation.io team**. Following up on the discussion in #101080 where you asked what other GeoIP sources people would like to see supported, and after seeing #149885 recently add support for the IPInfo Plus database, we wanted to put in a request (and offer to help) with adding support for IPGeolocation.io as well.

Wanted to be upfront that we work on this product, so happy to answer any questions about the data or format, and we're glad to provide test databases, documentation, or engineering support to help this move forward if useful.

**What source:** IPGeolocation.io (https://ipgeolocation.io). We offer downloadable IP to location, company, abuse, and ASN databases in CSV and MMDB formats, similar in structure to what MaxMind provides, along with an API.

**Why we think it would be a nice addition for Elasticsearch users:**
1. We include a few fields that MaxMind's standard database doesn't cover out of the box, like currency, calling code, and time zone, which some users currently need a second lookup or provider to fill in.
2. Having a second self-hosted database option gives Elasticsearch users more resilience generally. If a team's current provider changes pricing, terms, or update cadence, having an alternative already supported means less disruption to their pipeline.

**Security and threat intelligence fields:**
Beyond core geolocation, we also maintain a dedicated IP Security database that a lot of Elasticsearch users doing fraud prevention, bot filtering, or access control would likely find useful to have natively available in the ingest pipeline. This includes:
- `threat_score`, a 0 to 100 composite risk score for the IP
- Boolean flags for `is_vpn`, `is_proxy`, `is_residential_proxy`, `is_tor`, `is_relay`, `is_anonymous`, `is_bot`, `is_spam`, `is_known_attacker`, and `is_cloud_provider`
- Named attribution fields like `vpn_provider_names`, `proxy_provider_names`, and `cloud_provider_name`, rather than just boolean flags
- Confidence scores and last seen dates for VPN and proxy detections
- This data is updated daily and ships in the same MMDB/CSV format as our location database, so it could realistically be added as its own `Database` type alongside geolocation

We'd be glad to provide sample databases and documentation so the team can get a better sense of the format and fields firsthand, whatever is most useful for evaluating this. Since #149885 already set a solid precedent with a dedicated Database variant, lookup class, and field mapping tests for IPInfo Plus, we imagine IPGeolocation.io support could follow a similar pattern, and we're happy to help with sample data, implementation details, or even a PR if that's the preferred path.

Implement a configurable ES|QL query timeout.

Today ES|QL queries do not have their own timeout, they just get interrupted if top layer timeouts trigger (client, proxy and so on), so probably a sensitive default is no timeout at all.

We probably need options to configure query timeout both globally (cluster setting) and per query (query parameter/setting).

More fine-grained options are also possible, eg.
- per command/query type
- per user/role

For reference https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/99526

issues.body:
### Description

This is a fairly simple idea:

There are times when a specific shard of a larger index (or all of them) are lost. For example, if you have a readonly index and you ever remove your replica(s), then lose the primary shard(s) on a specific node, it may not be a serious concern other than the need to perform a partial restore.

In this scenario, when the cluster knows that it lost shards (the index is red), we should be able to perform a snapshot-restore without closing the index first.

The current approach requires:

```http
POST /.ds-my-red-index-from-days-ago/_close

POST /_snapshot/my-snapshot-repo/my-snapshot/_restore
{
  "indices": ".ds-my-red-index-from-days-ago",
  "include_aliases": true
}
```

I am proposing that this be simplified:

```http
POST /_snapshot/my-snapshot-repo/my-snapshot/_restore?missing_shards_only
{
  "indices": ".ds-my-red-index-from-days-ago",
  "include_aliases": true
}
```

I don't care about the added field name or whether it's a querystring parameter or body parameter, but something to a signify that this is okay and expected to be partial. This would seemingly help most red-index scenarios where a snapshot is available.

_Even better_ would be if we could do something where we don't even need to lookup the snapshot:

```http
POST /_snapshot/my-snapshot-repo/_restore?missing_shards_only
{
  "indices": ".ds-my-red-index-from-days-ago",
  "include_aliases": true
}
```

with the implication being that it comes from the latest successful snapshot for the index, per index if multiple are passed.

issues.body:
## Description
 
ES|QL provides regex matching via RLIKE and substitution via REPLACE, but lacks a function to count how many times a pattern matches a string (a per-row function that returns an integer).
 
A match count function is needed for detection logic that depends on frequency, not just presence:
 
- Trigger only when a pattern appears at least N times.
- Compute ratios (e.g., "numeric characters / total length") to detect obfuscation.
- Score patterns by occurrence count.

## Impact
 
- **Detection quality**: Many detections require thresholds (>= N matches) or ratios. Without counting, we are unable to develop the detections we plan, or we need to use hacky stopgaps that rely on unclear syntax and are therefore difficult to maintain.
- **Maintainability**: The stopgap is not obvious, requires comments, and is easy to copy incorrectly.
- **Performance**: Multiple regex passes over large strings and intermediate string manipulations (painful for large PowerShell script blocks).
- **Harder reviews**: The stopgap logic obscures the actual detection intent, slowing code review. Customers also have difficulty reviewing our detections to respond to alerts.

## Use Cases / Examples
 
Detection Rules using the stopgap:
 
- https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/blob/main/rules_building_block/defense_evasion_posh_obfuscation_proportion_special_chars.toml
- https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/blob/main/rules/windows/defense_evasion_posh_obfuscation_char_arrays.toml
- https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/blob/main/rules/windows/defense_evasion_posh_obfuscation_string_concat.toml
- https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/blob/main/rules/windows/defense_evasion_posh_obfuscation_concat_dynamic.toml
- https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/blob/main/rules/windows/defense_evasion_posh_obfuscation_string_format.toml
- https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/blob/main/rules/windows/defense_evasion_posh_obfuscation_index_reversal.toml
- https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/blob/main/rules/windows/defense_evasion_posh_obfuscation_reverse_keyword.toml
- https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/blob/main/rules/windows/defense_evasion_posh_obfuscation_iex_env_vars_reconstruction.toml
- https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/blob/main/rules/windows/defense_evasion_posh_obfuscation_backtick.toml
- https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/blob/main/rules/windows/defense_evasion_posh_obfuscation_backtick_var.toml
- https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/blob/main/rules/windows/defense_evasion_posh_obfuscation_whitespace_special_proportion.toml
- https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/blob/main/rules/windows/defense_evasion_posh_obfuscation_iex_string_reconstruction.toml
- https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/blob/main/rules/windows/defense_evasion_posh_obfuscation_high_number_proportion.toml
### Example 1: High numeric character ratio
 
Current logic:
 
```esql
| eval Esql.script_block_length = length(powershell.file.script_block_text)
| eval Esql.script_block_tmp = replace(powershell.file.script_block_text, """[0-9]""", "🔥")
| eval Esql.script_block_pattern_count = Esql.script_block_length - length(replace(Esql.script_block_tmp, "🔥", ""))
| eval Esql.script_block_ratio = Esql.script_block_pattern_count::double / Esql.script_block_length::double
| where Esql.script_block_ratio > 0.35
```
 
Desired logic:
 
```esql
| eval Esql.script_block_length = length(powershell.file.script_block_text)
| eval Esql.digit_count = REGEXP_COUNT(powershell.file.script_block_text, """[0-9]""")
| eval Esql.digit_ratio = Esql.digit_count::double / Esql.script_block_length::double
| where Esql.digit_ratio > 0.35
```
 
### Example 2: Count complex multi-character patterns
 
Current logic:
 
```esql
| eval tmp = replace(
    powershell.file.script_block_text,
    """((\{\d+\}){2,}["']\s?-f|::Format[^\{]+(\{\d+\}){2,})""",
    "🔥"
  )
| eval count = length(tmp) - length(replace(tmp, "🔥", ""))
| where count >= 5
```
 
Desired logic:
 
```esql
| eval count = REGEXP_COUNT(
    powershell.file.script_block_text,
    """((\{\d+\}){2,}["']\s?-f|::Format[^\{]+(\{\d+\}){2,})"""
  )
| where count >= 5
```
 
## Stopgaps
 
As a stopgap, we use REPLACE + LENGTH to simulate a match count by:
 
1. Replacing each regex match with a single-character marker (🔥)
2. Measuring the length difference to count how many markers were inserted
Example: Count pattern matches in a PowerShell script
 
```esql
// replace the patterns we are looking for with the 🔥 emoji to enable counting them
// The emoji is used because it's unlikely to appear in scripts and has a consistent character length of 1
| eval Esql.script_block_tmp = replace(powershell.file.script_block_text, """[A-Za-z0-9_-]`(?![rntb]|\r|\n|\d)[A-Za-z0-9_-]""", "🔥")
 
// Count inserted markers
| eval pattern_count = length(Esql.script_block_tmp) - length(replace(Esql.script_block_tmp, "🔥", ""))
```
 
This is necessary because ES|QL does not expose:
 
- The number of replacements performed by REPLACE, or a direct match count function

## Asks / Recommendations
 
- Add a REGEXP_COUNT(field, pattern) function that returns an integer count per row. It should count non-overlapping matches (consistent with REPLACE), use the same regex engine as REPLACE, and handle null/empty values.

## References
 
- https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/query-languages/esql/functions-operators/string-functions#esql-replace
- [TRaDE Gaps and Blockers](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MWhqjiDonIC2NwxCm8rYodcBVrK1-6-Isw2LEredUlY/edit?usp=sharing)
issues.title: [ES|QL] Add a regex match count function (e.g. `REGEXP_COUNT`)

issues.body:
## Description
 
EQL has a mechanism to reference fields that may not exist in the dataset. By default, EQL returns an error if a query references a non-existing field. To avoid this, you can mark a field as optional using the `?` operator, so EQL then treats it as null and the query continues to run.
 
ES|QL doesn't have an equivalent operator. If a query references a missing field, whether it doesn't exist or only exists in some index patterns, it fails with an error like "verification_exception: Unknown column".
 
[#140463](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/140463) introduces support to nullify mapping-unavailable fields via the unmapped_fields setting (for example, `SET unmapped_fields="nullify"`). But it is a "global" query behavior and not a per-field opt-in mechanism. For our detection rules, we need a granular per-field syntax (EQL-like `?`) so only explicitly marked fields become null, while other missing fields still fail verification.
 
Until a per-field optional fields mechanism exists, ES|QL remains less flexible than EQL when querying across datasets with different schemas.
 
## Impact
 
- **Multi Domain Analytics Blocker**: Our MDA queries use multiple data sources in different domains, so it's unrealistic to expect them to have 1:1 field parity.
- **Advanced Data source usage Blocker**: Queries that have logic or exclusions that rely on fields that require advanced configuration to be enabled (such as Linux session view, dynamic parsed Windows events, etc.) cannot be used without rendering the rule incompatible for a part of our users.
- **Detection parity**: EQL rules that use optional fields can't be migrated 1:1 to ES|QL.
- **UX and onboarding**: Users coming from EQL expect optional-field behavior, and this can cause frustration.

## Use Cases / Examples
 
- We had to remove one of the indices supported in a web server detection rule because a field was missing in one of the index patterns ([ref](https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/issues/5376)). This also made us restrict the data sources used in new ES|QL rules.

## Stopgaps
 
- `SET unmapped_fields="nullify"` ([#140463](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/140463)) can be used to bypass missing-field verification by nullifying unmapped fields, but this is not a viable stopgap for detection rules because it disables runtime verification for missing fields and can hide typos.

## Asks / Recommendations
 
- Add ES|QL support for per-field optional fields similar to EQL, treating missing fields as null instead of causing the query to fail. This should be granular so only explicitly marked fields become null, and other missing fields still fail verification.

## References
 
- https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/query-languages/eql/eql-syntax#eql-syntax-optional-fields
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/112912
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/138888
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/140463
- https://github.com/elastic/kibana/issues/246587
- [TRaDE Gaps and Blockers](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MWhqjiDonIC2NwxCm8rYodcBVrK1-6-Isw2LEredUlY/edit?usp=sharing)
issues.title: [ES|QL] Support per-field optional fields (EQL-like `?` operator)

issues.body:
## Description
 
Endpoint EQL (and legacy Endgame EQL) includes relationship operators like `descendant of`. This lets you filter events to those where a process is anywhere under another process in the process tree, not just a direct child.
 
In Elastic Defend data, ancestry is represented by:
 
- `process.entity_id`: A stable identifier for the process instance.
- `process.Ext.ancestry`: A multivalue field listing ancestor `process.entity_id` values (parent, grandparent, etc.).

ES|QL does not provide a native way to materialize a set of entity IDs from one query and use it to filter another (for example, matching those IDs against `process.Ext.ancestry`).
 
## Impact
 
- **Detection parity**: Endpoint EQL rules that use `descendant of` can't be migrated 1:1 to ES|QL.
- **Detection coverage**: We cannot create detection-focused equivalents of Endpoint EQL lineage logic. Endpoint rules are prevention-focused and not tolerant of false positives, so they are more restrictive than detection-focused content, reducing our overall threat coverage.
- **Performance**: The stopgap is memory-intensive and can timeout in high-volume environments.
- **Maintenance**: The stopgap can be harder to review and maintain.
- **Customer Support**: Deep process relationships allow for powerful correlation, differentiating us from competitors, and providing the right tools for our customers to protect their environments.

## Use Cases / Examples
 
### Example 1: Match descendants of an "ancestor" process set (EQL vs ES|QL intent)
 
Endpoint EQL logic:
 
```eql
process where process.name == "schtasks.exe" and
  descendant of [process where process.name in ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "mshta.exe")]
```
 
Desired logic (ES|QL - hypothetical syntax):
 
```esql
FROM logs-endpoint.events.process-*
| WHERE event.type == "start" AND process.name == "schtasks.exe"
| WHERE DESCENDANT_OF(
    process.Ext.ancestry,
    process.name IN ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "mshta.exe") | KEEP process.entity_id, host.id
  )
```
 
## Stopgaps
 
As a stopgap, ES|QL can approximate `descendant of` by using INLINE STATS to materialize a set of ancestor `process.entity_id` values, then comparing that set against each event's `process.Ext.ancestry`. If `MV_INTERSECTION()` returns any shared values, the event is treated as a descendant of the selected ancestor process.
 
This pattern is shipping today in production prebuilt detection rules, for example [Elastic Defend Alert from Package Manager Install Ancestry](https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/blob/main/rules/cross-platform/initial_access_elastic_defend_alert_package_manager_ancestor.toml) (condensed version, see the linked rule for the full query):
 
```esql
FROM logs-endpoint.alerts-*, logs-endpoint.events.process-* METADATA _id, _version, _index
 
| EVAL is_pkg_install = CASE(
    // npm  npx  yarn  pnpm (Node.js ecosystem)
    process.parent.name IN ("node", "node.exe") AND (
      process.parent.command_line LIKE "*npm install*" OR
      process.parent.command_line LIKE "*yarn add*" OR
      process.parent.command_line LIKE "*pnpm install*"
    ), true,
    // ... additional CASE branches for pip/pipx/poetry/uv and cargo elided ...
    false
  )
 
| WHERE process.Ext.ancestry IS NOT NULL AND (data_stream.dataset == "endpoint.alerts" OR is_pkg_install)
 
// Capture entity_ids for package install parent processes
| EVAL all_entity_id = CASE(is_pkg_install, process.parent.entity_id, "null")
 
// Collect all package install entity_ids globally
| INLINE STATS all_pkg_entity_ids = VALUES(all_entity_id) WHERE all_entity_id != "null"
 
// Find which package install entity_ids appear in this process's ancestry
| EVAL Esql.pkg_ancestor_ids = MV_INTERSECTION(all_pkg_entity_ids, process.Ext.ancestry)
 
// Elastic Defend alerts descended from a package install process
| WHERE Esql.pkg_ancestor_ids IS NOT NULL AND data_stream.dataset == "endpoint.alerts"
 
| KEEP *
```
 
Another production example: [Elastic Defend Alert from GenAI Utility or Descendant](https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/blob/main/rules/cross-platform/initial_access_elastic_defend_alert_genai_utility_descendant.toml).
 
Limitations:
 
- **Memory**: INLINE STATS must compute VALUES(all_entity_id) across the working set, which can require large in-memory state for wide time windows or high-cardinality matches.
- **Query planning**: Descendant filtering cannot be pushed down early, because the ancestor entity id set is materialized inside the same pipeline.

A potential alternative is to use subqueries to materialize the entity id set, once the technical preview capability is available for testing.
 
## Asks / Recommendations
 
- Add an ES|QL feature that is optimized for process relationship queries similar to Endpoint EQL `descendant of`.

## References
 
- https://www.elastic.co/blog/introducing-event-query-language
- https://www.elastic.co/docs/explore-analyze/query-filter/languages/eql
- https://github.com/endgameinc/eql/blob/master/docs/query-guide/basic-syntax.rst
- https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/query-languages/esql/commands/inlinestats-by
- https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/query-languages/esql/functions-operators/mv-functions
- https://github.com/search?q=repo%3Aelastic%2Fprotections-artifacts%20%22descendant%20of%22&type=code
- https://github.com/search?q=repo%3Aelastic%2Fdetection-rules%20MV_INTERSECTION&type=code
- [TRaDE Gaps and Blockers](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1MWhqjiDonIC2NwxCm8rYodcBVrK1-6-Isw2LEredUlY/edit?usp=sharing)
issues.title: [ES|QL] Add support for process relationship queries (EQL-like `descendant of`)

issues.body:
## Description

ES|QL already supports null-column suppression through the `drop_null_columns=true` request parameter. This removes columns that are null for the entire result set, reducing sparse output payloads.

The gap is that this behavior cannot be expressed in the ES|QL query itself. Query authors must rely on the caller, such as an agent or application layer, to remember to set the request parameter. For agent/LLM workflows, where ES|QL output may be passed directly into a model, this makes payload shaping less visible and less portable.

We want equivalent query-level syntax, preferably as a DROP-style command such as:

```esql
FROM logs-*
| KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, source.ip, destination.ip, *
| DROP NULL COLUMNS
```

or:

```esql
FROM logs-*
| KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, source.ip, destination.ip, *
| DROP WHERE NULL
```

The expected behavior should match the existing `drop_null_columns=true` response option: remove columns that are null for every row in the result set.

Note: this is not a blocker for us, the request parameter works today, but query-level syntax would make the behavior portable and easier for LLM agents to discover.

## Importance

For agent/LLM use cases, sparse ES|QL outputs can include many `field: null` values that add payload size without useful context. Having this behavior in the query makes output-shaping explicit, portable, and owned by the query author rather than each caller.

There is also a potential cost dimension for LLM callers: in the ES|QL response format, an all-null column contributes a `null` entry to every row in `values`, and `FROM logs-*` unions mappings across integrations, so sparse results can carry many such columns. The extra nulls count toward token costs and context window. We haven't benchmarked the impact.

## Stopgaps

- Ask agents to explicitly set `drop_null_columns=true`

## Asks / Recommendations

- Add ES|QL syntax for the existing null-column suppression behavior, preferably through a DROP-style command such as `| DROP NULL COLUMNS` or `| DROP WHERE NULL`.
issues.title: [ES|QL] Query-level syntax for null-column suppression (e.g. `DROP NULL COLUMNS`)

issues.body:
### Description

Elastic's Threat Research and Detection Engineering team (TRaDE) manages nearly 2,000 prebuilt detection rules. As we migrate rules to ES|QL, we need a programmatic capability to validate each query offline — for syntax, semantics, and schema — across multiple stack versions, without requiring a running Elastic Stack.

Today, ES|QL rules can only be validated remotely against a live cluster. We currently do this via remote validation (https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/pull/5222), which requires spinning up Elastic containers in CI, only validates against the latest stack version, and adds significant build time and infrastructure cost.

We have prototyped a Java wrapper around the ES|QL validation code in the Elasticsearch repo (POC: https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/pull/6207). It works well:

- Validating all ES|QL rules went from ~10min (remote) to ~4min, fully local
- We can validate against specific stack versions locally, closing a major gap (today we only validate against latest, so we don't catch ES|QL function backporting issues)
- It retains our required-fields population functionality

However, the POC depends directly on internal Elasticsearch Java interfaces (Analyzer, Verifier, function registry internals), which are not a stable contract and can change between versions — so it isn't a safe long-term integration point.

Following discussion with the ES|QL team (internal: https://github.com/elastic/ia-trade-team/issues/840), the proposed direction is a **well-defined, lean API — effectively the Analyzer + Verifier packaged as a standalone JAR** — that:

- Takes as input: index mappings, and an ES|QL query (including per-query SET settings)
- Returns: success, or VerificationException(s) pointing to the respective parts of the query that are invalid
- Is reflected in Elasticsearch's code as a supported API surface, so consumers aren't broken from one ES version to the next

This issue is to formalize that request and capture the full set of requirements.

## Requirements

Beyond the core validate(mappings, query) → ok | VerificationExceptions contract, our detection rules tooling needs:

- **Referenced-field extraction**: a way to enumerate the fields a query references and outputs. With EQL/KQL we extract fields from the parser AST; for ES|QL we currently return no AST and fall back to fragile regex patterns. This drives Kibana rule features such as required_fields and related_integrations, and validation of rule-type-specific fields (e.g., that alert_suppression.group_by fields exist in the query output). Note: the Analyzer + Verifier does not currently return a list of required fields.
- **Schema validation**: validate field keys and types against different schemas (ECS, integration schemas, beats), supplied as mappings.
- **Version-aware validation**: validate a query against a specific stack version (e.g., 8.19, 9.x), so a single toolchain can validate rules for all supported versions.
- **Semantic/lint-style diagnostics** (nice to have): warnings for ES|QL best practices we currently enforce with regex (e.g., required metadata fields, presence of keep commands) and expensive query patterns.
- **Published, versioned artifact**: released alongside Elasticsearch versions so grammar/verifier parity is maintained as ES|QL evolves.
- **Stability guarantee**: an agreed API surface that Elasticsearch commits to not breaking silently between versions.

## Impact

- Customers may inadvertently receive faulty rules that downstream impact their experience, workloads, or ability to detect & prevent threats
- ES|QL rules cannot be validated offline during development, requiring a running Elastic Stack instance
- CI/CD pipelines require spinning up entire Elastic containers to validate ES|QL queries, adding significant build time and infrastructure costs
- Field extraction from ES|QL queries (required_fields, related_integrations) relies on fragile regex patterns rather than proper AST traversal
- Cannot validate ES|QL queries against specific stack versions without running that version
- Rule authors receive validation feedback late in the development cycle (at CI time) rather than locally during authoring
- Index templates for integrations can have nuances that are only realized upon installing a given integration. Catching these nuances manually and adding fields to a static schema (non-ecs) creates significant manual overhead for our rule developers.

## Use Cases / Examples

- **AST-based field extraction**: With EQL/KQL, we use the parser's AST to extract all referenced fields via `[str(f) for f in self.ast if isinstance(f, eql.ast.Field)]`. For ES|QL, we currently return None from the ast property with a comment: "*Return the AST of the ESQL query. Dependant on an ESQL parser, which is not implemented*"
- **Integration detection**: For EQL/KQL, we parse event.dataset and data_stream.dataset values from the AST. For ES|QL, we use fragile regex patterns that can miss edge cases (e.g., `get_esql_query_event_dataset_integrations()` uses regex like `r"event\.dataset\s+in\s*\(\s*([^)]+)\s*\)"`)
- **Semantic validation**: Currently we validate ES|QL using regex patterns to check for required metadata fields and keep commands - patterns that can easily miss valid ES|QL syntax variations. A concrete example where the regex approach broke down and a proper parser would have made the fix much simpler to build and maintain: https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/issues/4575
- **Schema validation**: EQL and KQL validators can validate queries against ECS, beats, and integration schemas offline.
- **Alert suppression field validation**: Cannot validate that fields referenced in alert_suppression.group_by exist in the query output without parsing the query
- **Early error detection**: with offline validation in place, issues like https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/issues/6177 would have been caught early in development instead of after release.
- A large enterprise customer has told us they resorted to reimplementing their own ES|QL parser from the grammar to overcome the same gaps.

## Stopgaps

- **Remote validation** (https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/pull/5222): requires managing a combination of infrastructure — N stack releases, N integrations per rule, N rule variations and indices — causing significant overhead and complexity, leading to many issues that require investigation and manual work to resolve

## Asks / Recommendations

- Define and expose the Analyzer + Verifier as a standalone, supported API/JAR with the contract outlined above (mappings + query in; ok/VerificationExceptions out)
- Include or complement it with referenced-field/AST access so downstream tooling can extract fields without regex
- Support validation against specific stack versions, and publish the artifact per release so grammar parity is maintained
- Document the supported API surface and its stability guarantees

## References

- Internal (Elastic): https://github.com/elastic/security-team/issues/11554 (Epic: ES|QL python parser — original requirements), https://github.com/elastic/ia-trade-team/issues/840 (Meta: Java ES|QL validation — POC and API discussion with the ES|QL team)
- POC: https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/pull/6207
- Remote validation: https://github.com/elastic/detection-rules/pull/5222
