issues.body:
## Problem

PR #153462 adds `on_failure=ignore` for columnar mode. The question "a value could not be indexed normally, where should it go?" is answered in at least four places independently: `DocumentParser.parseObjectOrField` pre-captures to `_ignored_source` based on `syntheticSourceMode()` and `sourceKeepMode`; `DocumentParserContext.enforceSingleValue` writes to the `._on_failure` failure column based on source mode; `IgnoreMalformedStoredValues` call sites write to `._ignore_malformed` or stored fields based on source mode and index version. None of these were designed to own routing decisions, yet all of them do. This makes the routing logic impossible to test in one place: covering all combinations of source mode, failure reason, and call site requires tests scattered across the codebase, and the interactions between call sites fall through the gaps entirely.

The known instance is `parseObjectOrField` pre-capturing to `_ignored_source` before calling `fieldMapper.parse()`, while `enforceSingleValue` inside `fieldMapper.parse()` also writes the violated value to the `._on_failure` failure column. For fields with fallback synthetic source mode or `sourceKeepMode == ARRAYS`, both paths fire for the same violation. This will not be the last such interaction as the feature grows.

## Goal

The storage routing responsibility needs a single owner so that adding a new mechanism cannot silently interact with an existing one. The `parseObjectOrField` pre-capture pattern is the most concrete place to address, as it makes a storage decision independently of the field mapper. Any solution should guarantee that a value is written to exactly one fallback location regardless of source mode.

The storage invariant tests from #153767 should be in place first: any change to storage routing that breaks storage uniqueness or semantic equivalence will be caught without manual inspection of `parsedDoc.rootDoc()`.

## Benefits

- **Synthetic source reconstruction**: the read side has a single authoritative answer for where a redirected value lives, rather than reconciling multiple columns.
- **Block loaders**: a central routing owner provides the natural place to define the read contract, so block loaders do not re-derive source-mode branching independently.
- **New failure reasons**: adding a constraint type is one additional case in one place rather than a new instance of scattered branching.
- **New source modes**: branching logic changes in one place rather than across every call site.
issues.title: Consolidate fallback value storage routing to prevent source-mode interaction bugs

issues.body:
## Problem

PR #153462 adds `on_failure=ignore` for columnar mode. When a field constraint fires and the violating value is redirected to the `._on_failure` failure column, `parseObjectOrField` may also pre-capture the same value to `_ignored_source` via `addIgnoredFieldFromContext` before calling `fieldMapper.parse()`, for fields with fallback synthetic source mode or with `sourceKeepMode == ARRAYS`.

One confirmed instance: a field in FALLBACK synthetic source mode (e.g. keyword with a normalizer) that also has `multi_value=false` and `on_failure=ignore` will pre-capture the violated value into `_ignored_source` and also write it to `._on_failure`, wasting disk since only one copy is emitted in the output. The same double-storage risk applies to `ignore_malformed` and any future fallback mechanism. The existing tests cover whether the feature fires (failure column is populated, `_ignored` is marked) but not whether it stores correctly. No test parameterizes over `synthetic` and `columnar_stored` source modes. No test asserts that `_ignored_source` is not simultaneously written for the same field and value, or that the violated value is absent from the main field doc values. No test verifies that `GET _source` returns identical results across source modes.

## Goal

**Storage uniqueness tests** (`MapperServiceTestCase`, parameterized over `synthetic` and `columnar_stored`). For each source mode and each violation type (`multi_value=false` and `nullability=false`), parse a document that triggers `on_failure=ignore` and inspect `parsedDoc.rootDoc()` directly: the main field doc values contain exactly the valid value; the `._on_failure` sidecar field is present; `_ignored_source` does not also contain the violated value; `_ignored` is populated.

**Semantic equivalence tests**. `SyntheticVersusColumnarStoredSourceIT` already verifies equivalence between `synthetic` and `columnar_stored` for the general case but `buildSpec()` does not set `multi_value=false`, `nullability=false`, or `on_failure=ignore`. Extend the generator to exercise violation scenarios and assert that `GET _source` returns an identical document from both indices and that `_ignored` contains the field name in both cases. These tests also provide the safety net for the routing abstraction refactoring described in #153765, and will extend naturally to cover the `._on_failure` read path once synthetic source reconstruction is wired.
issues.title: Verify fallback value storage uniqueness and equivalence across source modes

issues.body:
### Description

Several binary doc-values queries construct their doc-values readers inside `Weight#scorerSupplier` rather than in `ScorerSupplier#get`:

- `BinaryDvConfirmedQuery#scorerSupplier` builds the `SortedBinaryDocValues` used for wildcard confirmation before returning the supplier: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/db81aa43468d65dca016ed88400129413007dc2b/x-pack/plugin/wildcard/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/wildcard/mapper/BinaryDvConfirmedQuery.java#L186-L188
- `BinaryDocValuesContainsTermQuery#scorerSupplier` calls `getBinaryDocValues` and builds the two-phase iterator eagerly: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/db81aa43468d65dca016ed88400129413007dc2b/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/lucene/queries/BinaryDocValuesContainsTermQuery.java#L59
- `ScanningBinaryDocValuesTermQuery#scorerSupplier`: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/db81aa43468d65dca016ed88400129413007dc2b/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/lucene/queries/ScanningBinaryDocValuesTermQuery.java#L57
- `BinaryDocValuesLengthQuery#scorerSupplier`: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/db81aa43468d65dca016ed88400129413007dc2b/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/lucene/queries/BinaryDocValuesLengthQuery.java#L55

On TSDB/logsdb segments, `getBinaryDocValues` constructs an `AbstractTSDBDocValuesProducer$BinaryDecoder` per query clause per segment: `IndexInput` clones, `DirectMonotonicReader` block tables, a per-block offsets array, and until #153903 also a decompression buffer sized to the largest uncompressed block in the segment (128k minimum).

This runs during query planning. `BooleanScorerSupplier` instantiates suppliers for every clause in order to compare costs before pulling any scorer, so for a query with many such clauses over many segments all of this **state is allocated up front and held for the whole planning phase, including for clauses that never execute**. Under high search concurrency this multiplies across threads; it contributed to the heap exhaustion investigated in https://github.com/elastic/incident-management/issues/2277, where the failing allocation was inside `BinaryDvConfirmedQuery$1.scorerSupplier` while threads were still in `BooleanScorerSupplier.computeCost`. #153903 mitigates the largest single allocation by allocating the buffer lazily, but the reader construction itself is still eager in all four queries.

### Lucene contract

The `ScorerSupplier` API exists to separate cost estimation from scorer construction. From the Lucene 10.5 javadoc:

- `ScorerSupplier`: "A supplier of `Scorer`. This allows to get an estimate of the cost before building the `Scorer`."
- `ScorerSupplier#get(long leadCost)`: "Get the `Scorer`. This may not return `null` and must be called at most once."
- `Weight#scorerSupplier(LeafReaderContext)`: "Get a `ScorerSupplier`, which allows knowing the cost of the `Scorer` before building it. A scorer supplier for the same `LeafReaderContext` instance may be requested multiple times as part of a single search call."

Since `get` is called at most once and only for clauses that actually execute, **expensive per-leaf setup belongs there**; work done in `scorerSupplier` is paid for every clause during planning and may even be paid multiple times per leaf. `IndexOrDocValuesQuery` is the canonical consumer of this split: it requests both suppliers, compares costs, and discards one without ever calling `get` on it.

### Proposal

Move the doc-values reader construction (and iterator setup where applicable) from `scorerSupplier()` into `ScorerSupplier#get(leadCost)` in the four queries above. `cost()` needs none of it: in `BinaryDvConfirmedQuery` it delegates to the approximation's supplier, and in the other three it derives from `maxDoc`. The existing null/early returns for leaves without the field keep working as is.

There is precedent for this kind of deferral in `BinaryDvConfirmedQuery`: #136086 delayed automaton creation for the same reason (OOM on queries against wildcard fields).

Relates to #153903.
issues.title: Binary doc-values queries create doc-values readers in `scorerSupplier` instead of `ScorerSupplier#get`

issues.body:
### Description

Right now enabling/disabling directory metrics requires a feature flag - which means there is a default on/off setting that can be overridden on a per deployment base. As this has a performance impact it would be great to only enable/disable this behavior at runtime. The task is to investigate if this is possible, and if so, implement.

The current implementation is doing the accounting by using a special IndexInput in `StoreMetricsDirectory` - which in turn is only used when the feature flag is enabled and is wrapping `ByteSizeDirectory`. This does not work with dynamic updating.

Few options to explore and check how big the performance impact is:

* Wrapping the index input with a `volatile` that is updated when a new dynamic setting is changed
* Wrapping the directory with a live setting, so that accounting is only enabled/disabled if a segment is reopened, which may not happen for big/old segments, but only for smaller newer ones or when they are merged - this means you do not have a hundred percent guarantee that a search is fully accounted  for
* A third option that I may have missed that is safe to implement, has less of a performance impact and is exact
issues.title: Directory Metrics: Investigate to move from feature flag to dynamic setting

issues.body:
### Description

The decision to pre or post filter is made most optimally within a segment, since that is the most granular place to make the decision and would allow for different execution paths based on the per-segment selectivity of the filter instead of the aggregated selectivity of the filter at the shard level. At the moment, we make the decision at the shard level. We discussed this possible improvement here https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/148876#discussion_r3243808579

Additional benefits of per-segment pre/post filtering is that it allows for easier/earlier resume query logic because it would be done on the search thread (based on the current design) instead of the query thread.

Note that I mention only disk bbq here because that is the only segment search code we have control over. The HNSW is in lucene.

Further, it seems plausible that a codec might make different decisions about when to pre/post filter, especially as we trend towards possible other implementations that might merge filtering with vector index exploration.

issues.body:
In https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/150193 we implemented the lucene pushdown when the left field is pushable field attribute and the right argument is foldable. We push down MV_CONTAINS as a `TermsSetQuery`.

However, we can also push down in the case where the left argument is foldable and the right one is a pushable field attribute, e.g. `MV_CONTAINS(["python", "c++"], programming_languages)`.
In this case we won't have a clear equivalent like `TermsSetQuery`.
The most obvious way would be to push it down as a `TermsQuery`, but still recheck (use `Translatable.RECHECK`). This would still provide a better performance than not pushing down MV_CONTAINS, since it would filter out any docs that don't contain any of the given values.

**EDIT: !!!!!** One problem is that `MV_CONTAINS(["python", "c++"], NULL)` returns true, so we can't just use `TermsQuery`, we would need a boolean query **!!!**

It would be nice if we can use a `QueryBuilder` such that we don't need to recheck. I assume we can, but needs more thought.
issues.title: ES|QL: MV_CONTAINS pushdown for foldable left/pushable right args

issues.body:
## Problem

When using `drop_null_columns=true` with `format=json`, the response body still enumerates **every** mapped column in the `all_columns` metadata array — even those that were dropped because they were null. For wide, sparse indices this metadata alone can be enormous.

Example: an index pattern with 345,327 mapped fields (only ~84 populated per document). The `all_columns` array in every response lists all 345k column names + types, adding significant wire size and parsing overhead that is entirely wasted for clients that don't use it.

## Context

`all_columns` was added so clients (e.g. Kibana Discover) could show the full schema alongside the projected result. That's useful in the Discover use case, but it is actively harmful for programmatic/data-pipeline clients that just want the data without the bulk metadata overhead.

## Request

Provide a way to suppress `all_columns` from the response — for example:
- A new request parameter `include_all_columns=false` (opt-out, default `true` for backwards compatibility), or
- Honour an existing content-negotiation or request flag to omit it.

This is orthogonal to `drop_null_columns`: a client may want drop + no metadata, drop + metadata, or keep + no metadata.

## Impact

For the 345k-field case, not sending `all_columns` would eliminate a large chunk of response size entirely and remove a significant per-request CPU cost on the server side (serialising 345k entries).

## Related

- Slack thread: https://elastic.slack.com/archives/C02TBFZFYSD/p1784553318112749
- Companion issue (Arrow format ignores `drop_null_columns`): https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/154522
issues.title: ES|QL: all_columns metadata is prohibitively expensive for wide/sparse indices and cannot be suppressed

issues.body:
Tracking Kibana side: https://github.com/elastic/kibana/issues/257804

## Summary

We're evaluating whether the Security Solution **Indicator Match** detection rule type can be reimplemented on top of ES|QL. This epic captures the ES|QL/Elasticsearch capabilities that would be required, each broken out as a sub-issue with the detection-rule behavior it maps to.

## Primer: what is an Indicator Match rule?

A **detection rule** runs on a schedule, queries user data, and creates **alerts** when it finds something. Different **rule types** have different matching logic.

**Indicator Match (IM)** correlates a customer's **event data** (logs, network traffic, endpoint events) against a **threat-intelligence index** ("indicators" = known-bad IPs, file hashes, domains, etc.). It alerts when an event matches a known indicator.

The rule config is a **threat mapping**: a list of field pairs like `event.source.ip  ↔  threat.indicator.ip`. The rule answers: *"Is this event's `source.ip` present in my threat-intel list of bad IPs?"* — which is exactly a semi-join / membership test.

Threat-intelligence feeds are large — commonly **millions of indicators**, sometimes 10M+. An Indicator Match rule matches customer events against that entire set on every run. The current implementation handles this by **paging** through both the event side and the threat side (PIT + `search_after`, no total-size cap), so feed size doesn't cause a hard failure.

Key properties of the **current** (DSL) implementation that any migration must preserve:

1. **The threat index is an ordinary index / data stream** (can be cross-cluster).
2. **The alert carries "enrichment"**: which specific indicator matched, from which feed, its document id/index — pulled from the matched threat document.
3. **Multiple fields can be required together** (tuple/AND matching): "same indicator must match on `source.ip` AND `source.port`."
4. **The threat index is deliberately NOT time-filtered.** The rule's lookback window bounds which *events* to scan, not which *indicators* are still valid (a 6-month-old IOC is still valid).
5. **Threat feeds are large** (millions of indicators) and often **multi-valued** (one indicator listing several IPs).
6. **Cross-cluster search works on any license today.**

## Current ES|QL options and where they fall short

We looked at the two membership/join constructs ES|QL offers:

| Requirement | `LOOKUP JOIN` | `WHERE … IN (<subquery>)` |
|---|---|---|
| Reads an ordinary threat index / data stream | ❌ requires `index.mode=lookup` (reindex/mirror) | ✅ any ordinary index |
| Cross-cluster / remote threat index | ❌ right side can never be remote-qualified | ✅ works in every combination |
| Returns the matched indicator row (enrichment) | ✅ returns right-side columns | ❌ semi-join, no right-side identity |
| Multi-field (tuple) AND matching | ✅ multi-key `ON` | ❌ single-column, non-correlated |
| Scale / large threat sets | ✅ streams + probes, no size cap | ⚠️ coordinator-materialized, ~1M keyword ceiling @ default |

**The problem:** the two constructs' strengths are **mutually exclusive within one clause**.
- Need ordinary/remote threat indices → `IN`, but you lose tuple matching + enrichment.
- Need tuple matching or enrichment → `LOOKUP JOIN`, but you're back to lookup-mode + no-remote.

Plus a third class of issues sits **outside** the `IN`-vs-`JOIN` choice (filter scoping, range matching, MV/NULL semantics, CCS licensing, scale).

## The asks (sub-issues)

**Would unblock a general-purpose migration:**
- [ ] https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/154846 
- [ ] https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/154847
- [ ] https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/154849

**Feature/semantic gaps that apply regardless of which construct we use:**
- [ ] https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/155881
- [ ] https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/154851
- [ ] https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/154852

## Glossary

- **Event index**: the customer's data being monitored.
- **Threat index / indicators**: the threat-intel list being matched against.
- **Threat mapping**: the field-pair config defining what "matches."
- **Enrichment (`threat.enrichments`)**: metadata about *which* indicator matched, attached to the alert.
- **Lookback window**: the rule's event time range per run.
issues.title: [Epic] ES|QL capabilities needed for a native Indicator Match detection rule

issues.body:
## Context (Indicator Match)

Our Indicator Match rule matches customer events against a threat-intel index. When an event matches an indicator, the resulting alert must include **enrichment**: *which* indicator matched — the threat document's `_id`, `_index`, the feed name, and selected fields copied from the indicator doc (`threat.enrichments`). Analysts rely on this to triage ("this IP matched the AbuseCH feed, indicator doc X").

## What we need

A join/lookup construct that:
1. Returns **columns from the matched right-side (threat) row**, like `LOOKUP JOIN` does, AND
2. Works against an **ordinary index or data stream** (NOT `index.mode=lookup`), AND
3. Allows the right side to be **remote / cross-cluster qualified**.

## Why the existing constructs don't cover it

- `WHERE … IN (<subquery>)` is a **semi-join**: it returns qualifying left-side (event) rows and *nothing* about which right-side (indicator) row caused the match. No enrichment source.
- `LOOKUP JOIN` **does** return right-side columns, but requires the right index to be `index.mode=lookup` and the right side **can never be remote-qualified**. Threat indices are frequently remote and ordinary-mode.

## How this maps to current rule behavior

Today enrichment is produced by a **separate follow-up search** using Lucene named queries (`matched_queries`) against the threat index, because the detection query alone can't return the matched indicator identity. That works but keeps a second round-trip and its scaling limits. A join that returns the matched row would let enrichment come from the detection query itself.
issues.title: [ES|QL] Join form that returns the matched right-side row against an ordinary/remote index

issues.body:
## Context (Indicator Match)

An Indicator Match "threat mapping" can require **multiple fields to match the same indicator document at once**. Example: a mapping group of `{ event.source.ip = threat.ip } AND { event.source.port = threat.port }` means: *alert only when there exists a single indicator doc whose `ip` AND `port` both match this event.* This "tuple / AND" matching is a core, first-class feature of the rule type.

## What we need

A way to express **correlated multi-column membership** — the same right-side (indicator) row must match on multiple columns simultaneously — against **ordinary / remote** indices. Semantically equivalent to `LOOKUP JOIN`'s multi-key `ON a = x AND b = y`, but without the lookup-mode + no-remote constraints.

## Why the existing constructs don't cover it

- `WHERE … IN (<subquery>)` is **single-column and non-correlated**. This produces false positives (e.g. event
  matches ip from indicator A and port from indicator B, which is not a real match). `postAnalysisVerification` also fails on any multi-field subquery config.
- `LOOKUP JOIN` supports multi-key `ON`, but only against lookup-mode, non-remote indices
  (see https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/154846).

## How this maps to current rule behavior

The current engine expresses tuple matching by materializing one boolean clause per (threat document × mapping group), embedding the concrete field values and requiring all entries in the group to match on the same doc. Every multi-entry mapping group uses this path. There is no ES|QL construct that reproduces it against ordinary indices.

## Impact if unmet

Multi-field IM rules (a large, security-relevant class — e.g. IP+port, user+host) simply cannot migrate. Any ES|QL IM variant would be limited to **single-field** mappings.
issues.title: [ES|QL] Correlated multi-column (tuple) membership / join against ordinary indices

issues.body:
## Context

Kibana's detection rules pass a single **request-level DSL filter** on the ES|QL query request, carrying the rule's **time-range (lookback) window** plus exception filters. Today Elasticsearch applies that filter to **every** source in the plan — including a `WHERE … IN (<subquery>)` subquery.

## What we need

A way to scope the request filter to the **outer `FROM`** only so a filter meant for the primary source does not silently apply to a subquery/right-side source.

## How this maps to current rule behavior 

In the current Indicator Match implementation, the threat index is **deliberately NOT time-filtered**. The rule's lookback window bounds which **events** to scan; it must NOT bound which **indicators** are valid — a threat indicator ingested 6 months ago is still a valid match against an event from 5 minutes ago.

If the request time-range filter leaks into the threat subquery:
- Only indicators *ingested within the lookback window* would qualify — for a typical feed, essentially none.
- And it fails **silently**:
  - empty subquery → `field IN (<empty>)` folds to `FALSE` → **zero alerts**
  - negated mapping → `field NOT IN (<empty>)` → **every event alerts**

No error is raised — the rule just silently produces wrong results.
issues.title: [ES|QL] Scope the request-level filter to the outer FROM only (don't leak into subqueries)

issues.body:
## Context (Indicator Match)

Threat-intel indicators are sometimes **ranges**, not exact values — most commonly `ip_range` (a CIDR block like `10.0.0.0/8`), and numeric ranges. Indicator Match today matches an event's value **inside** such a range (containment), e.g. "does this event's `source.ip` fall within any bad CIDR block?"

## What we need

A membership/containment construct in ES|QL that can test whether a scalar value is **contained within a range** sourced from another index — the range analog of `WHERE field IN (<subquery of exact values>)`.

## Why the existing constructs don't cover it

Both `WHERE … IN (<subquery>)` and `LOOKUP JOIN` are **equality / key-based**. Neither expresses range containment. ES|QL has no range membership type for this shape.

## How this maps to current rule behavior

The current engine matches events against range-typed indicators via range queries. Range lists (`ip_range` and numeric ranges) are a supported indicator/value-list type.

## Impact if unmet

CIDR/range-based IM rules and range value-lists cannot migrate.
issues.title: [ES|QL] Range / CIDR containment matching (e.g. ip_range indicators)

issues.body:
## Context (Indicator Match)

Threat indicators are frequently **multi-valued**: one indicator document may list several IPs, hashes, or domains in a single field, e.g. `threat.ip = ["1.1.1.1","2.2.2.2"]`. The rule should match an event if it hits **any element** of such a list.

## The behavior difference

**`WHERE … IN (<subquery>)` today:**
- Multi-valued values on **either side collapse to NULL and never match**. A threat  indicator with an array field is silently ignored unless flattened with `MV_EXPAND`  inside the subquery.
- **`NOT IN` with any NULL in the subquery result matches zero rows** — a single NULL in the  threat set turns a whole negated rule into "matches nothing."

**How Indicator Match behaves today (the semantics we'd be changing):**
- On the side being matched against, arrays "just work" — an event matches if it hits **any element** of a multi-valued indicator field (Lucene terms semantics).
- "Does not match" (negation) degrades gracefully — missing fields fall back to a sensible existence check rather than nullifying the whole clause.

## Why it matters

Both differences fail **silently** (no error), which is the dangerous part:
- Common multi-value threat-intel data would quietly stop generating alerts.
- One NULL in a threat feed could silently disable an entire "does-not-match" rule.

## What we need

One of:
1. `IN`/`NOT IN` semantics that match Lucene terms behavior for multi-valued fields (any-element match), and non-catastrophic NULL handling for `NOT IN`; **or**
2. Clear, documented guidance + a supported, ergonomic pattern (e.g. blessed `MV_EXPAND` usage inside subqueries) that reproduces any-element matching, plus documented `NOT IN` NULL behavior so clients can guard against it.
issues.title: [ES|QL] Multi-valued / NULL matching semantics for IN / NOT IN

issues.body:
## Summary

We're evaluating whether the Security Solution **New Terms** detection rule type can be reimplemented on ES|QL. A POC that replaced an original `INLINE STATS` approach with `STATS … BY` + `FIRST(...)` clears the original failure mode and is a real improvement, but it still doesn't match the current (`_search`-based) implementation at the high-cardinality end, and it surfaced a correctness question around `FIRST` tie-breaking.

This issue is to share our findings and the blockers we hit. We'd value your read on what's expected behavior, what's tunable, and what (if anything) is on the roadmap that could help.

## Primer: what is a New Terms rule?

A **detection rule** runs on a schedule, queries user data, and creates **alerts**. The **New Terms** rule type alerts when a field value (or combination of values) appears that has **not been seen before** within a configured historical baseline.

Config:
- `new_terms_fields`: 1–3 fields (e.g. `host.name`, or `[user.name, host.name]`).
- `history_window_start`: start of the baseline window (e.g. `now-14d`).

Behavior, per run:
1. Establish a **baseline** = the distinct values (or value-combinations, for multiple fields) of `new_terms_fields` seen in the **history window** (`history_window_start` → detection interval start).
2. In the **detection interval**, find values/combinations **absent** from the baseline — those are "new terms."
3. For each genuinely-new term, emit an alert attributed to the **introducing document** (the first doc that produced that value), copying its fields into the alert.

Equivalent ES|QL shape (single pass over baseline + interval): group by the fields, compute `first_seen = MIN(@timestamp)` per group, keep groups whose `first_seen` falls in the detection interval (i.e. not present in history), and extract the introducing doc's fields.

## Two characteristics that make this hard in ES|QL

1. **We need a coherent "first document per group," not just aggregates.** The alert is built from the *introducing* document — its `_id`, `_index`, and multiple source fields — and they must all come from the **same** document.
2. **It's inherently high-cardinality.** The rule enumerates distinct values/combinations of the grouping fields; multi-valued fields multiply that cardinality. The current engine is **bounded per request** (paged); a single ES|QL aggregation query has no equivalent bound.

## Current (V1) implementation, for reference

Three-phase, **memory-bounded-per-request** pipeline:
1. Composite aggregation over the rule interval, paged at `PAGE_SIZE = 10000`.
2. For each batch of candidate terms, a history-window composite agg with `include` restriction, batched at `BATCH_SIZE = 500`, filtered via `bucket_selector: first_seen > start_time`.
3. Terms agg with `include` + `top_hits size:1` to fetch the introducing document. Phase 1 paging stops once `createdSignalsCount > maxSignals`.

There is no equivalent to this bounded, paged architecture in a single ES|QL query.

## POC approaches

**V2a — `INLINE STATS` (original POC):**
```sql
| INLINE STATS first_seen = MIN(@timestamp) BY <fields>
| WHERE @timestamp == first_seen
| INLINE STATS min_doc_id = MIN(_id) BY <fields>
| WHERE _id == min_doc_id

**Test environment:** Elastic Cloud, ES `9.4.2`, 2 data nodes × 408 MiB heap, sub-plan cap `esql.intermediate_local_relation_max_size ≈ 8.16 MiB` (~2% heap).

Single-valued (500k docs, 100k cardinality):

| Fields | INLINE STATS (V2a) | STATS + FIRST (V2b) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ✅ 2.53 s | ✅ 1.15 s |
| 2 | ❌ `sub-plan [8.9 MB] > 8.1 MB` | ✅ 1.24 s |
| 3 | ❌ `sub-plan [9.2 MB] > 8.1 MB` | ✅ 1.43 s |

Multi-valued, mv=3 (200k docs, 50k cardinality/field):

| Fields | INLINE STATS + MV | STATS + FIRST + MV |
|---|---|---|
| 1 MV | ✅ 1.13 s | ✅ 0.52 s |
| 2 MV | ❌ `sub-plan [14.8 MB] > 8.1 MB` | ✅ 4.23 s |
| 2 MV + 1 SV | ❌ `sub-plan [41.6 MB] > 8.1 MB` | ❌ `[parent] data for [First] would be [387.7 MB] > [387.5 MB]` |

**Net status:** unblocked from the POC's original failure mode, but performance does not yet match V1 at the high end, and `FIRST` tie-breaking is an open correctness question.
issues.title: [ES|QL] New Terms detection rule: findings and blockers from a V1 → ES|QL migration POC

issues.body:
## Summary

We're migrating the Security Solution **Threshold** detection rule type to ES|QL. The ES|QL query works and passes our tests — Threshold is the closest to ready of the rule types we've looked at — but we've hit a few blockers, most of which depend on ES|QL/Elasticsearch. This epic gives the domain context and links each specific language/capability gap as a sub-issue.

Related prior tracking: elastic/kibana#257810.

## Primer: what is a Threshold rule?

A **detection rule** runs on a schedule, queries user data, and creates **alerts**. The **Threshold** rule type alerts when the number of events matching a query — grouped by zero or more fields — meets or exceeds a configured count within the rule's time interval.

Config:
- A query/filter selecting events.
- `threshold.field`: 0–N group-by fields. (Zero fields = a single count over all matching events.)
- `threshold.value`: the minimum event count for a group to alert.
- `threshold.cardinality` (optional): a secondary condition — the number of **distinct** values of another field in the group must also meet a value (e.g. "≥ 5 distinct `source.ip`").

Behavior, per run: group matching events by `threshold.field`, count events per group (and optionally the distinct count of the cardinality field), and emit **one alert per group** that meets the count (and cardinality) condition.

Equivalent ES|QL shape:
```sql
FROM <indices>
| WHERE <rule query>
| STATS count = COUNT(*),
        distinct = COUNT_DISTINCT(<cardinality_field>)
  BY <threshold_fields>
| WHERE count >= <value> AND distinct >= <cardinality_value>
issues.title: [Epic] Threshold detection rule → ES|QL: findings and blockers

issues.body:
## Context (Threshold)

Threshold rules support an optional **cardinality** condition: a group alerts only if the number of **distinct** values of a chosen field meets a configured value (e.g. "≥ 10 distinct `user.name`"). In ES|QL we express this with `COUNT_DISTINCT(<field>) BY <threshold_fields>`.

## What we're seeing

The Threshold ES|QL query works and passes tests in general, but with the cardinality condition it **fails with performance errors on high-cardinality data**, and `COUNT_DISTINCT` carries a documented **accuracy limit around 40,000** distinct values.

Two distinct concerns for this rule type:
- **Failures at high cardinality** make otherwise-valid cardinality-threshold rules unrunnable on realistic data.
- **Approximate counts are boundary-sensitive here.** Unlike a dashboard where a ~1% error is cosmetic, a Threshold rule compares the distinct count directly against the configured value — so an approximate count near the threshold can flip an alert on or off (false positives/negatives) rather than just being slightly off.

## How this maps to current rule behavior

The current (`_search`-based) implementation uses a `cardinality` aggregation for this condition; the migration relies on `COUNT_DISTINCT` as the equivalent.
issues.title: [ES|QL] COUNT_DISTINCT accuracy and performance on high-cardinality data (Threshold rule)

issues.body:
## Context (Threshold)

Threshold rules routinely query **many indices at once**, and the same field name often has **different mappings across those indices** — e.g. `source.ip` mapped as `ip` in one index and `keyword` in another. The field may be a group-by (`threshold.field`) or the cardinality field, so it ends up in `STATS … BY` / `COUNT_DISTINCT`.

## What we're seeing

ES|QL queries **fail when a field has conflicting mapping types across the queried indices**. Our current workaround is to cast the field to a string (e.g. `TO_STRING(...)`) so the query passes verification — but casting introduces its own problems:

- `TO_STRING` gets the query **past the type verifier** in all cases we've tested.
- **But for a `date + keyword` conflict it produces duplicate buckets**: the date side serializes with `.000` precision while the keyword side keeps the raw input string, so the *same logical value* lands in two different groups. For a rule that counts per group, that splits a group's events across two buckets and changes the counts — i.e. it affects correctness, not just formatting.
- `TO_DATETIME(TO_STRING(...))` re-normalizes both sides to the same instant and collapses the buckets — but that remedy is **type-specific**.
- Because the correct cast depends on the actual conflicting types, the cast strategy has to be **decided at the moment the ES|QL query is constructed** (from `field_caps`), per field. That makes it a per-type-pair workaround we'd own and maintain, and one that's easy to get subtly wrong (the `date + keyword` case above).

The epic notes the string-cast workaround "may impact performance" as well.

## How this maps to current rule behavior

The current (`_search`-based) implementation aggregates across mixed-mapping indices without the query author having to reconcile per-index types; grouping/counting behaves consistently. The ES|QL path requires us to detect conflicts and hand-pick casts up front to get equivalent bucketing.
issues.title: [ES|QL] Multi-index mapping type conflicts (same field, different types) — Threshold rule

issues.body:
## Context 

Detection rules can be defined against a **data view**, and that data view may include **runtime fields**. As an example, these runtime fields can be used in the rule query, as a group-by (`threshold.field`), or as the cardinality field.

## What we're seeing

Rules that rely on data-view runtime fields **do not work in ES|QL**: the runtime fields aren't available/extracted, so a field the rule depends on effectively isn't there. 

## How this maps to current rule behavior

The current (`_search`-based) implementation resolves the data view's runtime field definitions into `runtime_mappings` on each search, so runtime fields behave like any other field for querying, grouping, and cardinality. The ES|QL path has no equivalent, so those rules can't migrate as-is.
issues.title: [ES|QL] Dataview runtime-field support for detection rules migration

Integer fields mapped with index_terms: true (introduced in #153163) are indexed as terms in the inverted index instead of BKD points (doc values are still kept). Range queries therefore go through the terms dictionary (cost grows with the number of matching terms) or fall back to doc values, rather than through points.

We should investigate whether enabling a doc-values skipper by default for these fields is worthwhile — i.e. whether it meaningfully speeds up range queries enough to justify the extra write/storage cost.

issues.body:
## Summary

When Elasticsearch successfully indexes a Prometheus remote write request but the client times out, the client can retry the same write. That retry can then hit `VersionConflictEngineException` for documents already inserted by the first request.

The version-conflict pattern is not unique to Prometheus remote write, but PRW amplifies it because one request can contain many samples and the protocol/exporter behavior can turn a duplicate conflict into confusing permanent-failure reporting.

## Problem

- A retried request that was already indexed can return HTTP 400/version-conflict responses for duplicate documents.
- Prometheus itself may not report HTTP 400 in this path: https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/v2.55.1/tsdb/head_append.go#L979
- OTel Prometheus remote write exporter can treat the response as permanent failure and report dropped data.
- Initial investigation found HTTP 400s correlated with timeout/load spikes: Elasticsearch indexes the request, the client times out, the client retries, and the retry conflicts with already stored documents.
- There was no evidence of whole-batch data loss in the repro, but current behavior makes retry/partial-failure semantics hard to reason about.

## Proposal

Evaluate whether the Prometheus remote write endpoint should:

1. Treat identical retries as idempotent when the generated document ID/content matches an already-indexed sample.
2. Improve partial-failure reporting so duplicate-on-retry conflicts are distinguishable from real ingestion failures.
3. Confirm the behavior for both direct Prometheus remote write clients and OTel Collector PRW exporter paths.

## Expected outcome

Retries of already-successful PRW writes should not look like data loss or permanent ingestion failure when the only failures are duplicate documents from the original successful write.
issues.title: PromQL: Prometheus remote write retries should be idempotent when the original request succeeded

issues.body:
### Description

When a text embedding request exceeds a model's token limit, inputs are silently truncated. The caller receives a successful response with embeddings derived from a fraction of the submitted text, with no indication that truncation occurred.

This is a correctness problem: search quality degrades silently, and there is no signal to the caller that they should chunk their input or switch to a field type that handles chunking automatically (e.g. `semantic_text`).

ES should surface truncation to callers so that users are not left to discover the problem through degraded recall.

I realize that exact token counts require model-specific tokenization, but character length is a usable order-of-magnitude proxy for detecting likely truncation. We don't need to be precise, but a user who sends a 100 page PDF and only gets inference on the first paragraph should get a warning.

Some actionable options to notify could include:
* HTTP Warning header
* Configurable parameter (`throw_on_likely_truncation` ?): 422, opt-in would be non-breaking (and probably useless), opt-out would be breaking.

This would have to be transmitted through the inference pipeline, obv.

I don't know what the best way to notify the user would be, but we should try to do something more than truncate silently.


Relates to #138700 (inconsistent `max_input_tokens` handling across services).
issues.title: [Inference API] Silent truncation of inputs exceeding model token limits should be surfaced to callers

issues.body:
## Context (Indicator Match)

Our Indicator Match rule correlates a customer's **event data** against a **threat-intelligence index** on a configured field pair, e.g. `event.source.ip ↔ threat.indicator.ip`. It alerts when an event's value is present in the threat set, which is a membership test on that field pair.

The two sides of a pair are not guaranteed to share a type. The most common shape of this is `ip` on one side and `keyword` on the other, but it also occurs *within a single side* when the field is queried across multiple indices that mapped it differently (e.g. `keyword` in one index, `ip` in another). Today these rules match correctly with no special handling.

Whether a given rule is affected depends on the live index mappings, not the rule configuration: the field pair and index patterns are declared in the rule, but the resolved types come from the data on that cluster at execution time.

## What we need

A join / membership construct whose **key can span fields that resolve to different types across the queried indices** (e.g. `keyword` vs `ip`) and still match correctly, **without requiring a lossy, whole-column cast** of the key to a common type.

Concretely: we want to answer "is this event's `source.ip` in the set of `threat.indicator.ip` values?" when the two fields are `keyword` and `ip`, the way the current implementation does.

## Why the existing constructs don't cover it

Both `WHERE … IN (<subquery>)` and `LOOKUP JOIN` require the join/membership key to resolve to a **single type across the whole query**. When the two sides resolve to different types, the query fails at plan verification:

```esql
FROM events | WHERE source.ip IN (FROM ti | KEEP threat.indicator.ip)
-- verification_exception: left field [source.ip] of type [KEYWORD]
-- is incompatible with right field [threat.indicator.ip] of type [IP]
```

One could work around this by casting the key to a common type, but not simply by adding a cast to the membership test:
- An **inline** cast in the `WHERE` (`source.ip::ip IN (...)`) is rejected ("Complicated IN subquery is not yet supported in the WHERE command").
- The cast has to be applied in a separate `EVAL` that first writes the converted value into its own column (on either side) before the membership test.
- Casting to a common type can flatten it and change matching semantics. For example, the IPv6 addresses `2001:db8::1` and `2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001` are equal under `ip` comparison but are different strings, so casting the key to `keyword` no longer matches them.
- Materializing large threat/event fields into a cast column also has a performance cost, on data volumes that are already large (feeds of millions of indicators).

## How this maps to current rule behavior

The current (DSL) implementation matches using **two separate searches**: it reads the indicator values from the threat index, then feeds those values into a second query against the event index. Because these are two independent searches, each field is only ever evaluated against **its own index's mapping**:
- The threat field is read under its own type and handed over as plain canonical string values.
- The event field then matches those values under *its* own type: a `keyword` field compares them as exact strings, an `ip` field parses them as addresses.

Neither field ever needs to know the other's type. `keyword` on one side and `ip` on the other is transparent, because the value crosses from one query to the other as a string and is re-coerced by whichever mapping receives it.

A native ES|QL migration collapses this into **one query**, where the join key must be a single resolved type across both sources, so the mismatch the two-query approach absorbs silently becomes a type conflict.

## Impact if unmet

This is a supported configuration that works transparently today. Under a single-query model it either fails loudly at plan verification (the no-cast case) or requires an `EVAL`-materialized cast on every run, with the semantic and performance trade-offs above. The dangerous case is silent: once the cast is applied, flattening the type can change which values match without raising an error. Because the condition depends on live mappings, it is per rule and per cluster, and a migration would have to inject the cast per cross-type pair based on types that are not derivable from the rule configuration. Any rule with a cross-type pair is a migration regression for that rule.
issues.title: [ES|QL] Join / IN key on a field with conflicting types across indices (e.g. keyword vs ip)

issues.body:
### Description

When a SAML realm is configured with the same key pair for both signing.key/signing.certificate and encryption.key/encryption.certificate, Elasticsearch accepts the configuration silently. In FIPS mode (BouncyCastle FIPS), the same RSA key cannot be used for both signing and decryption — the library throws IllegalKeyException: Attempt to sign/verify with RSA modulus already used for encrypt/decrypt at runtime.

This produces an intermittent 500 Cannot construct SAML redirect that is very hard to diagnose. The failure is intermittent because it depends on whether both operations happen within the same session context.

Expected behavior: SamlRealm should compare the RSA modulus of the signing private key against the encryption private key during realm initialization and fail fast with a clear message when they match and FIPS mode is active — e.g., "SAML realm signing and encryption keys must be distinct in FIPS mode".

Where to fix: SamlRealm.create() / buildSigningCredential + buildEncryptionCredential in x-pack/plugin/security/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/security/authc/saml/SamlRealm.java.
issues.title: SAML realm should reject duplicate signing/encryption keys at startup in FIPS mode

issues.body:
## Motivation

As of 9.4, `bbq_disk` became the default index type for float vectors with `dim >= 384`, replacing the graph-based defaults used in earlier versions. This is a good default for most workloads, but it creates two decision points that don't have great tooling today:

1. **Migration decisions for existing indices.** Indices created before 9.4 don't automatically move to the new default — upgrading a cluster doesn't change existing mappings. Users now have to decide whether reindexing to `bbq_disk` is worth it, and today that decision requires actually reindexing to see the memory/disk impact.
2. **Opting out of the default when it doesn't fit.** `bbq_disk` trades some recall ceiling for much lower memory usage ([Elastic's own docs note](https://www.elastic.co/search-labs/blog/diskbbq-elasticsearch-introduction) that HNSW with quantization is still preferable when very high recall, ample off-heap memory, and low update rates are all true). Deciding whether to deviate from the default — or which `bits` setting to use within `bbq_disk` — still requires the same kind of before/after comparison.

Elasticsearch already ships this "preview before you commit" pattern in a few places — the Analyze API for tokenization, and the Ingest Simulate API for pipelines. A capacity estimator for vector quantization would fit the same philosophy: let users see the projected outcome without mutating any data or consuming extra cluster resources.

The docs page on tuning approximate kNN search ([Ensure data nodes have enough memory](https://www.elastic.co/docs/deploy-manage/production-guidance/optimize-performance/approximate-knn-search#_ensure_data_nodes_have_enough_memory)) already documents the exact formulas used internally for RAM sizing per element_type/quantization combination, plus the disk overhead percentages (int8 ~25%, int4 ~12.5%, bbq ~3.125%). This proposal is essentially about exposing those existing, documented formulas as a queryable API instead of a manual calculation users have to do themselves.

Separately, `bbq_disk` already allows changing the `bits` parameter in `index_options` without reindexing, showing the team is already investing in reducing the reindex burden for vector tuning. This estimator would extend that same direction to the initial choice of quantization type and to the pre-9.4 → 9.4+ migration decision specifically.

## Proposed API

```
GET /<index>/_knn_capacity_estimate?field=<field_name>
```

Given an existing `dense_vector` field, return the current memory footprint plus projected footprints for each alternative quantization, computed from:
- vector count and dimensionality (from field mapping + doc count)
- the documented RAM formulas per element_type/quantization
- the documented disk overhead percentages

No reindexing, no sampling, no actual vector processing — purely arithmetic over existing mapping/stats metadata, so it's safe to run against production indices.

### Example response

```json
{
  "field": "my_vector",
  "current": {
    "element_type": "float",
    "quantization": "none",
    "num_vectors": 1000000,
    "dims": 1024,
    "estimated_ram_bytes": 4160000000
  },
  "estimates": [
    { "quantization": "int8", "estimated_ram_bytes": 1004000000, "ram_reduction_pct": 75.9, "disk_overhead_pct": 25 },
    { "quantization": "int4", "estimated_ram_bytes": 516000000, "ram_reduction_pct": 87.6, "disk_overhead_pct": 12.5 },
    { "quantization": "bbq_hnsw", "estimated_ram_bytes": 142000000, "ram_reduction_pct": 96.6, "disk_overhead_pct": 3.125 },
    { "quantization": "bbq_disk", "estimated_ram_bytes": 9800000, "ram_reduction_pct": 99.8, "note": "Only a fraction of cluster/centroid data needs to be resident; actual RAM depends on query access patterns." }
  ],
  "disclaimer": "These are memory/disk estimates derived from documented sizing formulas, not measured recall or query latency. For recall/QPS comparisons, use Rally's vector search tracks."
}
```

Notes on the response design:
- Disk usage is reported as going **up** with quantization (extra storage for the quantized copy alongside the original), not down — this mirrors the actual documented behavior, since the two are frequently conflated.
- No recall prediction is included. Recall depends heavily on data distribution and isn't something we can honestly estimate from mapping metadata alone; the response explicitly disclaims this and points to Rally for empirical measurement.
- Naming: `_knn_capacity_estimate` rather than `_simulate_*`, to avoid implying that anything is actually executed — this is a pure calculation over existing metadata.

## Scope / what this is not

- Not a replacement for Rally-based benchmarking (recall, QPS) — this is explicitly out of scope and should stay that way.
- Not a reindexing or migration tool.
- No changes to indexing or search behavior; read-only, computed from mapping + doc count.

## Open questions for maintainers

1. Should this live as a standalone endpoint, or as an extension to the existing [[Analyze Index Disk Usage API](https://www.elastic.co/docs/api/doc/elasticsearch/operation/operation-indices-disk-usage)](https://www.elastic.co/docs/api/doc/elasticsearch/operation/operation-indices-disk-usage) response instead of a new route?
2. Is `num_vectors` best sourced from `_count` or from per-shard doc stats to avoid an extra query?
3. Any preference on including `bbq_disk`'s cluster/centroid formula (which is a bit more involved than the flat per-vector formulas) in v1, or shipping HNSW-only quantization estimates first and following up with DiskBBQ?

Happy to put together a draft PR with the estimator logic as a self-contained, unit-testable utility class once there's rough agreement on the API shape.
issues.title: Add a dry-run capacity estimator for dense_vector quantization (int8/int4/bbq/bbq_disk)

issues.body:
## Context

PR #155586 fixes the request circuit breaker accounting for `TDigestPercentilesAggregator` on the data node (shard level). Two related gaps remain out of scope for that PR and are tracked here.

## 1. Coordinator-side accounting

The coordinator path uses `NOOP_BREAKER` throughout, so coordinator memory is invisible to the request circuit breaker:

- `AbstractInternalTDigestPercentiles(StreamInput)` — deserialised shard sketches are allocated with `NOOP_BREAKER`
- `getLeaderReducer` — the merge accumulator is also allocated with `NOOP_BREAKER`
- `MovingPercentilesPipelineAggregator` — same pattern

In a high-cardinality `terms` + `percentiles` query the coordinator holds *all* shards' sketches simultaneously, so this gap is where the headroom matters most.

## 2. Shard-level siblings: boxplot and exponential merging

`AbstractBoxplotAggregator.getExistingOrNewHistogram` and `AbstractTDigestOrExponentialMergingAggregator.getExistingOrNewHistogram` are copies of the method fixed in #155586 — same `NOOP_BREAKER`, same pattern. Their `doClose()` also only closes the `ObjectArray` container, not the individual elements. A high-cardinality `terms` + `boxplot` query can still OOM the data node after #155586 merges.

## What needs to be done

- Decide the accounting strategy for the coordinator path (e.g. charge the REQUEST breaker on deserialisation, or introduce a coordinator-scoped breaker)
- Apply the same `doClose` and breaker-charging fixes to `AbstractBoxplotAggregator` and `AbstractTDigestOrExponentialMergingAggregator`
issues.title: Track TDigest percentiles memory on coordinator and fix shard-level siblings (boxplot, exponential)

issues.body:
LOAD/LOAD_ALL read unmapped fields from `_source`. Assembling `_source` is very expensive in columnar mode, and proceeding row-by-row is also not ideal.

Let's see if we can do better:
- Can we track which unmapped fields there are in a given index? This would unlock great local physical optimizations.
- Can we store unmapped fields efficiently in columnar mode?
- Can we switch to a more optimized retrieval mode?
  - Esp. for LOAD, we should check if we can extract columns at a time, rather than row-by-row extracting from `_source`.
  - Can we avoid constructing and parsing `_source`?
issues.title: ESQL: Efficient LOAD/LOAD_ALL in columnar mode

issues.body:
Reindex retries failed bulk requests, with this backoff-and-retry policy:
https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/6338e5c7a7bcf7a3315546fef23cb13322f76abb/modules/reindex/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/reindex/AbstractAsyncBulkByPaginatedSearchAction.java#L986-L991

I believe that the total accumulated backoff time is 59,460ms, i.e. just less than a minute. We believe this is too short. Bulk requests at the REST level have a 260s timeout by default. We have seen occurrences of such failures in production — perhaps due to a bug (now fixed), but it would be good for reindex to be resilient in the face of such bugs.

It's worth bearing in mind that, most of the time, the only thing a client can do when failures are reported by reindex is to retry the whole operation themselves. A more persistent retry policy within reindex, which only retries the failed documents or batches, would be a better user experience.

Actions proposed are:
1. Change the default retry policy so that it persists for longer. Details of the new policy TBD (but please bear the discussion above in mind).
2. Probably make the retry policy configurable. I would say that making the parameters (backoff interval, number of retries, etc.) into node or cluster settings is low-effort and provides a useful tool when dealing with production incidents. TBD whether we should also make them configurable via REST query parameters (though I'd lean towards not complicating the public API, at least not for now).
3. Consider switching to a true exponential backoff as it is normally understood, i.e. a delay of $t = t_0 k^{(i-1)}$ before the _i_ th retry. The current `BackoffPolicy.exponentialBackoff()` method does, if I'm reading it correctly, $t = t_0 + 10\mathrm{ms} * e^{0.8 * (i-1) }$, which is... something different. I don't see why that should be better — and, if we are exposing parameters as settings, it seems better to do so in a standard way. (That method has other callers, so I suggest that it should be renamed to something like `legacyDecayingBackoff()` so that we can leave the other callers unaffected by this work.)
issues.title: Improve bulk retry policy for reindex

issues.body:
When a user issues a bulk request, the coordinator will fan out to nodes it believes to be primary shards. If a shard is no longer the primary when it receives the request, it will throw a `ShardNotInPrimaryModeException` (see `IndexShard.wrapPrimaryOperationPermitListener()`). This will be caught and wrapped in a `RetryOnPrimaryException` with `possiblyExecutedOnPrimary = false` (see `TransportReplicationAction.AsyncPrimaryAction.doRun()`). The coordinator will retry, up to some timeout (see `TransportReplicationAction.ReroutePhase.performAction()`). If it hits the timeout, the `RetryOnPrimaryException` will be returned to the user, with a status of 500. This is actually retryable by the client, so a 429 is more appropriate. Additionally, `retry_on_primary_exception` is an odd top-level error to return to the user. Perhaps wrapping in a `ElasticsearchTimeoutException` might be appropriate?

There are other places that `RetryOnPrimaryException` is used (that's just the one that occurred in the instance that prompted this issue). The above likely applies for all of them so long as `possiblyExecutedOnPrimary() == false`, though we should check this.

We should also consider the impact on reindex, which issues bulk requests (at the transport layer). That retries on 429s, but only on 429s (see `org.elasticsearch.action.bulk.Retry.RetryHandler`). So the `RetryOnPrimaryException` wrapping a `ShardNotInPrimaryModeException` in the above scenario is not retried, and returned to the user. If we make the above change return a 429 in this case (and if this happens at the transport rather than the REST layer) then reindex will see it and retry. We need to think about whether or not this is desirable, given that this will already have been retried in the `TransportReplicationAction` layer. However, the concerns around returning a better error type than `retry_on_primary_exception` to the user in the event that we run out of retries does apply here.

To summarize:
 - Consider wrapping a `RetryOnPrimaryException` that runs out of retries in a `ElasticsearchTimeoutException` before returning to the user.
 - Consider making it a 429 rather than a 500 when `possiblyExecutedOnPrimary() == false`.
 - Verify that, when the bulk request is coming from reindex, the error type returned to the user gets wrapped the same as it does for a bulk request directly from a user.
 - Think about whether the change to 429 would cause an additional round of retries in the reindex layer, after it's already retried at the `TransportReplicationAction` layer, and whether or not that is desirable.
issues.title: Improve handling of `RetryOnPrimaryException` in bulk requests and reindex

issues.body:
## Problem

Elasticsearch reindexing can reintroduce documents that were deleted while a reindex operation was in progress. Example:
1. Start reindex a → b
2. Document is deleted from a
3. The deleted document might still be copied onto B during the reindex process

## Current Workaround

A few but all annoying:
* Pause writes during reindex (annoying because results are stale for many hours)
* Never delete docs from elasticsearch directly, use soft-deletion (e.g. `deleted` boolean field keyword) and period cleanup via cronjob (complexity)
* Write to the old index and at the same time collect all operations that happen during the reindex. Replay every operation to the new index after reindex is complete (complexity)

## Requested Behavior

It would be useful if Elasticsearch's reindexing functionality had a built-in mechanism for handling documents deleted from the source while a reindex is running.

For example, Elasticsearch could track deletes occurring during the reindex and reconcile them before considering the operation complete, or provide another mechanism that gives equivalent consistency guarantees.

## Why This Would Help

This would make online index migrations substantially simpler and safer. Applications could rely more directly on Elasticsearch's reindexing process rather than implementing a separate catch-up/replay mechanism
issues.title: Add option to handle deleted documents during reindex

issues.body:
## 🎯 TL;DR

Widening the LogsDB binary doc values block **and** raising zstd to level 3 cuts a large non-indexed `text` payload roughly **in half** on disk. Neither lever does anything alone.

The trade-off is narrower than it first looks: full-scan and session-at-a-time reads are **neutral**, only random point lookups regress (~7×) — and that cost comes from the block size, not the zstd level.

POC + benchmarks: #157246 (changes no production default).

## 🔍 The problem

A non-indexed `text` field under LogsDB is retained as binary doc values in `<field>._original`. For payload-heavy workloads that field *is* the index — for browser session replay (rrweb DOM snapshots, ~256 KB/doc) it measures at **~96% of on-disk bytes** after merge.

That payload has an awkward profile:

- **Individually near-unique** → per-doc compression finds little. Measured ~4.5× on a real replay stream, vs ~12–16× for ordinary logs on the same cluster.
- **Collectively very redundant** → the same tag soup, class names and JSON keys recur across docs. Sampling a real stream, many ~256 KB chunks were *byte-identical* to another chunk.

Today's codec can't see that second part. LogsDB uses ES819 `Version3` (`useES95()` is TSDB-only) with **zstd-1 / 512 KB blocks**, and `CompressedBinaryBlockWriter.addDoc` flushes *after* appending — so with ~256 KB values a block holds **at most 2 docs**. The window never spans enough documents for the repetition to be visible, and level 1 isn't searching for long-range matches anyway.

> `index.codec: best_compression` is unrelated — that's stored fields. This payload is binary doc values.

## 📊 Storage

`testLargeBinaryBlobZstdWindow` — Lucene `Directory` + `IndexWriter`, no node, `forceMerge(1)`, round-trip asserted on every value:

| Config | Mode | Block | Size | vs today |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|
| today | zstd-1 | 512 KB | 30,397,784 B | — |
| window only | zstd-1 | 4 MB | 28,892,103 B | −5.0% (wash) |
| **window + level** | **zstd-3** | **4 MB** | **15,353,655 B** | **−49.5% (~1.98×)** |

Stable across seeds and 200–320 docs. Cross-checked against two real corpora (neither committed — internal telemetry):

| Real corpus | Docs | Sessions | window-only | window+level |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| CCS cluster, random sample | 198 | n/a (recycled) | 89% | 58% (~1.73×) |
| **PR-cloud, sorted by real `session.id`** | **710** | **86** | 91.8% | **44.8% (~2.23×)** |

The second run — bigger, real per-session grouping instead of recycled content, natural size distribution (196 B–2.26 MB) — came out **better**, not worse. Real successive snapshots of the same evolving DOM apparently share more structure than a hand-built vocabulary does. The test in the PR is synthetic and self-contained.

**Both levers are required** — that's the finding.

## ⚖️ Read & write cost

A reader caches exactly **one** decompressed block and searches forward only, so read cost follows the access pattern, not the block size alone. 256 docs × 256 KB, best of three, warm:

| Config | full scan | one session | random single doc |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| today (zstd-1, 512 KB) | 23.4 ms | 1.46 ms | **0.195 ms** |
| window-only (zstd-1, 4 MB) | 22.3 ms | 1.44 ms | 1.454 ms |
| window+level (zstd-3, 4 MB) | 21.8 ms | 1.40 ms | **1.372 ms** |

- **Scan / session-at-a-time: neutral.** Under an index sort a session's blobs are contiguous, share blocks, and each block is decompressed once.
- **Random point lookup: ~7× slower** — tracks the ~8× more uncompressed bytes per cold lookup (512 KB holding 2 values → 4 MB holding 16).
- **Write: no measurable penalty** at this size (indexing/merge varied more between repeats than between configs).
- 💡 **The level is free on reads.** At an equal 4 MB block, zstd-3 reads *marginally faster* than zstd-1. So: **block size buys storage and costs point-lookup latency; zstd level buys storage for nothing.**

## 💰 What it's worth

Applied to that ~96%-of-bytes field, across the ~1.7×–2.23× range measured so far:

| | Today | Projected |
|---|---:|---:|
| Replay primary | 173 GB | ~82–103 GB |
| Per session on disk | 4.46 MB | ~2.1–2.7 MB |
| Blended ratio, all RUM streams | ~6× | ~9–11× |

⚠️ This helps **disk** — hot-tier footprint and infra cost. It does **nothing** for ingest-metered billing, which meters enriched `_source` *before* compression.

## 🚧 Open questions

1. **Where should this knob live?** `libs/columnar`'s `BlockBytesCodec` is already designed as a per-column, type-agnostic terminal byte stage with frozen ids — but the only implementation today is identity, and ColumNAR has no opaque-bytes column type yet (`LONG`/`DOUBLE`/`STRING` only; `addBinaryField` decodes numeric payloads). So it looks like the right long-term home, not a near-term one.
2. **Scoping is mandatory, not optional.** One binary DV format serves *every* field, and the read numbers show a global flip would be wrong — point-lookup fields would pay the ~7× for nothing.
3. **BWC** — old nodes can't read a `code = 2` segment. Needs an index version + codec-version discussion.
4. **Locality is load-bearing twice** — it's what makes the compression reachable *and* what keeps reads neutral. One real replay stream already sorts on `session.id` in its index template (that's where the 710-doc/2.23× result above came from) — but not every replay stream does yet. Where it's still `host.name`/`@timestamp`, this would take the ~7× read penalty *without* the compression win. The sort has to land first, wherever it hasn't.
5. **If this becomes automatic** (statistics captured at flush/merge): the trigger can't be mean value size alone. While building the corpus, a first design with heavy *intra*-document redundancy already compressed ~15× at today's settings and gained nothing from the wider window — only *cross*-document redundancy benefits. A useful heuristic needs a cross-block similarity signal, or it'll fire on large fields that don't benefit.
6. **Block-size safety** — #137139 avoided multi-MB blocks because a *fixed* 32-values/block OOMs on large values. Variable blocks allow 1 doc/block so 4 MB at ~256 KB values (~16 docs/block) stays bounded, but shouldn't be raised blindly.

Happy to hear this is the wrong layer — capping/sampling the payload upstream is the competing option, and the only one that helps ingest-metered deployments.
issues.title: LogsDB: wider binary DV blocks + zstd-3 halves large non-indexed text payloads

issues.body:
## Problem

Under `SET unmapped_fields="LOAD_ALL"`, the `$$unmapped_fields` blob attribute must be extracted on data nodes and sent to the coordinator. https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/156945 doesn't need special treatment for LOOKUP JOIN because `ProjectAwayColumns` forces an extraction on the data node.

However, the extraction point is suboptimal for **row-expanding commands** such as `MV_EXPAND` and `LookupJoinExec` (data-node join): without a hint, `InsertFieldExtraction` places the `FieldExtractExec` **above** the expanding node, re-parsing `_source` once per *output row* instead of once per *input document*. For a command that expands `N` values per field, this is an `N`-fold read amplification.

The fix belongs in `InsertFieldExtraction.missingAttributes` (which filters `p.rehttps://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/156917ferences() − p.inputSet()` to `FieldAttribute | MetadataAttribute | TemporalityAttribute | UnmappedFieldsAttribute`): add a positive **row-expanding** notion that causes the extractor to be placed *below* the expanding node, so `_source` is read once per input document.

## Affected commands

- `MvExpandExec`: `computeReferences()` returns `target.references()` only — no `UnmappedFieldsAttribute`.
- `LookupJoinExec` (data-node join): `computeReferences()` returns `Expressions.references(leftFields)` only.

## Design notes

No positive "row-expanding" marker exists in the physical layer today:
- `RowCountPreserving` (`plan/physical/RowCountPreserving.java`) is the **wrong polarity** and strictly stronger than needed (`LimitExec`, `TopNExec`, `AggregateExec`, `SampleExec` also lack it).
- The concept currently exists only as duplicated `instanceof` checks in `PushDownAndCombineLimits`.
- `InsertFieldExtraction` runs `Limiter.ONCE` (single bottom-up pass), placing the extractor on the first child whose `outputSet()` contains `_doc`.

Options:
1. **Marker interface** `RowExpanding` on `MvExpandExec` and `LookupJoinExec`, checked in `InsertFieldExtraction`.
2. **Explicit `instanceof` list** in `InsertFieldExtraction`, analogous to `PushDownAndCombineLimits`.
3. **Override `inputSet()`** in the expanding nodes to exclude `$$unmapped_fields`, forcing the extractor below them.

Whichever mechanism is chosen, it should be covered by tests on both plan branches (`MV_EXPAND` and data-node LOOKUP JOIN), and `MV_EXPAND` should be admitted to the LOAD_ALL allow-list once the performance issue is fixed.
issues.title: ES|QL: extract $$unmapped_fields below row-expanding nodes
