issues.body:
Currently, when you cancel a reindex task (or any `BulkByPaginatedSearchTask`), it does a `rethrottle(Float.POSITIVE_INFINITY)`, so it will wake up if it's sleeping due to throttling, but otherwise it just checks for cancellation at various points between requests: it does not attempt to cancel any in-flight search or bulk requests. We occasionally see cancellation taking a long time, so this could help, if it's feasible.

In particular, `ShutdownPrepareService` will wait `node.maximum_reindexing_grace_period` (defaults to 10s on stack) for tasks to relocate, and if that doesn't work then it cancels them and waits `REINDEXING_CANCELLATION_TIMEOUT` (hardcoded to 10s) for them to finish. The cancellation would allow it to write the result into the `.tasks` index in time (we get `NodeClosedException` if we leave it too late) and hence for subsequent `GET /_tasks` or `GET /_reindex` calls to return something. But right now, if it fails to relocate during the grace period, there's a very good chance that it will fail to cancel as well. More aggressive cancellation would help with that.

We may also want to replace `REINDEXING_CANCELLATION_TIMEOUT` with a node setting, and consider a higher value in serverless.
issues.title: Improve cancellability of reindex (incl. on shutdown)

issues.body:
## Summary

The `SpatialDocValuesExtraction` optimizer rule marks `geo_point`/`cartesian_point` fields for Lucene doc-values extraction (producing `LongBlock` instead of `BytesRefBlock`) when those fields are consumed by spatial aggregations (`ST_CENTROID_AGG`, `ST_EXTENT_AGG`) or certain spatial functions that prefer doc-values.

A bug fix in #141300 introduced a conservative guard: if the same spatial field is also referenced by a *non-spatial* function in an `EVAL` or `FILTER` — for example `TO_STRING(location)` — the doc-values optimization is suppressed entirely for that field, so the field is extracted from source (WKB / `BytesRefBlock`) for all consumers.

This is correct but lossy: a query like

```esql
FROM airports
| EVAL location_str = SUBSTRING(TO_STRING(location), 1, 5)
| STATS centroid = ST_CENTROID_AGG(location) BY location_str
```

loses the `LongBlock` doc-values path for `ST_CENTROID_AGG`, even though only `TO_STRING` is the incompatible consumer.

## Root cause

All non-spatial functions that accept `geo_point` / `cartesian_point` currently expect their input blocks to be `BytesRefBlock` (WKB-encoded). When `SpatialDocValuesExtraction` marks a field for doc-values, *every* consumer of that field gets a `LongBlock` instead, which those functions cannot handle.

## Proposed optimization

Teach each affected non-spatial function to additionally support a `LongBlock` (doc-values) input path. Concretely, for each function that has a `@ConvertEvaluator`-generated evaluator, add a second static method annotated with `@ConvertEvaluator(extraName = "FromGeoPointDocValues")` (or `FromCartesianPointDocValues`) that takes a `long` parameter and decodes it via `SpatialCoordinateTypes.GEO.longAsWkb(encoded)` before applying the existing logic.

Then update `SpatialDocValuesExtraction` to call `withDocValues()` on these functions (analogous to how it handles `SpatialDocValuesFunction` implementations today), so the planner switches each function's evaluator factory to the doc-values variant when the field is extracted from doc-values.

## Scope

A survey of the codebase identified approximately 25 non-spatial functions that accept `geo_point` or `cartesian_point` and use `BytesRef` block inputs:

| Category | Functions |
|---|---|
| Convert | `TO_STRING`, `TO_GEOSHAPE`, `TO_CARTESIANSHAPE`, `TO_GEOPOINT`, `TO_CARTESIANPOINT` |
| Aggregate | `VALUES`, `FIRST`, `LAST`, `EARLIEST`, `LATEST`, `SAMPLE` |
| MV scalar | `MV_FIRST`, `MV_LAST`, `MV_DEDUPE`, `MV_APPEND`, `MV_CONTAINS`, `MV_DIFFERENCE`, `MV_INTERSECTION`, `MV_INTERSECTS`, `MV_SLICE`, `MV_UNION` |
| Other scalar | `COALESCE`, `CASE`, `DECAY` |

A few functions (`COUNT`, `COUNT_OVER_TIME`, `ABSENT`, `PRESENT`, `MV_COUNT`) operate only on value counts and are already safe with any block type — no changes needed for those.

A reasonable starting point for this optimization would be `TO_STRING`, as it is the function most likely to appear alongside a spatial aggregation in a real-world query and the one that triggered the original bug report (#141300).

## Related

- Bug fixed by: #141300
- `SpatialDocValuesExtraction` rule: `x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/optimizer/rules/physical/local/SpatialDocValuesExtraction.java`
- `SpatialDocValuesFunction` interface: already used by spatial functions that support the `LongBlock` input path
- Encoding/decoding: `org.elasticsearch.xpack.esql.core.util.SpatialCoordinateTypes`
issues.title: ES|QL: Preserve spatial doc-values optimization when non-spatial functions also reference the field

issues.body:
## Summary

Query latency for federated datasets scales linearly with file count rather than with data volume. The default `schema_resolution: union_by_name` reads and merges schema metadata from every file before query execution begins, making file count the dominant performance factor — even for queries that touch no data (e.g., `LIMIT 0`).

This creates a poor out-of-the-box experience for the most common Parquet layout: Hive-partitioned directories with thousands of identically-schemaed files. Users must discover and set `schema_resolution: first_file_wins` to get acceptable performance.

## Evidence

Tested on a scaled ECH cluster (Azure eastus2, `9.6.0-SNAPSHOT` build 2026-08-27) with public S3 Parquet datasets.

### GBIF (9,705 Parquet files, 266 GB) — `union_by_name` (default)

| Files | LIMIT 0 | COUNT | WHERE | AGG | NEEDLE |
|-------|---------|-------|-------|-----|--------|
| 9 | 3.2s | 1.1s | 1.2s | 0.9s | 1.2s |
| 95 | 6.7s | 1.0s | 7.2s | 1.1s | 3.1s |
| 950 | 47.5s | 1.1s | 7.2s | 4.3s | 46.1s |
| 1,900 | 54.0s | 101.9s | 109.3s | 112.6s | 212.6s |
| 4,750 | 256.8s | 273.6s | 283.1s | 287.5s | >600s |
| 9,705 | 537.3s | 534.3s | 588.4s | 579.5s | >600s |

### Same GBIF dataset with `first_file_wins`

| Files | LIMIT 0 | COUNT | WHERE | AGG | NEEDLE |
|-------|---------|-------|-------|-----|--------|
| 9 | 2.7s | 1.2s | 4.2s | 0.2s | 2.7s |
| 95 | 1.0s | 4.7s | 6.5s | 1.6s | 2.6s |
| 950 | 1.1s | 45.0s | 52.3s | 7.0s | 59.9s |
| 1,900 | 1.1s | 99.9s | 61.4s | **13.2s** | 116.1s |
| 4,750 | **1.1s** | 253.9s | 286.2s | **25.3s** | 413.4s |
| 9,705 | **1.0s** | 517.1s | 555.3s | **62.3s** | >600s |

Key observations:
- **LIMIT 0** (pure metadata, zero data scanning): 537s → 1.0s (**537x improvement**) at 9,705 files. This isolates the schema resolution overhead.
- **AGG queries** (which benefit from column pruning): 580s → 62s (**9x improvement**) at 9,705 files.
- **WHERE/COUNT/NEEDLE** (full data scan): negligible change — the bottleneck shifts to I/O, confirming the overhead is schema resolution, not data reading.

### BTC (6,427 Parquet files, ~200 GB) — same pattern

| Files | LIMIT 0 (default) | LIMIT 0 (FFW) | Speedup |
|-------|--------------------|---------------|---------|
| 1 | 0.4s | 2.3s | — |
| 30 | 1.1s | 0.7s | 1.6x |
| 365 | 1.8s | 0.8s | 2.3x |
| 723 | 2.6s | 0.8s | 3.3x |
| 6,427 | 28.8s | 0.7s | **41x** |

### Default-size cluster: CBE at moderate file counts

On default-size ECH clusters, the schema resolution overhead consumes enough JVM heap to trigger circuit breaker exceptions at 723 files (see #157885). Queries that completed in 2-22s on prior builds now fail.

## Impact

The most natural way to set up federated data — pointing at a Hive-partitioned S3 prefix — produces datasets with hundreds or thousands of files that all share the same schema. In this common case:

1. `union_by_name` does redundant work: it reads N schemas to confirm they're identical, when reading 1 would suffice
2. LIMIT 0 and metadata queries become unusable above ~1,000 files
3. Default-size clusters hit circuit breakers above ~700 files (#157885)

## Suggestions

Consider one or more of:

1. **Smarter default**: If the first N files have identical schemas, skip the remaining files (adaptive short-circuit)
2. **Warn when a dataset resolves to many files with `union_by_name`**, suggesting `first_file_wins`
3. **Reduce per-file heap cost** of schema metadata to push the circuit breaker threshold higher
issues.title: ES|QL data federation: query latency scales linearly with file count due to per-file schema resolution

issues.body:
### Description

The Elasticsearch clients accept a bearer token (e.g., an OAuth access token) for authentication, but have no built-in support for acquiring or refreshing tokens from an OAuth 2.0 / OIDC Identity Provider 

Every application using the client must therefore implement its own token lifecycle management:

Acquiring tokens from the IdP using client credentials
Securely storing access/refresh tokens
Detecting expiration and refreshing (or reacquiring) tokens
Handling acquisition/refresh failures

This duplicates the same logic across every integrating application, adds complexity, and increases the risk of inconsistent or insecure implementations.

This capability is a common pattern in other client SDKs (e.g., Azure SDK TokenCredential, Google Cloud client libraries) and would align the Elasticsearch clients with established practices for enterprise identity integration. Elasticsearch's server-side OIDC realm already supports token-based authentication; this request addresses the client-side gap in acquiring and maintaining those tokens.
issues.title: Native OAuth 2.0 / OIDC token acquisition and refresh in Elasticsearch clients

issues.body:
## Summary

ES|QL does not preserve the order of a multivalued field, and it removes duplicate values from `keyword` fields. This is documented behavior: the relative order of a multivalued field is undefined, and some types like `keyword` remove duplicate values on write ([ES|QL multivalued fields](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/query-languages/esql/esql-multivalued-fields)). There is no way to get a multivalued field back in its source order, or to keep its duplicate values, except `METADATA _source`, which returns the whole document as one opaque `_source` column rather than typed fields. `_search` (Query DSL) returns `_source` verbatim and does not have this limitation.

This is most damaging when **two arrays are aligned by position** - element `N` of one array corresponds to element `N` of another. Reordering each array independently, or dropping a duplicate from only one of them, silently destroys the pairing.

## Reproduction (verified on 9.6)

Two parallel arrays where `value[i]` belongs to `key[i]` (the shape cloud audit logs use):

```
PUT mv-demo
{ "mappings": { "properties": { "key": { "type": "keyword" }, "value": { "type": "keyword" } } } }

POST mv-demo/_doc?refresh
{ "key":   ["User-Agent","AppId","AppOwnerOrganizationId","ServicePrincipalProvisioningType"],
  "value": ["kiota-go/1.5.4","e0fd3ac6-8927-4e1d-a68e-14bf2deb0522","4fa94b7d-a743-486f-abcc-6c276c44cf4b","Other"] }

# Query DSL - verbatim, key[i] pairs with value[i]
GET mv-demo/_search
# key   -> ["User-Agent","AppId","AppOwnerOrganizationId","ServicePrincipalProvisioningType"]
# value -> ["kiota-go/1.5.4","e0fd3ac6-...","4fa94b7d-...","Other"]
# pairs -> User-Agent=kiota-go/1.5.4, AppId=e0fd3ac6-..., AppOwnerOrganizationId=4fa94b7d-..., ...

# ES|QL - each array reordered independently, pairing broken
POST _query
{ "query": "FROM mv-demo | KEEP key, value" }
# key   -> ["AppId","AppOwnerOrganizationId","ServicePrincipalProvisioningType","User-Agent"]
# value -> ["4fa94b7d-...","Other","e0fd3ac6-...","kiota-go/1.5.4"]
# pairs -> AppId=4fa94b7d-... (wrong), AppOwnerOrganizationId=Other (wrong), ...
```

Every key is now mapped to the wrong value. A duplicate value breaks it the same way: ES|QL drops the duplicate from that array only, shifting everything after it out of alignment with the other array.

## Why it matters

Cloud audit logs commonly store event details as parallel key/value arrays. Azure in particular splits fields into `azure.auditlogs.properties.additional_details.key` and `...additional_details.value`, where `value[i]` belongs to `key[i]`. Read via `_search` (Query DSL) the association is preserved; read via ES|QL each array is reordered and keyword duplicates removed, so the key-to-value mapping is silently corrupted.

We are evaluating running Security detection rules as ES|QL queries. Today they run as Query DSL and the alert copies `_source`, so paired arrays stay aligned; on ES|QL the alerts would carry mismatched pairs.

## Current workaround and why it is insufficient

`METADATA _source` returns the document verbatim (order and duplicates preserved), but as a single opaque `_source` column, not as individual typed fields. That is not usable for queries that need to `KEEP`, filter, or display specific fields with their real types.

## Ask

A way to return selected multivalued fields in **source order, preserving duplicates** - for example an option to load specified fields from `_source` instead of doc_values, or a per-field / per-query setting that disables the sort+dedup for chosen columns. Single-valued fields and the default behavior can stay as they are.
issues.title: [ES|QL] Preserve multivalued field order and duplicates when returning fields

issues.body:
As a user we can now write queries to query histogram data (tdigest, exponential histogram, or classic histogram with `TO_TDIGEST`) in this way:

**Query 1. Distribution (bar)**

```esql
TS metrics-*
| STATS count = COUNT(histogram_field, bucket)
    BY bucket = BUCKET(histogram_field, 20, 1.2, 1400)
```

**Query 2. Distribution over time (heatmap)**

```esql
TS metrics-*
| STATS count = COUNT(histogram_field, bucket)
    BY bucket = BUCKET(histogram_field, 20, 1.2, 1400), TBUCKET(100)
```

However, as you might have noticed we have 4 values hardcoded:

- `100`: target number of time buckets (`TBUCKET(100)`).
- `20`: target number of buckets for `histogram_field`. This does not fully depend on the data; the user can pick how many bars they want.
- `1.2`: minimum of `histogram_field` in the current data.
- `1400`: maximum of `histogram_field` in the current data.

The min and max you can only set if you have information from the data. Right now, as a user, you have to:

**a) Put whatever you think.** Guess min and max and hope they fit.

**b) Run another query first**, then paste the numbers into Query 1 / Query 2:

```esql
TS metrics-*
| STATS min = MIN(histogram_field), max = MAX(histogram_field)
```

This process is not straightforward, but it does not end there. If the user puts a visualization on a dashboard with this query, changing the time range or filters will not make the chart adapt to the data in view, because min and max are hardcoded. Time already adapts (`TBUCKET(100)`). The `histogram_field` axis does not. The shape squishes into one bar / one heatmap row, or grows a long empty tail.

## Proposal

When querying histograms under `TS`, `BUCKET(histogram_field, 20)` should take min and max from the current data. That is different from time, where `TBUCKET(100)` / `BUCKET(@timestamp, 100)` already take from and to from `?_tstart` and `?_tend`. Explicit min and max stay available when the user wants a fixed range: `BUCKET(histogram_field, 20, 1.2, 1400)`.

**Query 1. Bar**

```esql
TS metrics-*
| STATS count = COUNT(histogram_field, bucket)
    BY bucket = BUCKET(histogram_field, 20)
```

**Query 2. Heatmap**

```esql
TS metrics-*
| STATS count = COUNT(histogram_field, bucket)
    BY bucket = BUCKET(histogram_field, 20), TBUCKET(100)
```

The user still chooses how many buckets they want (`20` and `100`). They do not have to know min and max. A saved dashboard recomputes them on every run.

One way this could work is translating `BUCKET(histogram_field, 20)` to:

```esql
INLINESTATS min = MIN(histogram_field), max = MAX(histogram_field)
| STATS ... BY BUCKET(histogram_field, 20, min, max)
```
issues.title: ES|QL: auto-detect min and max for numeric BUCKET() so histogram bars and heatmaps adapt to the current data

issues.body:
## Summary

CSV and TSV files from government and vendor exports often start with a few non-data lines (generation timestamp, legal disclaimer) and only then the real header row. Federation today treats the first line as the header when `header_row` is true, so those files parse as garbage or fail.

Request: Databricks-style behavior — skip a fixed number of leading rows, then treat the next remaining row as the header.

This is table stakes vs Databricks, Athena/Hive, BigQuery, and DuckDB. Snowflake has `SKIP_HEADER`, but it cannot be combined with `PARSE_HEADER`. Databricks is the model we want: `skipRows` and `header=true` work together.

## Current behavior

Dataset CSV/TSV settings today ([docs](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/query-languages/esql/esql-data-federation-datasets)):

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `header_row` | `true` | First row names the columns |
| `comment` | `//` | Skip lines that begin with this prefix |
| `error_mode` | `fail_fast` | Malformed-row handling |

There is no count of leading rows to ignore. A prose disclaimer is not a `//` comment, so `comment` does not help. With `header_row: true`, line 1 becomes the column names.

## Requested behavior (Databricks)

From the [Databricks Spark CSV options](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/spark/api-options):

> `skipRows` — The number of rows from the beginning of the CSV file that should be ignored, including commented and empty rows. If `header` is true, the header will be the first unskipped and uncommented row.

Proposed dataset setting, e.g. `skip_rows` (integer, default `0`), combined with existing `header_row` and `comment`:

1. Ignore the first `skip_rows` lines of the file (including blank and comment-prefixed lines in that count).
2. If `header_row` is `true`, the next remaining non-comment line is the header.
3. Remaining lines are data rows.

Example file:

```
File generated 2026-09-11
CONFIDENTIAL — authorized use only
state,ip,user_agent
TX,1.2.3.4,Mozilla/5.0
```

```json
{
  "settings": {
    "format": "csv",
    "skip_rows": 2,
    "header_row": true
  }
}
```

Expected columns: `state`, `ip`, `user_agent`. Expected first data row: `TX`, `1.2.3.4`, `Mozilla/5.0`.

Today this dataset either fails or invents columns from `File generated 2026-09-11`.

## What we are not asking for

- Auto-detecting which line is the header (DuckDB `sniff_csv` / unknown-length preambles). Athena documents that variable-length headers are out of scope. Field users who hit this already know N.
- Parquet / Iceberg / NDJSON. Schema lives in file metadata or every line is a record. This is a delimited-text problem.

## Impact

Field testing of Experimental federation hit this on public government CSV in S3. The workaround is to copy the object and hand-delete the preamble, which defeats query-in-place.

Same pattern shows up in agency extracts, vendor reports, and Excel-exported CSVs. Without `skip_rows`, those objects are not queryable as datasets even when the data rows themselves are well-formed.

## Suggestions

1. Add `skip_rows` (non-negative integer, default `0`) on CSV/TSV dataset settings.
2. Apply it before `header_row` resolution, matching Databricks: skip N, then first remaining uncommented row is the header when `header_row` is true.
3. Document interaction with `comment` (does `skip_rows` count comment lines, as Databricks does?).
4. Out of scope for this issue: sniffer / “find the column labels.”
issues.title: ES|QL data federation: skip leading CSV/TSV rows before the header (Databricks skipRows)

issues.body:
PromQL's `topk` / `bottomk` ranking functions exist in Elasticsearch (see `PromqlBuiltinFunctionDefinitions`), but there is no ES|QL equivalent that preserves full rows. The closest options today fall short:

- `STATS … | TOP(field, k)` packs the winning values into a multivalue array, losing the rest of each row.
- `SORT field DESC | LIMIT k BY group` gives the right rows, but it is verbose, splits one intent across two commands, and (unlike PromQL) does not read as ranking.

### Proposal

Add row-preserving ranking commands:

```esql
FROM k8s
| TOPK network.bytes_in, 3 BY pod      -- 3 highest rows per pod
| BOTTOMK network.bytes_in, 3 BY pod   -- 3 lowest rows per pod
| LIMITK 3 BY pod                      -- arbitrary 3 rows per pod
```

The `BY` clause is optional; without it the commands apply globally. `k` must be a non-negative integer, like `LIMIT`.

Example:

```esql
FROM employees
| TOPK salary, 1 BY gender
| KEEP first_name, last_name, salary, gender
| SORT gender
```

| first_name | last_name | salary | gender |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tzvetan | Zielinski | 74572 | F |
| Otmar | Herbst | 74999 | M |
| Lillian | Haddadi | 73717 | null |

### Implementation sketch

The commands desugar in the parser to exactly what the equivalent `SORT | LIMIT [BY]` parses to (`OrderBy` + `LimitBy`/`Limit`), so analysis, optimization (`ReplaceLimitAndSortAsTopN` folds them into `TopNBy`/`TopN`), and distributed execution are reused with no new execution code. New `TOPK`/`BOTTOMK`/`LIMITK` lexer keywords plus a gating capability (e.g. `ESQL_TOPK_COMMAND`).

### Status

- Supersedes the `STATS`-aggregate approach in #159219 (closed): aggregates collapse each group into a multivalue array and cannot preserve rows, so they don't match PromQL ranking semantics.
- Draft implementation: #159228.

### Open questions

- Syntax/naming: is `TOPK <field>, <k> [BY <groups>]` the right surface?
- `LIMITK k [BY …]` is a pure alias of `LIMIT k [BY …]` — keep for PromQL-family symmetry or drop?
- Telemetry currently reports the desugared `LIMIT BY`/`SORT` nodes rather than `TOPK`; acceptable or worth a dedicated label?
issues.title: ESQL: TOPK

issues.body:
In a `FORK` query every data driver loads the projected fields, so field extraction is multiplied by the Lucene slice s.  `SORT ... | LIMIT n` does not, it defers the loading to the `node_reduce` driver. 

Measured on the `msmarco-hybrid-search` nightly across #143133, which took data drivers
per shard from ~1 to ~10 (`esql-profile` metrics, same query):

- FORK `data.ValuesSourceReaderOperator.process_ms`: **6.73 → 48.60**
- FORK `node_reduce.ValuesSourceReaderOperator.process_ms`: 12.46 → 14.05 (flat)
- non-FORK TopN: no `data`-side reader before or after

**Cause:** late materialization does run for FORK branches, but the field-pruning filter in `LateMaterializationPlanner#planReduceDriverTopN` keeps any attribute in `topLevelProject.outputSet()`. A FORK branch has no narrowing `KEEP`, so `ProjectAwayColumns` makes that set the whole relation and nothing is pruned.

Relates to #141770.
issues.title: ES|QL: `FORK` branches load projected fields in every data driver instead of deferring to `node_reduce`

issues.body:
### Description

Tests that assert on recovery type, shard location, or other placement-sensitive state should disable rebalancing (e.g. `index.routing.rebalance.enable: none` or `cluster.routing.rebalance.enable: none`) unless the test is *intentionally* exercising rebalance/relocation.

Today this is handled ad hoc: each flake gets a one-off fix after CI mutes it. The same class of race keeps recurring because sibling scenarios or related suites omit the setting.

### Why

Rebalancing can start a PEER recovery or move shards between setup and assertion. That races with tests that expect:

- snapshot recovery stats (e.g. `type: SNAPSHOT`, `stage: DONE`)
- a stable shard copy for reads (term vectors, field caps, etc.)
- specific shard allocation (e.g. testing local/non-local specific behavior, specific transport layer interaction)
- no-relocating within a short timeout after the real work is done

### Proposed approach

1. Let an agent go over resent test failures and look for common patterns where the test fix has been to disable relocations.
2. Look for the most common patterns and apply the fix pro-actively where applicable.

Another approach could be to disable relocation as the default for tests and only enable relocation for tests that specifically test relocation behavior. This seems a lot more invasive though and there is a point to be made about keeping integration tests as close as possible to production setup.

### Evidence / related failures

Same snapshot.restore PEER-vs-SNAPSHOT race (recurring):

- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/159161 (open; muted) — restore path missing `rebalance.enable: none` while siblings in the same file already set it
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/157984 (closed duplicate)
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/157065 → fix https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/157424 (setting added on create only; restore gap left #159161)
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/94354 → fix https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/108768 (original pattern: disable rebalance after restore so `_recovery` is not overwritten by PEER)

Related placement/rebalance flakes and fixes:

- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/98746 / https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/95889 — `tsdb/30_snapshot` restore asserts (same PEER/SNAPSHOT class)
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/148096 → https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/153153 — mtermvectors BWC race when creating a second index triggers rebalance mid-test
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/131394 → https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/133036 — `DataStreamLifecycleDownsampleDisruptionIT` `ensureGreen` timeout from post-work rebalancing (Distributed suggested disable rebalance)
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/85169 — disable rebalancing in `IndexDiskUsageAnalyzerIT`
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/61068 — disable rebalancing in searchable snapshot tests

Counterexample (when re-enabling is fine): https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/122889 — ES|QL REST tests re-enabled rebalance once query execution no longer failed under relocation.

In-progress fix for the latest snapshot.restore instance: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/159172

### Relates to

- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/159161
issues.title: Disable rebalancing in tests that assume shard placement

issues.body:
## Observed

No ES|QL function converts an IPv4 address stored as a number to the `ip` type. An IPv4 address is
32 bits, so it can be written as dotted text, `192.168.1.1`, or as the single integer those bits
form, `3232235777`.
`TO_IP` and the `::ip` cast accept only text and the `ip` type itself.

Reproduced on `main` at `fa290247433fe578902f065aa104c66f0776199a`. From an empty cluster, with no
setup:

```
POST _query
{ "query": "ROW src_ip_int = 3232235777 | EVAL src_ip = TO_IP(src_ip_int) | KEEP src_ip" }
```

Result:

```
Found 1 problem
line 1:45: argument of [TO_IP(src_ip_int)] must be [ip or string], found value [src_ip_int] type [long]
```

Expected `192.168.1.1`. `3232235777` is `0xC0A80101`, that address with its first octet in the most
significant byte. Both comparable engines convert it in one call: ClickHouse's
`IPv4NumToString(3232235777)` returns the string `192.168.1.1` and `toIPv4` returns the typed value,
and BigQuery's `NET.IPV4_FROM_INT64` returns the address as `BYTES`, its reference defining the
encoding as "the least significant bit of the IP address is stored in the least significant bit of
the integer … 1 means 0.0.0.1, and 0x1FF means 0.0.1.255".

## Impact

Affects every user whose IPv4 data is stored numerically, on indices and external datasets alike.
Reaching the `ip` type at all requires rebuilding the dotted quad arithmetically and parsing it back
as text:

```
ROW n = 3232235777
| EVAL src_ip = TO_IP(CONCAT(
    TO_STRING(n / 16777216 % 256), ".",
    TO_STRING(n / 65536 % 256), ".",
    TO_STRING(n / 256 % 256), ".",
    TO_STRING(n % 256)))
| KEEP src_ip
```

That query resolves, and `CIDR_MATCH` and `IP_PREFIX` work on its output, so the data is reachable —
at three divisions, four modulos, four string conversions and a seven-argument concatenation per
row, which the user must write correctly for every column holding an address. Scope is the conversion surface
only: the `ip` data type, its storage and its functions are unaffected, and IPv6 does not arise
because it does not fit an integer.

## Structural cause

The conversion functions derive their accepted input types from a map of evaluators keyed by input
`DataType`, and a type absent from that map is rejected during type resolution, before planning. The
`ip` conversions register evaluators for the string-shaped inputs and for `ip` itself. The numeric
encoding of an address therefore has no entry point into the type: the gap is not in the `ip`
representation, which is a fixed binary value, but in the absence of any mapping from a 32-bit
integer onto it.

## Mechanical cause

[`ToIp`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/fa290247433fe578902f065aa104c66f0776199a/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/expression/function/scalar/convert/ToIp.java#L78-L124)
declares `type = { "ip", "keyword", "text" }` on its `field` parameter, and its `resolveType` calls
`isTypeOrUnionType(field, ToIpLeadingZerosRejected.EVALUATORS::containsKey, …)`. That map's keys are
`IP`, `KEYWORD` and `TEXT`, so `INTEGER`, `LONG` and `UNSIGNED_LONG` are all rejected at one site.

The `::ip` cast reaches the same accepted set by a different route: `EsqlDataTypeConverter` maps the
`ip` target to `ToIpLeadingZerosRejected::new`, so the cast builds that function directly rather than
`ToIp`, and inherits the same evaluator keys.

## Structural fix

Give the numeric encoding an entry point into the type where the string shapes and `ip` itself
already have one: an evaluator keyed by the numeric `DataType`, in the maps the `ip` conversions
share. The
declaration that an integer is an address belongs at the point of use, as an explicit conversion the
user writes, rather than as an implicit coercion driven by a declared field type. That is where both
comparable engines put it: ClickHouse exposes `IPv4NumToString` and `toIPv4`, and BigQuery exposes
`NET.IPV4_FROM_INT64`.

## Mechanical fix

- Add the whole-number input types to the evaluator maps the `ip` conversions share
  (`ToIpLeadingZerosRejected`, `ToIpLeadingZerosDecimal`, `ToIpLeadingZerosOctal`), and widen the
  `field` parameter's declared types on `ToIp` to match.
- Read the number as a 32-bit IPv4 address with the first octet in the most significant byte.
- A number that does not represent an address takes the path the function already uses for an
  unparseable string: `null` with a warning header.
- The `leading_zeros` option applies to text parsing only.

## Acceptance

- `ToIpTests` covers each numeric input type, asserting the converted address for representative
  values including the lowest and highest address, and asserting `null` with a warning for a number
  that does not represent one.
- `ip.csv-spec` covers an end-to-end conversion of an indexed numeric column, and a `CIDR_MATCH`
  over the converted column. No existing `ip.csv-spec` fixture carries a numeric column, so the case
  brings its own fixture.

## Related

- elastic/elasticsearch#137172 — added a `base` argument to `TO_LONG` and `TO_INTEGER`. It widened a
  conversion function's surface by adding a parameter rather than a new input type, so it is
  precedent for the shape of the change and not for its mechanism.
issues.title: ES|QL: TO_IP should support numerics

issues.body:
### Description

When a client (e.g., Kibana) times out waiting for an ES|QL query response, the server-side query continues running indefinitely, consuming S3 connections and memory. There are two related gaps:

**1. Sync `_query` — client disconnect detection**

When a sync `_query` client disconnects (e.g., Kibana's 30s HTTP timeout fires), the ES transport layer eventually detects the broken connection and cancels the task, but this takes 5-8s. During this window, the query continues consuming S3 connections from the shared pool. For dashboards with many concurrent panels, this can exhaust the connection pool and cascade failures to other panels.

Investigate whether disconnect detection can be made faster, and whether the S3 connection permits should be released immediately on task cancellation rather than waiting for in-flight requests to complete.

**2. Async `_query/async` — no server-side timeout**

Async queries have no server-side execution timeout. A query submitted via `_query/async` with `wait_for_completion_timeout=1s` returns an async handle immediately, but the query itself runs until completion or explicit `DELETE`. If Kibana times out polling, the query keeps running.

Kibana should be instructed to `DELETE _query/async/{id}` during cleanup when a panel times out, to release server-side resources. Additionally, consider adding an optional server-side execution timeout for async queries (e.g., `execution_timeout`) that would auto-cancel queries that exceed a deadline.

### Impact

On workloads with many small S3 files (e.g., VPC Flow Logs with 10,000+ tiny Parquet files), a timed-out query can hold S3 connections for minutes. With 14 dashboard panels and a 24-connection pool, a single stalled query can block other panels from acquiring connections (60s connection-acquire timeout), cascading into dashboard-wide timeouts.

### Context

Identified while investigating #159688. The connection-acquire timeout (60s) combined with no async cancellation explains the "never completed" behavior reported on older builds where queries took 500+ seconds.
issues.title: [ES|QL:DS] Detect client timeout/disconnect and cancel server-side query

issues.body:
### Description

The Inference API has first-party services for Amazon Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, Azure AI Studio, Google Vertex AI, Google AI Studio and IBM watsonx, but none for **Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Generative AI**, Oracle's managed model service. It serves Cohere Command and Embed (including `cohere.embed-v4.0` with selectable output dimensions and `cohere.rerank-v4.0-fast`), Meta Llama, OpenAI, xAI Grok and Google Gemini models behind one regional endpoint, on demand or through dedicated AI clusters.

Today an Elasticsearch user on OCI cannot use it from semantic_text, the inference processor or the retrievers at all: OCI authenticates with its own HTTP request-signature scheme (RSA signature over `(request-target) host date x-content-sha256 content-type content-length`), which none of the existing services or the `custom` service can produce. The workaround is to run a separate proxy that re-signs requests, which means another component to operate and secure.

I would like to add an `ocigenai` service supporting `text_embedding`, `completion`, `chat_completion` (streaming and non-streaming) and `rerank`:

- **Authentication** with an OCI API signing key (`tenancy_id`, `user_id`, `fingerprint`, `private_key` PEM) using the OCI request-signature scheme, implemented in the plugin on top of the existing `HttpRequestSender` stack rather than by adding the OCI Java SDK and its Jersey HTTP client, so there are no new dependencies, licenses, entitlements or third-party audit allow-lists. This is the same approach the Vertex AI service takes for its credentials.
- **Service settings**: `region` (or `url` for private endpoints and other OCI realms), `compartment_id`, `model_id`, optional `endpoint_id` for dedicated AI clusters, `rate_limit`; embeddings also `dimensions`, `similarity`, `max_input_tokens`. **Task settings**: `input_type` and `truncate` for embeddings, `top_n` and `return_documents` for rerank.
- **Chat formats**: Cohere Command models use OCI's `COHERE` chat format; every other family uses `GENERIC`, which maps the unified chat request one to one, including image content, function tools and tool choice, with SSE streaming mapped to unified chunks.

I have an implementation ready on a branch, with unit tests for the signer (verified against the public key), PEM parsing, settings serialization, both request formats, streaming and the service itself through `MockWebServer`, and I have verified it live against OCI Generative AI in `us-chicago-1` for embeddings, both chat formats (streaming and not), and rerank, with a tampered signature correctly rejected with 401. I will open the PR referencing this issue.
issues.title: Add an OCI Generative AI (ocigenai) inference service

issues.body:
### Description

There are some marker interfaces, that tag functions with properties, that are useful for optimization. E.g. `AnyNullIsNull` (indicating that a function evaluates to `null` is any of its arguments is `null`), which is useful for the optimization step `InferIsNotNull`.

Other places in the code use hardcoded allow/blocklists, which don't generalize well (easily forgotten, leading to suboptimal optimization) or are potential future bugs.

Examples are:

[InferNonNullAggConstraint](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/optimizer/rules/logical/local/InferNonNullAggConstraint.java#L64-L68): aggregations are more or less prepended with `WHERE argument IS NOT NULL`, because most aggs ignore `null`s. Exceptions (blocklist) are made for `FIRST` / `LAST`, which don't igores `null`s. When more aggs with this property are added, and they're not added to this list, that's a bug. To prevent this, add an interface `IgnoresNulls`, indicating that an agg has this property, and use that.

[ReplaceStatsFilteredOrNullAggWithEval](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/optimizer/rules/logical/ReplaceStatsFilteredOrNullAggWithEval.java#L148-L150): the aggs `FIRST` / `LAST` are replaced by `null` iff the first argument is `null` (the second argument being `null` doesn't lead to a result of `null`). Maybe an interface `FirstNullIsNull` can be useful to generalize this concept.
issues.title: Add more function marker interfaces (IgnoresNull, FirstNullIIsNull, etc)
Snapshot restore should skip searchable-snapshot indices whose backing snapshot is missing

issues.body:
When serving a search, the coordinating node keeps the merged `top-K` hits in memory from the moment the shard results are combined until the HTTP response has been fully written to the client. For responses with large `_source` documents, this can be a lot of heap, and nothing on the coordinator charges it to the request circuit breaker. A single large search can therefore drive the node out of memory before any breaker trips.

During the streaming fetch, it does charge the request breaker per shard, as it accumulates that shard's `SearchHits`. The problem is that this reservation is released once the shard's result is built and handed off to the `FetchSearchPhase,` that is, before the cross-shard merge happens. From that point on the hits are untracked. 

The merge itself doesn't copy hits - it reuses the same `SearchHit` objects and hands them to the `SearchResponse`, which holds them until the response is sent and released. So there's a window - merge, serialize, wait for the network to drain - where a large amount of hit memory is resident and invisible to the breaker. The result is that the breaker's reported usage doesn't reflect what's actually on the heap during a search, and it can't reject an oversized result set.
issues.title: Coordinator does not account merged search hits against the request circuit breaker

issues.body:
It can happen that LOAD_ALL circuit breaks before being assigned an async id. In this case, the query is aborted with an error but there is no way for the user to understand the cause of the query not going through at all.

Let's make sure we still assign an async id in this case so the user can retrive the (error) result and retry at a later time.
